course_facts.scope_summary: MIT 10.626 Electrochemical Energy Systems, Spring 2014, Prof. Martin Bazant, Department of Chemical Engineering, graduate level. The Instructor Insights page states that the class contains both graduate and undergraduate students and that students taking the graduate version complete additional assignments; the course number 10.426 appears only in the course's data.json as recorded in references/mit-ocw-verification.json (observed.extra_course_numbers), not on any of the eight fetched HTML pages. The course teaches the physics and mathematical modelling of electrochemical energy conversion and storage in five parts: I Introduction (galvanic cells, conversion, storage), II Circuit Models (equivalent-circuit dynamics and impedance), III Thermodynamics (statistical thermodynamics and solution models, Nernst equation and open-circuit voltage, Pourbaix diagrams, metal-acid and Li-ion cells, pseudocapacitance, phase separation), IV Kinetics (Faradaic reactions, Butler-Volmer equation, electrocatalysis, electrochemical phase transformations, charge-transfer theory) and V Transport Phenomena (concentration polarization, transient diffusion, Warburg impedance, forced convection, transport in solids and bulk electrolytes, double layers, porous media, scaling analysis, porous electrodes). Applications named on the pages are batteries, fuel cells, supercapacitors and electrokinetics. Inference from the session titles only: no session title mentions power-electronic interfaces, battery management systems or grid-level storage operation; the pages make no statement about these topics.
stated_prerequisites: Syllabus page: 10.50 Analysis of Transport Phenomena (MIT's graduate transport course) is the only prerequisite listed.

Instructor Insights page: graduate students need 10.50 Analysis of Transport Phenomena or the instructor's permission; undergraduate students need 10.302 Transport Processes. The page does not name an undergraduate course number.

Implied by the reading list and session titles (inference, not stated on any page): working knowledge of thermodynamics, physical chemistry, ordinary and partial differential equations and basic circuit theory.

mapped_modules.rationale: The course's central subject is the physics and modelling of electrochemical cells: open-circuit voltage from thermodynamics, activation and concentration overpotentials, diffusion limits, phase-separating Li-ion electrodes and porous electrodes (characterisation from session titles; no lecture content was opened). This is the 'electrochemical cells and battery chemistries' half of re.batteries and gives the physical basis for OCV-versus-state-of-charge curves, internal resistance and impedance-based state estimation. The management half of the module (state-of-charge algorithms, ageing, battery management systems) does not appear in any session title.

mit_topics: Basic physics of galvanic cells, Electrochemical energy conversion
mapped_modules.rationale: Substantial treatment of three storage technologies (batteries, supercapacitors, fuel cells) from first principles, including how energy and power capability scale with electrode structure. The system-level content of re.storage - roles of storage in the grid, system round-trip efficiency, comparison with non-electrochemical technologies and bidirectional converter interfaces - is absent from the session titles, so the coverage is substantial but not central.

mit_topics: Basic physics of galvanic cells, Electrochemical energy conversion
mapped_modules.rationale: Sessions 2, 9 and 10 (calendar page) give the thermodynamic voltage, efficiency limits and loss mechanisms of one conversion channel (chemical to electrical and back), and part III (thermodynamics, 8 sessions) supplies the underlying thermodynamics. The supplementary prior-year note '2011 Lecture 31: Electrokinetic Energy Conversion', listed under the 'Electrokinetics' heading of the study-materials page (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/10-626-electrochemical-energy-systems-spring-2014/pages/study-materials/), also supports the label; it is not a 2014 session, so it is cited here rather than in mit_topics (see topic_outline S2.3). re.conversion is broader (all physical conversion processes, renewable resources and limits), so this course supplies depth on one slice rather than the module's breadth.

Part II builds RC equivalent circuits of electrochemical cells and studies their transient and frequency response - the same mathematics as AIPE's RC/time-constant foundations - but the course assumes that mathematics and applies it at graduate level, extended to distributed (diffusion) elements. Labelled background because the course does not teach the basics; it is an advanced-application reference for f.dynamics, not a source for teaching the module.

Complex impedance and phasor reasoning are assumed and applied to electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (the lecture-notes page lists the reading '2011 Lecture 5: Impedance spectroscopy' for session 5); AC fundamentals themselves are not taught.
Frequency-response and step-response reasoning for linearised systems is used as a tool throughout the circuit-model and transport parts but is assumed rather than taught.

The course's electrostatics content (double layers, diffuse charge in electrolytes and membranes) assumes the basic field, potential and capacitance concepts of f.electromagnetism and goes well beyond them; it does not teach basic electromagnetism. Beyond the two 2014 sessions listed, the study-materials page (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/10-626-electrochemical-energy-systems-spring-2014/pages/study-materials/) offers four prior-year notes under the heading 'Electrostatics' ('2011 Lecture 26: Compact Part of the Double Layer', '2011 Lecture 27a: Diffuse Charge at Electrode', '2011 Lecture 27b: Diffuse Charge in Membranes', '2011 Lecture 28: Electrostatic Correlations').

The syllabus page (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/10-626-electrochemical-energy-systems-spring-2014/pages/syllabus/) states the prerequisite 10.50 Analysis of Transport Phenomena, a graduate transport course, which implies fluency with ordinary and partial differential equations and asymptotic/scaling methods far beyond AIPE's first-order-ODE foundation; the transport sessions listed here apply that mathematics. Calculus is assumed, not taught.

Supercapacitor physics (double-layer capacitance, distributed resistance of porous electrodes) underlies the ESR and frequency-dependent capacitance that pe.passives treats at component level; the lecture-notes page (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/10-626-electrochemical-energy-systems-spring-2014/pages/lecture-notes/) lists the reading '2011 Lecture 6: Impedance of Electrode' for sessions 6-7. Tangential to the module's converter-component focus.

mit_topics: 2009 Lecture 19: Electronic Contributions to OCV in Batteries and Solar Cells
mapped_modules.rationale: A single supplementary 2009 note, listed under the 'Quantum Mechanics' heading of the study-materials page, relates electronic structure to open-circuit voltage in both batteries and solar cells (inference from the title only); a tangential cross-link, not PV teaching.

concepts_missing_in_aipe: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and equivalent-circuit elements of a cell (series resistance, charge-transfer resistance, double-layer capacitance, Warburg/diffusion impedance) - AIPE's f.ac covers impedance only for ideal R, L and C elements (ps.per-unit uses per-unit impedances) and no lesson covers cell impedance.
Nernst equation and open-circuit voltage as a function of composition - the physical basis of OCV versus state-of-charge curves - is not named in any AIPE module summary or lesson.
Pourbaix diagrams and electrochemical stability windows (electrolyte and electrode stability, corrosion) - no AIPE coverage.
Activation overpotential and Butler-Volmer / Tafel kinetics, exchange current density and electrocatalysis - no AIPE coverage.
Concentration polarization, diffusion limitation and limiting current as the origin of rate capability and capacity fade at high C-rate - no AIPE coverage.

Fuel cells (thermodynamic voltage, polarization curve, transport losses) - fuel cells, electrolysers and hydrogen storage appear in no AIPE module summary at all, a module-level gap in the energy-storage and energy-conversion tracks.

Supercapacitors: double-layer capacitance, pseudocapacitance and porous-electrode (RC-ladder) behaviour - re.storage names 'storage technologies' generally but no lesson or sub-module treats supercapacitors.

Phase-separating intercalation electrodes and electrochemical phase transformations (why some Li-ion chemistries have flat voltage plateaus) - graduate-level; an advanced sidebar candidate for re.batteries.
Porous electrode theory and scaling analysis of energy versus power (Ragone-type reasoning from first principles) - AIPE has 'energy and power ratings' but not the physics behind them.

Solution thermodynamics (ideal and regular solution models, statistical thermodynamics) (the energy-conversion track summary names physical and thermodynamic foundations generally, but no module summary names solution models or statistical thermodynamics), linear sweep voltammetry, homogeneous/heterogeneous charge-transfer theory, forced convection in electrochemical cells, electrokinetics and quantum theory of electrodes - chemical-engineering depth that is outside AIPE's electrical-engineering scope and should stay as 'further reading' only.
modern_gaps_not_covered_by_mit: Battery management systems: cell voltage/temperature monitoring, passive and active balancing, protection, and state-of-charge / state-of-health estimation algorithms (Coulomb counting, model-based observers) built on equivalent-circuit models.
Battery ageing and degradation (calendar and cycle ageing, SEI growth, lithium plating), thermal runaway and safety engineering - no session title on ageing or safety.
Pack-level engineering: series/parallel configuration, cell-to-pack, thermal management, contactors and pre-charge, fusing and isolation.
Power-electronic interfaces for storage: bidirectional DC/DC stages, grid-tied inverters, CC-CV and fast-charging profiles, charger topologies.

Grid-scale storage roles and system metrics: frequency regulation, arbitrage, capacity firming, system round-trip efficiency, levelised cost of storage, and comparison with non-electrochemical storage (pumped hydro, flywheels, thermal, hydrogen).
Post-2014 chemistries and formats: high-nickel NMC/NCA, LFP at pack level, sodium-ion, silicon anodes, solid-state electrolytes - only Li-ion and metal-acid cells are listed.

Engineering-level battery test methods: capacity and C-rate tests, HPPC-type pulse tests for internal resistance, cycle-life testing and datasheet reading. The course does cover laboratory electroanalytical characterisation (electrochemical impedance, sessions 5-7 and 27; linear sweep voltammetry, session 14), so the gap is the engineering test protocols, not characterisation as such.
Hydrogen and fuel-cell system integration (electrolysers, fuel-cell stacks with power electronics) beyond the electrochemistry of the cell.

Open-source simulation tooling for storage (Python equivalent-circuit model fitting, physics-based battery model packages) and reproducible labs - the course has no computational component visible on its pages.
Second-life use, recycling, sustainability and standards/grid-code requirements for stationary storage.
recommended_lessons: electrochemical-cell-fundamentals (re.batteries; curriculum/renewable-energy/energy-storage/): galvanic cell anatomy, why a cell has a voltage, Nernst equation at the level of 'voltage depends on composition', OCV versus state of charge - mirrors MIT sessions 2-3 and 9 at undergraduate depth.
battery-equivalent-circuit-models (re.batteries, f.dynamics): Thevenin and 2-RC cell models, internal resistance, time constants, identifying parameters from a pulse test - mirrors MIT session 4.

battery-impedance-spectroscopy-basics (re.batteries, f.ac, f.signals): EIS as a frequency response, Nyquist plots, reading series, charge-transfer and diffusion regions - mirrors MIT sessions 5-7 and 27.

overpotentials-and-rate-capability (re.batteries): activation (Butler-Volmer), ohmic and concentration overpotentials; polarisation curve; why usable capacity falls at high C-rate - mirrors MIT sessions 17-18 and 25-26.
supercapacitors-and-double-layers (re.storage, pe.passives): double-layer capacitance, pseudocapacitance, ESR, energy versus power - mirrors MIT sessions 13, 35, 37-38.

fuel-cell-fundamentals (home module is a taxonomy decision to flag: fuel cells are a conversion device and taxonomy.json has no fuel-cell or hydrogen node, so the lesson belongs under re.conversion or a new energy-storage sub-module rather than re.storage): thermodynamic voltage, efficiency, polarisation curve, transport losses - mirrors MIT session 10 (Fuel cells and batteries); the link to sessions 28-30 (Forced convection I-III) rests on the lecture-notes page's prior-year reading titles '2011 Lecture 17: Forced Convection in Fuel Cells (I)' and '2011 Lecture 18: Forced Convection in Fuel Cells II', not on the 2014 session titles themselves; fills the module-level fuel-cell gap.

energy-storage-landscape-and-ragone (re.storage): energy and power ratings, round-trip efficiency, scaling of energy versus power, comparison across technologies - extends MIT session 37 to the system view.
battery-management-fundamentals (re.batteries): SoC estimation on an equivalent-circuit model, balancing and protection - AIPE-original gap filler, not sourced from the MIT course.

lithium-ion-phase-separation-sidebar (re.batteries, advanced optional): why LFP-type electrodes show flat voltage plateaus - a short advanced note pointing to MIT sessions 15 and 20-21 as further reading.
recommended_simulations: labs/battery_equivalent_circuit.py (Python): simulate a 2-RC Thevenin cell model under a pulse-discharge profile, estimate R0, R1C1, R2C2 from the step response by hand, then fit numerically and compare - reproduces the reasoning of MIT 'Equivalent circuit dynamics'.

labs/randles_impedance.cir + Python post-processing (ngspice): AC sweep of a Randles circuit (Rs in series with Rct parallel Cdl, Warburg element approximated by an RC ladder) to produce a Nyquist plot; students read off Rs and Rct and check against the netlist values.

labs/ocv_nernst_curve.py (Python): open-circuit voltage versus state of charge for an ideal-solution intercalation electrode, then a regular-solution variant showing the emergence of a voltage plateau; compare with a measured OCV curve supplied as CSV. The comparison OCV-vs-SoC curve must be AIPE-original (e.g. generated from the model with added noise, or measured by AIPE on a commercial cell) or taken from a CC BY-compatible open dataset with attribution; no data from MIT problem sets or lecture notes may be used.

labs/polarisation_curve.py (Python): Butler-Volmer current-overpotential curve and Tafel plot, then a full cell polarisation curve combining activation, ohmic and concentration losses with a limiting current - applicable to a battery or a fuel cell.

labs/transient_diffusion_1d.py (Python, f.computation): explicit finite-difference 1-D diffusion in an electrode under a current step, showing concentration polarization and a diffusion time constant; verify step-size and stability behaviour.

labs/supercapacitor_transmission_line.cir (ngspice): porous-electrode RC-ladder model of a supercapacitor showing frequency-dependent capacitance and ESR; Python script turns stored energy and deliverable power into a Ragone point.
labs/cccv_charge_and_soc.py (Python): CC-CV charging of the equivalent-circuit model with Coulomb-counting SoC estimation and a simple voltage-based correction - the AIPE-original BMS gap filler.
prerequisite_relationships: re.batteries requires re.storage in taxonomy.json, and f.dynamics and f.ac are already transitively required (re.batteries -> re.storage -> pe.topologies -> f.ac -> f.dynamics). The course structure confirms this order: it builds equivalent-circuit and impedance models (part II) before cell thermodynamics, kinetics and transport, so RC and impedance fluency is assumed before cell physics.

f.calculus is already transitively required by the taxonomy (re.batteries -> re.storage -> pe.topologies -> f.ac -> f.dynamics -> f.calculus); the course's graduate transport-phenomena prerequisite (10.50; 10.302 for undergraduates) confirms that differential-equation fluency is needed for the electrochemical content.

taxonomy.json lists no f.electromagnetism dependency for re.storage or re.batteries, directly or transitively (f.dc-circuits names it only as 'related'); the course's double-layer and electrostatics content implies one only for the supercapacitor/double-layer and EIS lessons. Proposed taxonomy change, not an existing edge: add f.electromagnetism to re.batteries 'related', or scope the requirement to those lessons.

A battery-impedance (EIS) lesson needs f.signals (frequency response, Nyquist/Bode reading) in addition to f.ac; f.signals is not in the taxonomy's requirement closure of re.batteries, so this is a proposed lesson-level prerequisite, not an existing edge.

re.conversion thermodynamics should precede re.batteries overpotential and rate lessons: the course orders thermodynamics (part III, OCV) before kinetics (part IV, overpotentials) before transport (part V, rate limits). taxonomy.json links re.conversion to re.storage only as 'related', so this is a proposed lesson ordering (OCV -> overpotentials -> diffusion limits), not an existing requires edge.

re.storage supercapacitor content relies on f.dynamics (RC ladders), which the taxonomy already requires transitively (re.storage -> pe.topologies -> f.ac -> f.dynamics), and relates to pe.passives (ESR, frequency-dependent capacitance), which is not currently linked to re.storage in taxonomy.json (proposed 'related' edge).

The course assumes physical-chemistry background (statistical thermodynamics, solution models, electroanalytical methods) that AIPE has no module for; AIPE lessons should introduce only the Nernst/OCV and Butler-Volmer results they need and point to this course for derivations.

course_facts.scope_summary: An undergraduate social-science survey course (Sloan School of Management, jointly offered with Economics, Anthropology, and Urban Studies and Planning; the OCW HTML pages show only the number 15.031J, while the project's verification record lists the additional numbers 14.43J, 21A.341J and 11.161J taken from the course data.json; a core subject of MIT's Energy Studies Minor) on how energy choices are made at every level from the individual household up to firms, movements and governments, drawing on economics, management, political science, sociology and anthropology. Six units run from an overview of the U.S. and comparative energy systems, through the climate problem (including a simulation-based negotiation role play), household and business decision-making (energy demand economics, financial and normative frameworks, cases on combined heat and power and biodiesel, strategy and business models), primary energy and the electric power system (non-renewable resources, shale, today's and tomorrow's grid), to public-policy processes and team paper presentations. Judging from session and reading titles (slides and videos were not opened), it is not an engineering course: no circuit, converter, machine or power-flow topics are listed; its relevance to AIPE is the economics, markets, resources and policy context of energy systems.

course_facts.scope_summary: MIT 18.01SC (OCW Scholar edition, Fall 2010, Prof. David Jerison) is a self-contained single-variable calculus course for independent learners. It runs through five units: differentiation (definition, rules, implicit differentiation, exponentials and inverses), applications of differentiation (approximation, curve sketching, optimization, related rates, Newton's method, Mean Value Theorem, antiderivatives and a first look at separable differential equations), the definite integral and its applications (Riemann sums, both Fundamental Theorems, areas, volumes, averages, probability, numerical integration), techniques of integration (trigonometric methods, partial fractions, integration by parts, arc length, parametric and polar curves), and infinite processes (L'Hospital's rule, improper integrals, series and Taylor series). The material is organised as 102 sequential sessions (Sessions 1-101 on the five unit pages, Session 102 on the final-exam page); most sessions pair segmented lecture-video clips with notes and a worked example, many add recitation videos or an interactive mathlet, each part ends with a problem set and each unit with an exam. Positioning stated in the syllabus: a first-year, first-semester MIT subject with an estimated total effort of about 150 hours; no textbook is required, the course being described as self-contained, with any single-variable calculus text usable as an optional companion.
stated_prerequisites: High-school algebra and trigonometry (the syllabus names these as the only prerequisites).
Earlier exposure to calculus is described as helpful but not necessary.

mapped_modules.rationale: AIPE's f.calculus module is defined in the taxonomy as slopes, areas, exponentials and first-order differential equations introduced through charging and discharging circuits. Those four ideas are exactly the spine of this course (Units 1-3 plus the separable-ODE Sessions 39-40), so the course is the central academic reference for the module. The course goes far beyond the AIPE module in breadth (techniques of integration, series, polar coordinates) and never uses circuits as motivation; AIPE's module is a circuit-motivated subset of it. Taylor series (Session 98) is deliberately not listed here: it is a proposed extension of f.calculus (see the Taylor-series recommended lesson), not current module content, and appears under pe.modelling as background.

AIPE f.computation covers scripts, plots and simulation models with numerical integration, step sizes and numerical error. The course treats numerical integration in two sessions (the Session 63 page lists clips titled Introduction to Numerical Integration, Riemann Sums, Trapezoidal Rule and Simpson's Rule, plus a Riemann Sums mathlet) and root finding in one session on Newton's method, as hand methods rather than scripts. This is a brief, theory-side treatment of what AIPE teaches computationally, hence introductory. Newton's method (Session 33) is proposed as a root-finding addition to f.computation; the current module summary lists numerical integration only.

The course has no electric or magnetic content, so it supplies mathematical background only.

mapped_modules.rationale: AIPE f.dynamics (RC/RL responses, time constants) requires f.calculus in the taxonomy. The separable first-order ODE method and the exponential function taught in Sessions 17 and 39-40 are the mathematics that solves the RC/RL charging problem, but the course contains no circuit or energy-storage content, so it is assumed background rather than coverage.

mapped_modules.rationale: Average and RMS values of periodic waveforms in AIPE f.ac are the average-value integral (Sessions 60-61) applied to trigonometric powers (Sessions 68-69), and the derivatives of sine and cosine (Session 7) underlie the phase relations between AC voltages and currents. The course never mentions waveforms, complex numbers or phasors (its polar-coordinate Sessions 82-84 treat curves in polar coordinates, not the polar form of complex numbers), so it only supplies the mathematical background.

The Laplace transform used in AIPE f.signals is an improper integral evaluated by integration by parts, and inverting rational transfer functions relies on partial-fraction decomposition; L'Hospital's rule handles the limits behind asymptotes and final values. The course teaches these as pure integration techniques with no transforms, systems or feedback, so the coverage is background only.

Linearisation of a converter around an operating point (small-signal modelling in AIPE pe.modelling) is the first-order Taylor or linear approximation taught in Sessions 23-26 and 36, with Taylor series (Session 98) giving the error terms. The course has no converter or circuit content, so it is tangential background for the module.

mapped_modules.rationale: re.conversion requires f.calculus directly in the taxonomy: energy as the integral of power, efficiency as a ratio of such integrals and average power over a period rest on the definite integral (Sessions 43-48) and the average-value integral (Session 60). The course has no energy-conversion content, so it supplies mathematical background only.

Locating the maximum power point is the derivative-equals-zero optimisation taught in Sessions 29-30 (dP/dV = 0); the course has no photovoltaic or converter content, so this is mathematical background only. Mapped so that the optimisation recommended lesson, which feeds re.mppt, points at a mapped module.

Numerical solution of differential equations: none in 18.01SC; the 18.03SC home page lists a 'Numerical Methods' session in Unit I (mit-18-03sc-2011) whose method names were not read for this record. RK4, step-size and stiffness choices and energy-conservation checks, which pe.simulation and f.computation rely on, remain a baseline-wide AIPE gap; AIPE's buck-converter-fundamentals lab already uses fixed-step first-order (semi-implicit Euler) integration without a lesson that teaches the method.

Discrete-time calculus: sampling, difference equations and discrete integrators for digital control: not in 18.01SC; the 6.003 syllabus names discrete-time signals, sampling and difference equations (mit-6-003-2011).

Calculus on piecewise and switched waveforms (averaging over a switching period, volt-second and charge balance, small-ripple approximation): not in 18.01SC; assigned in the catalogue to the 6.622 baseline record (mit-6-622-2023). The 6.622 home and syllabus pages read for this record do not name these topics, so the pointer is catalogue organisation to be evidenced in that record.

Multivariable calculus (partial derivatives, gradients and constrained optimisation for loss models, MPPT and design trade-offs): not in 18.01SC; the 18.02SC syllabus lists partial derivatives, gradient and directional derivatives, and Lagrange multipliers (mit-18-02sc-2010).

Vector calculus and the integral forms of Maxwell's equations needed by f.electromagnetism and f.magnetism: not in 18.01SC; assigned in the catalogue to the 8.02 and 6.013 records (mit-8-02-2007, mit-6-013-2005). The 8.02 home page and the 6.013 syllabus read for this record do not list these topics by name (6.013 names Maxwell's equations only as a prerequisite), so the pointer is catalogue organisation.
Computational tooling (Python/NumPy/SymPy) for symbolic and numeric calculus: the course's interactive tools are legacy Java mathlets; a baseline-wide AIPE gap.

Energy-domain applications: integrating power to energy (W to Wh), average and RMS of electrical waveforms, and small-ripple estimates in a circuit context: not framed this way in 18.01SC, so AIPE lessons must supply the circuit framing themselves; a baseline-wide AIPE gap.
recommended_lessons: f.calculus: Slope as a rate of change, introduced from a measured capacitor voltage so that i = C dv/dt is the first derivative a learner meets (parallels Sessions 1-3)
f.calculus: Area as accumulation, with energy as the integral of power and Wh as the unit of the result (parallels Sessions 43-48)
f.calculus: The exponential function and the RC charging curve, solving the separable first-order equation and reading the time constant (parallels Sessions 17, 39-40; feeds f.dynamics)
f.calculus: Average and RMS of sinusoidal, rectified and PWM waveforms as integrals over one period (parallels Sessions 60-61, 68-69; feeds f.ac)
f.calculus: Linear approximation and differentials, linearising a diode or PV current-voltage curve around an operating point (parallels Sessions 23-26, 36; feeds pe.modelling)
f.calculus: Taylor series for exp, sin and cos, the small-ripple approximation, and Euler's formula as the entry to complex numbers and phasors (parallels Sessions 97-100)
f.calculus: Optimisation with derivatives, from maximum power transfer to the photovoltaic maximum power point (parallels Sessions 29-30; feeds re.mppt)
f.computation: Numerical integration of a sampled power waveform with rectangle, trapezoid and Simpson rules, and how error scales with step size (parallels Sessions 46, 63-64)
f.computation: Newton's method for a root, applied to the diode equation and a PV operating point (parallels Session 33)
f.signals bridge: improper integrals, integration by parts and partial fractions as the mathematics behind Laplace transform pairs (parallels Sessions 74-76, 91)
recommended_simulations: Python (numpy, matplotlib): secant slopes converging to the tangent on a sampled capacitor voltage; compare the numerical derivative with the analytical i = C dv/dt and show how sample spacing changes the error
Python: rectangle, trapezoid and Simpson integration of p(t) = v(t) i(t) to energy in Wh, with a log-log plot of error versus step size
ngspice (.tran) plus Python: RC charging transient compared with the closed-form solution of dv/dt = (Vs - v)/(RC); residual plot and time-constant extraction from the simulated curve
Python: average and RMS of a sinusoid, a full-wave rectified sinusoid and a PWM pulse train computed by numerical integration and checked against the closed-form integrals of sin^2
Python with ngspice .op cross-check: Newton's method on a diode-resistor loop using the exponential diode equation, iteration count and convergence plot
Python (sympy, numpy): Taylor polynomials of exp, sin and cos with truncation-error plots, and the (1 + x)^n approximately 1 + n x approximation used in small-ripple analysis
Python: first-order (tangent-line) linearisation of a PV cell current-voltage curve around the maximum power point compared with the full curve, as input to re.mppt
Python: numerical evaluation of the improper integral of e^(-s t) f(t) for a step and a decaying exponential to verify basic Laplace transform pairs
Python: load-resistance sweep for maximum power transfer and a P(V) sweep for a PV module, locating the maximum where the derivative crosses zero
prerequisite_relationships: f.calculus requires f.quantities (taxonomy); consistent with the syllabus, which states only high-school algebra and trigonometry as prerequisites and assumes no prior calculus.

f.dynamics requires f.dc-circuits and f.calculus (taxonomy); the course places antiderivatives and separable differential equations in Unit 2 Part C (Sessions 37-40) before any application, and AIPE's RC/RL work depends on exactly those sessions.
f.electromagnetism requires f.quantities and f.calculus (taxonomy): Faraday's law and field energy need the derivative (Sessions 1-3) and the definite integral (Sessions 43-48).

re.conversion requires f.quantities and f.calculus (taxonomy): energy as the integral of power and efficiency ratios need the definite integral of Unit 3 Part A (Sessions 43-48) and the average-value integral (Session 60).

f.ac requires f.quantities and f.dynamics in the taxonomy, so it reaches f.calculus only transitively through f.dynamics; the average/RMS lessons should therefore assume the definite integral (Unit 3 Part A) and may introduce the trigonometric-power integrals (Unit 4 Part A) themselves.

f.computation requires f.quantities and f.dynamics in the taxonomy, so Riemann sums (Session 46) arrive via f.calculus -> f.dynamics; the course itself teaches Riemann sums (Session 46) before numerical integration (Sessions 63-64).

f.signals requires f.dynamics and f.ac, and pe.modelling requires pe.topologies and f.signals (taxonomy); both reach f.calculus transitively, so AIPE's linearisation and transform lessons sit after the calculus, dynamics and AC modules, matching the course order that places linear approximation in Unit 2 Part A and improper integrals and Taylor series in Unit 5.

re.mppt requires re.pv and pe.buck (taxonomy) and reaches f.calculus through re.pv -> f.electronics -> f.dynamics -> f.calculus; the derivative-equals-zero optimisation of Sessions 29-30 is therefore assumed, not taught, in re.mppt.

Course-internal order stated in the syllabus: Unit 1 differentiation, Unit 2 applications including the ODE introduction, Unit 3 definite integral, Unit 4 techniques, Unit 5 infinite processes; sessions are to be taken in order because each builds on the previous one.

Proposed taxonomy change (not current): f.computation could list f.calculus directly, because its numerical-integration content (Sessions 46, 63-64) depends on the Riemann-sum definition rather than on f.dynamics; f.ac's dependency can remain transitive.

course_facts.scope_summary: 18.02SC is the OCW Scholar (self-study) edition of MIT's second-semester freshman calculus, taught by Prof. Denis Auroux: vector and matrix algebra, calculus of functions of several variables (partial derivatives, gradient, chain rule, optimisation with and without constraints), double and triple integrals in several coordinate systems, and vector calculus in two and three dimensions culminating in Green's, Stokes' and the divergence theorems, with a short physics-applications coda on Maxwell's equations. It is organised into 4 units, 12 parts and 102 numbered sessions, of which Sessions 22-23, 45-46 and 73 are unit-exam reviews and Sessions 99-102 are final-exam reviews. A typical session (Session 1 sampled) links a segmented lecture-video clip (recorded fall 2007) with board images, lecture notes, worked examples, a recitation video and problems with solutions; the syllabus says most sessions include lecture clips and some include Mathlets. The course has 12 problem sets (one per part), 4 unit exams and a final exam; solutions are linked on every sampled problem-set and exam page and Problem Set Solutions / Exam Solutions are listed resource types. The syllabus describes the course as self-contained with no required textbook and estimates roughly 150 hours of study.

mit_topics: 2. Partial Derivatives (Sessions 24-46: functions of two variables, partial derivatives, approximation formula, chain rule, gradient, directional derivatives, optimization, least squares, Lagrange multipliers)
Unit 1, Part C: Parametric Equations for Curves (Sessions 15-21, including Session 19: Velocity and Acceleration and Session 20: Velocity and Arc Length)
mapped_modules.rationale: The course's central subject is differential and integral calculus of several variables. f.calculus is AIPE's only calculus node; its taxonomy summary (slopes, areas, exponentials and first-order differential equations introduced through charging and discharging circuits) is the single-variable base that this course assumes through its 18.01 prerequisite, so the multivariable content extends the module rather than being contained in it. The extension is itemised under concepts_missing_in_aipe. The evidence page (Unit 2) lists Sessions 24-46; the Unit 1, 3 and 4 items are listed on https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/pages/1.-vectors-and-matrices/ (Sessions 1-23), https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/pages/3.-double-integrals-and-line-integrals-in-the-plane/ (Sessions 47-73) and https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/pages/4.-triple-integrals-and-surface-integrals-in-3-space/ (Sessions 74-98), and the part titles also appear in the site navigation of every page. Taxonomy follow-up: the f.calculus summary describes only single-variable calculus and first-order differential equations; either widen it to name functions of several variables, partial derivatives and multiple integrals, or add a multivariable-calculus node, so that this core reference is described by the module it maps to.

mit_topics: Part A: Vectors, Determinants and Planes (Sessions 1-8: vectors, dot products, components, determinants in 2D and 3D, cross products, planes)
Part B: Matrices and Systems of Equations (Sessions 9-14: matrix multiplication, matrix inverses, linear systems and planes, solutions to square systems)
mapped_modules.rationale: One of the four units is vector and matrix algebra up to inverses and solvability of square systems, which is exactly what AIPE's node-equation and mesh systems need. The state-space descriptions named in the module summary, and the eigenvalue and diagonalisation machinery they rest on, are not covered here (they belong to 18.06SC/18.03SC). The evidence page (Unit 1) lists Sessions 1-23 and both part titles; the Part B page https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/pages/1.-vectors-and-matrices/part-b-matrices-and-systems-of-equations/ lists Sessions 9-14 alone.

mit_topics: Unit 3, Part B: Vector Fields and Line Integrals (Sessions 56-64, including Session 63: Potential Functions)
Unit 3, Part C: Green's Theorem (Sessions 65-72, including Session 69: Flux in 2D)
Part B: Flux and the Divergence Theorem (Sessions 79-87: flux through a surface, divergence theorem, del notation)
Part C: Line Integrals and Stokes' Theorem (Sessions 88-96, including Session 89: Gradient Fields and Potential Functions)
Physics Applications (Session 97: Curl and Physics; Session 98: Maxwell's Equations)
mapped_modules.rationale: The vector-calculus half of the course (line integrals, flux, Green's, divergence and Stokes' theorems) is the mathematical language of Gauss's, Faraday's and Ampere's laws, and Sessions 63 and 89 define potential functions in general. The module's physics (charge, electric field and potential, current, magnetic fields, Faraday's law, energy stored in fields) is not taught; only the two-session Physics Applications coda (Sessions 97-98) states Maxwell's equations, so the course is background for this module, on the same footing as f.magnetism, and a physics course such as 8.02 is the physics reference. The evidence page (Unit 4) lists Sessions 74-98 including the Unit 4 part titles and Sessions 89, 97 and 98; the Unit 3 items are listed on https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/pages/3.-double-integrals-and-line-integrals-in-the-plane/ (Sessions 47-73).

mit_topics: Session 95: Stokes' Theorem and Surface Independence
mapped_modules.rationale: Surface flux integrals and Stokes' theorem underlie flux linkage and induced EMF; magnetic circuits, saturation and measurement in the module summary are not course topics. The evidence page (Unit 4) lists all four sessions (80 and 81 in Part B, 91 and 95 in Part C).

mit_topics: Session 85: Physical Meaning of Flux; Del Notation
mapped_modules.rationale: Heat flux and the diffusion equation are the field-level basis of conduction and thermal resistance; junction temperature, heatsinks and cooling in the module summary are not course topics. Added so that the diffusion-equation lab recommended for pe.thermal rests on a mapped module; both sessions are listed on the Part 4B evidence page.

mit_topics: Session 32: Total Differentials and the Chain Rule
Session 34: The Chain Rule with More Variables
Session 35: Gradient: Definition, Perpendicular to Level Curves
mapped_modules.rationale: Linearising a converter's averaged model around an operating point is a tangent-plane approximation built from partial derivatives. The course teaches that mathematics; converters and small-signal models are not MIT topics here. The evidence page (Unit 2) lists all five sessions (26 and 27 in Part A, 32, 34 and 35 in Part B).

mit_topics: Unit 2, Session 34: The Chain Rule with More Variables
mapped_modules.rationale: Newton-Raphson power flow combines a Jacobian of partial derivatives with the solution of a square linear system at each iteration; the course supplies both ingredients but does not treat Newton's method for systems or any power network. Sessions 11 and 14 are listed on the evidence page (Part 1B); Sessions 26 and 34 are listed on https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/pages/2.-partial-derivatives/ (Session 26 in Part A, Session 34 in Part B). In AIPE terms the linear-system ingredient is f.linear-algebra, which the taxonomy does not list in ps.power-flow.requires (ps.three-phase, ps.per-unit, f.computation); recommended taxonomy addition.

mit_topics: Session 39: Statement of Lagrange Multipliers and Example
mapped_modules.rationale: Constrained optimisation with a multiplier is the classical basis of economic dispatch (equal incremental cost); dispatch, reserves and frequency control are not MIT topics in this course. All three sessions are listed on the Part 2C evidence page.

mit_topics: Session 35: Gradient: Definition, Perpendicular to Level Curves
mapped_modules.rationale: Maximum power point tracking is a numerical maximisation of power over operating voltage; the course gives the calculus of maxima and the gradient as steepest-ascent direction (the hill-climbing intuition), not photovoltaics or tracking algorithms. The evidence page (Unit 2) lists all four sessions (28 and 30 in Part A, 35 and 38 in Part B).

mit_topics: Session 24: Functions of Two Variables: Graphs
Session 25: Level Curves and Contour Plots
Unit 3, Session 47: Definition of Double Integration
Unit 3, Session 51: Applications: Mass and Average Value
mapped_modules.rationale: The course is analytic and uses interactive Java Mathlets (named on the home page and syllabus, https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/pages/syllabus/) rather than code; surface and contour visualisation, least-squares fitting, the Riemann-sum definition of a double integral and average values over a region are the points where AIPE's computation module would implement the same ideas numerically in Python. Sessions 24, 25 and 29 are listed on the evidence page (Part 2A); Sessions 47 and 51 are listed on https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/pages/3.-double-integrals-and-line-integrals-in-the-plane/part-a-double-integrals/ (Sessions 47-55).

concepts_missing_in_aipe: Vector geometry in 2D/3D: dot and cross products, determinants as areas and volumes, equations of lines and planes (no AIPE module summary lists vectors or determinants)
Parametric curves and trajectories: velocity, acceleration and arc length (Unit 1 Part C)
Functions of several variables: graphs, level curves and contour plots
Partial derivatives, total differentials and the multivariable chain rule

Gradient and directional derivatives; the tangent-plane (linear) approximation in its general mathematical form (pe.modelling names linearisation around an operating point as an engineering technique for converters, but no module teaches the underlying approximation formula)
Unconstrained optimisation in several variables: critical points, second-derivative test, least squares posed as an optimisation problem
Constrained optimisation: Lagrange multipliers and constrained differentials
Double and triple integrals set up in rectangular, polar, cylindrical or spherical coordinate systems; change of variables (Jacobian)

Integral applications over regions and volumes: mass, moment of inertia, gravitational attraction, and the average value of a function over a 2D/3D region (Session 51); f.ac covers only the average and RMS of a periodic waveform in one variable

Vector fields, work and line integrals, conservative fields, path independence and potential functions for a general vector field (Sessions 56-63, 88-89); f.electromagnetism names electric potential but no module defines a potential function or path independence

Flux defined as the line integral of a vector field across a plane curve (Session 69) or the surface integral of a vector field (Sessions 80-83), Green's theorem in tangential and normal forms, and the divergence theorem; f.magnetism names magnetic flux but no module defines flux as an integral of a field
Curl in 2D and 3D, Stokes' theorem, simply connected regions and surface independence
Del notation and the diffusion (heat) equation as a first partial differential equation (Sessions 85, 87); pe.thermal names thermal resistance but no module states the heat equation
Maxwell's equations as the vector-calculus synthesis (AIPE's f.electromagnetism lists Faraday's law but no module states Maxwell's equations in differential or integral form)
modern_gaps_not_covered_by_mit: Numerical multivariable methods used in power engineering: Newton-Raphson for nonlinear systems (power flow), numerical Jacobians, quadrature for multiple integrals, finite-difference solution of the diffusion equation; the course is analytic and provides no code

Linear algebra beyond 3x3 systems: eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalisation, matrix exponential and state-space models needed by pe.modelling, f.signals and ps.stability; Unit 1 stops at inverses of square systems

Complex numbers and phasors (f.ac), Laplace and Fourier transforms (f.signals) and ordinary differential equations for RC/RL/RLC dynamics (f.dynamics); 18.02SC assumes 18.01 and leaves ordinary differential equations to 18.03SC: although OCW tags the course with Differential Equations, its only differential-equation session is Session 87 (Diffusion Equation), a partial differential equation

Least squares in matrix/regression form and optimisation algorithms (gradient descent, KKT conditions, convex programming) used for parameter extraction, MPPT, economic dispatch and energy management; the course gives only the calculus statements

Engineering-contextualised field applications: Ampere's law and flux for inductor and transformer magnetics design, Gauss's law for cable and coaxial geometries, heat conduction in power devices; the course's applications are mass, moment of inertia, gravitation and generic Maxwell equations
Reproducible open-source computation (Python/NumPy/SciPy/Matplotlib, ngspice) in place of the 2010 Java-applet Mathlets for visualising surfaces, contours, vector fields and flux

recommended_simulations: labs/foundations/linear_systems_node_equations.py (Python): assemble the node-voltage matrix of a resistive network, solve with numpy.linalg.solve, compare determinant/inverse/Cramer paths and check KCL residuals (Unit 1 Part B -> f.linear-algebra, f.dc-circuits)

labs/foundations/ngspice_node_matrix_check.py (Python driver for labs/foundations/ngspice_node_matrix_check.cir): runs an ngspice .op analysis of the same resistive network, parses the node voltages and compares them with the NumPy solution (Unit 1 Part B -> f.linear-algebra, f.dc-circuits)

labs/power-electronics/tangent_plane_linearisation.py (Python): partial derivatives of a buck/boost steady-state output V(D, Vin) analytically vs finite differences; plot tangent-plane approximation error against perturbation size (Unit 2 Parts A-B -> pe.modelling)

labs/power-electronics/ngspice_small_signal_operating_point.py (Python driver for labs/power-electronics/ngspice_small_signal_operating_point.cir): ngspice .dc sweep of a diode or MOSFET circuit; the script extracts numerical partial derivatives (small-signal conductance) around a bias point (Unit 2 Part A -> f.electronics, pe.modelling)

labs/renewable-energy/contour_gradient_mppt.py (Python): contour plot of PV power P(V, G) with gradient arrows; gradient-ascent steps compared with perturb-and-observe hill climbing (Sessions 25, 35 -> re.mppt)

labs/foundations/least_squares_model_fit.py (Python): least-squares fit of a conduction-loss or simplified PV model to synthetic noisy data; closed-form normal equations vs scipy.optimize.least_squares with residual plots (Session 29 -> f.computation)

labs/power-systems/lagrange_economic_dispatch.py (Python): minimise quadratic generation cost of two or three units subject to demand balance via Lagrange multipliers; verify equal incremental cost against scipy.optimize.minimize (Unit 2 Part C -> ps.grid-control)

labs/foundations/multiple_integrals_field_energy.py (Python): scipy.integrate tplquad of the electric energy density (epsilon E^2 / 2) over a coaxial-cable volume compared with C V^2 / 2, and of B^2 / (2 mu) over a toroidal core volume compared with L I^2 / 2; grid-step convergence study of a Riemann-sum version (Units 3A, 4A -> f.electromagnetism, f.computation)

labs/foundations/flux_divergence_gauss.py (Python): numerical flux of a point-charge field through a sphere and a cube with matplotlib quiver/streamplot; divergence-theorem check (Unit 4 Part B -> f.electromagnetism)

labs/foundations/stokes_faraday_loop.py (Python): line integral of a vector field around a loop vs surface integral of its curl; a time-varying field gives an induced-EMF estimate (Unit 4 Part C, Session 98 -> f.electromagnetism, f.magnetism)

labs/power-electronics/diffusion_1d_heat_fd.py (Python): explicit finite-difference solution of the 1-D diffusion equation for heat spreading in a device die with a step-size stability demonstration (Session 87 -> pe.thermal, f.computation)
prerequisite_relationships: The syllabus states 18.01 Single Variable Calculus as the only prerequisite; in AIPE terms f.calculus (single-variable part) and f.quantities precede every unit of this course

Unit order implies f.linear-algebra basics (vectors, matrices, square systems) can be taught before partial derivatives; AIPE can introduce node-equation matrices (f.dc-circuits + f.linear-algebra) ahead of multivariable calculus
pe.modelling requires partial derivatives, total differentials and the tangent-plane approximation (Unit 2 Parts A-B) in addition to its stated requires pe.topologies and f.signals

ps.power-flow requires solving square linear systems (Unit 1 Part B: Session 11 Matrix Inverses, Session 14 Solutions to Square Systems) and partial derivatives for the Jacobian (Unit 2 Parts A-B: Session 26 Partial Derivatives, Session 34 The Chain Rule with More Variables) on top of its stated ps.three-phase, ps.per-unit and f.computation; in AIPE terms this means f.linear-algebra, which the taxonomy does not list in ps.power-flow.requires (recommended taxonomy addition)

f.electromagnetism (Faraday's law and field energy as stated in its summary; Gauss's law as AIPE's intended extension) requires flux and surface integrals, divergence, line integrals and curl (Units 3-4); the course places Maxwell's equations last (Sessions 97-98), after all three theorems
f.magnetism (flux linkage, induction) builds on surface flux integrals and Stokes' theorem (Unit 4 Parts B-C)

pe.thermal (thermal resistance, junction temperature) can draw on heat flux and the diffusion equation (Unit 4 Part B: Session 85 Physical Meaning of Flux; Del Notation, Session 87 Diffusion Equation) in addition to its stated pe.losses prerequisite; the course reaches the diffusion equation only after the divergence theorem (Session 84)

ps.grid-control and re.energy-management (dispatch, scheduling) rely on constrained optimisation; the course teaches unconstrained optimisation (Unit 2 Part A) before Lagrange multipliers (Unit 2 Part C)
re.mppt presupposes maximisation of a function of one or two variables and the gradient as direction of steepest ascent (Unit 2 Parts A-B)
ps.machines (force and torque as partial derivatives of co-energy) requires partial derivatives (Unit 2 Part A)

Within the course: vectors and matrices -> partial derivatives -> double and line integrals in the plane -> triple and surface integrals in space -> physics applications; each part ends with a problem set and each unit with an exam

courses.facts_vs_inferences: FACTS (read on 2026-10-20 from ocw.mit.edu HTML pages, all HTTP 200 unless noted, and re-read the same day during review): course number 18.02SC, title Multivariable Calculus, Fall 2010, Undergraduate, instructor Prof. Denis Auroux; learning resource types Lecture Videos, Lecture Notes, Problem Sets, Problem Set Solutions, Exams, Exam Solutions; the home-page description line naming Interactive Java Applets (Mathlets); the eight content developers and the image credit to John B. Lewis as listed on the home page; MIT topic tags Calculus, Linear Algebra, Differential Equations; the home page and syllabus structure of 4 units, 12 parts, Physics Applications and Final Exam; the 102 numbered session titles (Sessions 1-23, 24-46, 47-73 and 74-98 listed on the four unit pages, 99-102 on the Final Exam Review page), 12 problem-set pages, 4 unit exam pages (practice exam, review sessions where present, exam) and the final-exam section, read from the unit/part/exam listing pages; the syllabus statements that 18.01 is the prerequisite, that no textbook is required, that lecture clips were recorded in fall 2007 and appear in most sessions, that there are dozens of recitation videos, that some sessions include a Mathlet, that each part ends with a problem set and each unit with an exam, and that about 150 hours are expected; the per-page resource link counts sampled on the Session 1, Problem Set 1, Exam 1 exam, practice final exam and final exam pages; the footer link to CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; the 301 responses for pages/calendar/ and for other non-existent paths. course_facts.scope_summary: 18.03SC is the OCW Scholar self-study edition of MIT's undergraduate differential-equations course. It is built from four units: first-order ODEs (analytic, geometric and numerical methods, complex arithmetic, sinusoidal and exponential inputs, autonomous equations), second-order constant-coefficient linear equations (characteristic equation, damped oscillators, exponential response, gain and phase lag, resonance, frequency response, an LRC-circuit application), Fourier series and Laplace transform (periodic input, step and delta functions, impulse response, convolution, transfer functions, poles), and first-order 2x2 systems (matrix methods, eigenvalues, phase portraits, matrix exponentials, linearisation of nonlinear systems, limit cycles and chaos). The navigation lists 39 session pages plus three unit exams and a final. Most session pages link course-note PDFs, clips from Prof. Mattuck's lectures, recitation videos, Mathlet pages, practice problems and two-part problem sets with solutions; the Conventions and Preliminary Material, Linear vs. Nonlinear and Applications: LRC Circuits sessions carry no video links. The syllabus overview frames the course around linear ODEs and the ways scientists and engineers use them, and states that MIT students put about 150 hours into it across 38 sessions.
stated_prerequisites: Single-variable calculus (MIT 18.01) is a prerequisite; OCW users are pointed to 18.01SC as preparation.

Multivariable calculus (MIT 18.02) is a corequisite, i.e. it may be taken at the same time; from it the course assumes familiarity with vectors, basic matrix arithmetic and elementary facts about vector-valued functions, and OCW users are referred to 18.02SC.
The syllabus names no textbook; the course is meant to be worked through on one's own from its notes, videos, problem sets and exams.

mit_topics: First Order Constant Coefficient Linear ODE's
Exponential Input; Gain and Phase Lag
mapped_modules.rationale: AIPE's f.calculus module pairs calculus (slopes, areas, exponentials) with first-order differential equations introduced through charging and discharging circuits. MIT Unit I is a deep, twelve-session treatment of the ODE half (separable and linear equations, integrating factors, direction fields, autonomous equations, stability of critical points), while the calculus half is assumed as the 18.01 prerequisite and not taught. The label is 'partial' for the module as a whole, consistent with the f.ac rating below; for the first-order-ODE half alone the coverage would be core.

mit_topics: Exponential Input; Gain and Phase Lag
Step and Delta Functions: Integrals and Generalized Derivatives
Unit Step and Unit Impulse Response
mapped_modules.rationale: The module summary (LTI systems, step and frequency response, Laplace transforms, poles, Bode plots, negative feedback) is the central subject matter of Units II and III: LTI operators, amplitude and phase response, step and impulse response, convolution, Laplace-transform solution of initial value problems, transfer and weight functions and pole diagrams. The exponential response formula (Exponential Response, Undetermined Coefficients) is the transfer function evaluated at the input exponent, which the Poles, Amplitude Response, Connection to ERF session builds on, and the three Fourier-series sessions handle periodic input by superposition over Fourier components. The course lists a note on Bode plots (Amplitude Phase, Gain and Bode Plots, on the Exponential Input; Gain and Phase Lag page) but nothing on negative feedback, loop shaping or gain and phase margins, so one module item is not covered. The home-page navigation lists all the sessions named here; per-session URLs are in topic_outline.

mit_topics: First Order Constant Coefficient Linear ODE's
Exponential Input; Gain and Phase Lag
mapped_modules.rationale: The mathematics of RC/RL responses and time constants (first-order constant-coefficient linear ODEs with step, exponential and sinusoidal inputs) and of RLC ringing (damped harmonic oscillator, damping ratio) is central to the course, but the module's physical content, capacitors and inductors as energy-storage elements, appears only in the single Applications: LRC Circuits session (notes titled RLC Circuits and Impedance plus a Series RLC Circuits Applet note); the syllabus goals otherwise name driven spring-mass systems as the physical model, so coverage is substantial but not central.

mit_topics: Matrix Methods: Eigenvalues and Normal Modes
mapped_modules.rationale: Unit IV treats 2x2 constant-coefficient linear systems x' = Ax, i.e. the state-space description named in the module summary, with eigenvalues and eigenvectors, normal modes, fundamental matrices and the matrix exponential; the Linear Systems session page lists a note titled Review of Vectors and Matrices (also on the lecture-notes listing) and notes on matrix notation and the companion matrix. It is one unit of four and limited to 2x2 systems, and the module's node-equation and large-system solving content is not taught, so coverage is partial.

mit_topics: Exponential Input; Gain and Phase Lag
mapped_modules.rationale: Complex numbers, Euler's formula and the complex-exponential (phasor-style) method for sinusoidal inputs, amplitude-phase form, gain and phase lag, and the note titled Impedance on the Applications: LRC Circuits page cover the complex-number half of the module in depth. Period, frequency, duty cycle, average and RMS values and AC power are not listed anywhere in the course, so coverage is partial rather than core.

The Numerical Methods session page lists an introduction note, notes titled Motivation and Implementation of Euler's Method, Errors in Euler's Method and Further Numerical Methods, video resource pages titled Euler's Method, Example of Euler's Method, Better Methods and Pitfalls, an Euler's Method Applet note with an exploration page, a worked exercise, a recitation video and the usual practice-problem and problem-set files; the syllabus course goals also name Euler's method and direction fields. So Euler's method, its error and the existence of better methods are taught in one session. Programming, plotting and simulation-model building are not taught, and step-size and error discussion is confined to this session, so the treatment is introductory relative to the module summary.

mit_topics: Transfer (System) and Weight Functions, Green's Formula
Poles, Amplitude Response, Connection to ERF
mapped_modules.rationale: The course supplies the mathematical machinery the module relies on: linearisation of a nonlinear system around an equilibrium (critical point), transfer functions and pole diagrams of LTI systems. It contains no converter, averaging or small-signal-model content, so it is background for pe.modelling rather than coverage of it.

mit_topics: Poles, Amplitude Response, Connection to ERF
Exponential Input; Gain and Phase Lag
mapped_modules.rationale: Stability read from pole locations, amplitude and phase response, phase lag and the single note Amplitude Phase, Gain and Bode Plots are prerequisites for loop design and phase/gain margins, but the course lists no feedback loops, compensation, margins or digital implementation; tangential background only.

Second-order resonance mathematics (natural frequency, damping, pure versus practical resonance, LRC circuit response) is the analytical basis for resonant-tank behaviour, but resonant converters, LLC stages and soft switching are not part of the course.

Fourier series of a periodic (square- or PWM-like) input and the response of an LTI system to it by superposition over harmonics is the mathematics behind the inverter output harmonics and output filters named in the module summary; the course has no inverter, bridge or PWM content. URLs for the other two Fourier sessions are in topic_outline.

The same Fourier-series and periodic-input material underlies the rectifier line-current harmonics and power-factor analysis named in the module summary; the course has no rectifier, power-factor or three-phase content, so this is background only.

mit_topics: Limitations of the Linear: Limit Cycles and Chaos
mapped_modules.rationale: Equilibria, phase portraits, eigenvalue-based classification and linearisation of nonlinear 2x2 systems are the mathematics behind small-signal and rotor-angle stability studies; the course has no power-system content, so this is assumed background for ps.stability.

concepts_missing_in_aipe: First-order ODE theory beyond what the module summaries name: separable equations, integrating factors, existence and uniqueness, and superposition for linear equations. First-order differential equations are named generically in the f.calculus and f.dynamics summaries, but these techniques are not named and curriculum/catalogue.json attaches no lesson or lab to either module.
Geometric methods: direction fields and isoclines for first-order ODEs (named in no module summary and in no repository file).

Euler's method and its error as an explicitly taught foundations topic. The f.computation summary names numerical integration, step sizes and numerical error; the only implementation is the fixed-step semi-implicit Euler scheme inside labs/power-electronics/buck_switching.py, whose docstring documents its step-dependent error and which the buck fundamentals lesson (curriculum/power-electronics/dc-dc-conversion/buck-converter-fundamentals.md) describes in its lab-method paragraph. No lesson teaches the method, its error order or its step-size limits, and catalogue.json attaches nothing to f.computation.
First-order autonomous equations: phase lines, critical points and their stability; linear versus nonlinear behaviour (named in no module summary and in no repository file).

Second-order constant-coefficient theory: characteristic equation and modes, under-, critically and over-damped responses. The term damping ratio appears only in the buck fundamentals lesson, where zeta = sqrt(L/C)/(2R) is applied to the start-up transient of the output filter; no foundations lesson develops the general second-order theory.
Exponential response formula, undetermined coefficients and the amplitude-phase form of sinusoidal responses (named in no module summary; f.ac and f.signals have no lesson).

Pure versus practical resonance of a driven second-order system as general theory. LC resonance appears only applied to the buck output filter in the draft tutorial curriculum/03-converters/buck-converter.md (natural frequency, Q and the resonant peak of the duty-to-output transfer function) and in the buck fundamentals lesson's start-up transient; resonant converters are mentioned in the stage-03 outline; pe.resonant has no lesson.

Fourier series of periodic inputs, operations on Fourier series and the response of an LTI system to periodic input by superposition. No module summary names Fourier series, although pe.rectifiers and pe.inverters name harmonics; 'Fourier' appears in no repository file in English or Chinese.

Delta functions and generalised derivatives, the unit impulse response, the convolution integral and Green's formula. Step response is named in the f.signals summary, but these items appear in no module summary and in no repository file.

Laplace transform as a taught topic: transform tables, partial fractions and the inverse transform, solving initial value problems, weight and transfer functions, pole diagrams. Laplace transforms and poles are named in the f.signals summary and converter transfer functions in the pe.modelling summary (and the zh-CN prerequisite path lists the transform for F07), but catalogue.json attaches no lesson or lab to f.signals, and the only transfer-function derivation in the repository is the draft buck tutorial's duty-to-output function.

Bode plots as a taught foundations topic: named in the f.signals summary and the stage-04 outline, tabulated in the draft buck tutorial, but no lesson constructs or reads one (MIT lists a single note, Amplitude Phase, Gain and Bode Plots).

2x2 linear systems: eigenvalues and eigenvectors, normal modes, fundamental matrix, trace-determinant classification of phase portraits, matrix exponential, variation of parameters. The f.linear-algebra summary names state-space descriptions but nothing on eigenvalues; 'eigen', 'phase portrait' and 'matrix exponential' appear in no repository file and f.linear-algebra has no lesson.

Jacobian linearisation of general nonlinear 2x2 systems near critical points, limit cycles and chaos. Linearisation around an operating point is named in the pe.modelling summary (and the pe.modelling mapping above relies on it), but the qualitative theory of nonlinear systems appears nowhere in the repository.

Complex arithmetic, Euler's formula and the complex-exponential method as a self-contained lesson. Complex numbers, phasors and impedance are named in the f.ac summary, the three-phase lesson (curriculum/power-systems/ac-power-networks/three-phase-fundamentals.md) carries a short phasor recap that defers to f.ac, and labs/power-systems/three_phase.py does phasor arithmetic with cmath, but catalogue.json attaches no lesson to f.ac.
modern_gaps_not_covered_by_mit: Practical numerical ODE solving as engineers use it: adaptive step size, implicit and stiff solvers, the scipy.integrate.solve_ivp workflow and the stiffness of switching-converter models. (The Numerical Methods session page lists Errors in Euler's Method, a Better Methods video page and Further Numerical Methods, so higher-order fixed-step methods are at least named by the course.)
Gain and phase margins, loop shaping and negative-feedback design on Bode plots (the course lists a Bode-plot note, amplitude/phase response and pole diagrams, but no feedback loops).
Discrete-time dynamics: sampled systems, difference equations, z-transform and digital control implementation needed by pe.control.
Switched and piecewise-linear systems, state-space averaging and small-signal models of converters (the course treats continuous LTI systems only).
State-space modelling above 2x2 order and numerical eigenvalue analysis of large systems, as needed for converter-dominated grid stability studies.
Fourier transform, DFT/FFT, harmonic spectra and total harmonic distortion for measured waveforms (the course covers Fourier series only).
Phasor-domain AC power quantities: RMS and average values, real/reactive/apparent power, three-phase phasors.
Open computational tooling for verification: Python/NumPy/SciPy scripts and ngspice circuit simulation compared against hand analysis (the course relies on Java Mathlets).
Electromechanical dynamics (swing equation), frequency dynamics and small-signal stability in inverter-dominated grids as applications of the ODE theory.

numerical-ode-methods-euler-to-rk45 (f.computation): direction fields, Euler's method, step size and error, solve_ivp, stiffness; applied to RC, RLC and an averaged buck model

impulse-response-and-convolution (f.signals): step and delta functions, unit impulse response, convolution integral, response to a load-step train
fourier-series-and-harmonics (f.signals, background for pe.rectifiers and pe.inverters): Fourier series of square and PWM waveforms, LTI response to periodic input by superposition, THD

recommended_simulations: labs/foundations/rc_first_order_response.py (Python): RC circuit with step, exponential and sinusoidal sources; analytic solution versus Euler and solve_ivp, time-constant extraction, step-size sweep

labs/foundations/euler_step_size_error.py (Python): Euler versus RK45 global error against step size on y' = k y and on a series RLC; demonstrates instability of large steps and stiffness; should reuse or reference the fixed-step semi-implicit Euler integrator already in labs/power-electronics/buck_switching.py rather than introduce a second scheme

labs/foundations/rlc_damping_resonance.py (Python): series RLC second-order ODE; damping-ratio sweep (under/critical/over-damped), magnitude and phase response, practical-resonance peak versus natural frequency
labs/foundations/rlc_ngspice_compare.py (Python wrapper around ngspice -b): .tran step response and .ac sweep of a series RLC netlist compared with the Python analytic solution
labs/foundations/sinusoidal_steady_state_phasor.py (Python): complex-exponential method for RC/RL filters; gain and phase lag versus frequency overlaid on time-domain simulation

labs/foundations/laplace_transfer_function_poles.py (Python, sympy and scipy.signal): transfer function from an ODE, pole diagram, step and impulse responses; move poles across the imaginary axis to show instability
labs/foundations/convolution_load_step.py (Python): numerical convolution of an impulse response with arbitrary inputs (load-step train) compared with direct solve_ivp integration

labs/foundations/fourier_series_pwm_filter.py (Python, with ngspice .four counterpart): Fourier coefficients of square/PWM waveforms, per-harmonic LC-filter response by superposition, reconstruction versus time-domain simulation, THD

labs/foundations/state_space_phase_portrait.py (Python): 2x2 x' = Ax from LC/RLC state variables; eigenvalues, trace-determinant classification, phase portraits (node, saddle, spiral, centre), matrix exponential via scipy.linalg.expm

labs/foundations/linearisation_nonlinear_2x2.py (Python): nonlinear 2x2 system (pendulum, PV-fed converter equilibrium); critical points, Jacobian linearisation, linearised versus full trajectories, limit-cycle example
prerequisite_relationships: f.dynamics requires f.calculus, as the taxonomy already states (the course assumes single-variable calculus, MIT 18.01, before its first-order ODE unit).

f.linear-algebra should be in place before the systems part of f.signals and before ps.stability (the course expects vectors and matrix arithmetic from the 18.02 corequisite, and the Linear Systems session opens Unit IV with a Review of Vectors and Matrices note before the eigenvalue methods). The taxonomy currently lists f.linear-algebra only under f.signals.related and not among ps.stability's requirements, so this is a proposed promotion to requires.

f.ac (complex numbers and phasors) precedes sinusoidal-input dynamics and frequency response (Unit I places Complex Arithmetic and Exponentials and Sinusoidal Functions before Exponential Input; Gain and Phase Lag). This agrees with the taxonomy, where f.signals requires f.ac; since the taxonomy also places f.dynamics before f.ac, sinusoidal-input responses of RC and RL circuits belong after f.ac (in f.signals or at the end of f.ac) rather than in f.dynamics' step-response material.

f.signals requires f.dynamics and f.ac, consistent with the taxonomy (second-order response in Unit II builds on the first-order methods of Unit I; Laplace transforms and transfer functions in Unit III build on Units I and II).

pe.modelling requires f.signals (as in the taxonomy) and should additionally require f.linear-algebra, which the taxonomy does not list (current requires: pe.topologies, f.signals); Unit IV's Linearization Near Critical Points depends on Unit IV matrix methods and phase portraits as well as on Unit III transfer functions.

ps.stability should require f.linear-algebra explicitly, beyond its current ps.power-flow and pe.modelling requirements (phase portraits, eigenvalue classification and linearisation are the stability tools taught in Unit IV).

f.computation's numerical-ODE content can be taught alongside f.calculus/f.dynamics rather than after them (Numerical Methods is the fourth session of Unit I, immediately after Geometric Methods). The taxonomy currently lists f.dynamics as a requirement of f.computation; this proposes teaching the numerical-ODE part concurrently.

A future harmonics lesson for pe.rectifiers and pe.inverters depends on f.ac and the superposition content of f.signals, not on Laplace transforms (Unit III teaches Fourier series and periodic input before the Laplace transform). Both modules currently require pe.topologies and f.ac only, so f.signals would be a new dependency for that lesson.

courses.facts_vs_inferences: FACTS (read on 2026-10-20 from ocw.mit.edu HTML pages, all HTTP 200 unless stated): course title, number 18.03SC, Fall 2011, Undergraduate level, four instructors, MIT topic tags (Differential Equations, Linear Algebra) and seven learning resource types, as on the home page and in references/mit-ocw-verification.json (which records syllabus_status null for this course because the standard pages/syllabus/ path never returns 200); the four-unit structure, the 39 session page titles (each matching its page title), the three unit exam pages and the final exam page, with their URLs; the syllabus statements on prerequisites (18.01 prerequisite, 18.02 corequisite assuming vectors, matrix arithmetic and vector-valued functions, pointers to 18.01SC and 18.02SC), course goals (naming among others Euler's method, direction fields, stability of critical points, LRC circuits, amplitude and phase response, weight and transfer functions, pole diagrams, Laplace transform, convolution, Fourier series, the matrix eigenvalue method, phase portraits and linearisation), the 38-session and about-150-hour statements, the two-part problem-set format and the absence of a textbook section; resource counts from the listing pages (213 lecture-note PDF items, of which 209 carry session numbers s0-s38 and 4 are Laplace-table files, 78 lecture video clips, 35 problem-solving videos, 190 problem-set items, 97 problem-set-solution items, 114 exam items, 43 exam-solution items, 3 PDF links per unit exam page, 4 on the final exam page); the resource titles quoted in rationales (Amplitude Phase, Gain and Bode Plots on the Exponential Input; Gain and Phase Lag page; Motivation and Implementation of Euler's Method, Errors in Euler's Method, Further Numerical Methods and the video pages Euler's Method, Example of Euler's Method, Better Methods and Pitfalls on the Numerical Methods page; RLC Circuits and Impedance on the Applications: LRC Circuits page; Review of Vectors and Matrices on the Linear Systems page); the absence of video links on the Conventions and Preliminary Material, Linear vs. Nonlinear and Applications: LRC Circuits pages; and the redirect behaviour of pages/calendar/, pages/syllabus/ and video_galleries/ (301 to resources/calendar/index.html, resources/syllabus/index.html and resources/index.html respectively, each of which returns 301 to itself, so no 200 page exists). No MIT page lists negative feedback, gain or phase margins, logarithmic axes or decibels, nor any modern topic such as grid-forming converters, wide-bandgap devices, inverter-dominated grids, DC microgrids, Python/SciPy, ngspice, RK45, z-transform, FFT or THD, and none is attributed to MIT here. The topic-outline index values (I-1, II-3, final, etc.) are positional labels derived from the navigation order, not MIT session numbers; the lecture-note filenames carry their own numbering s0-s38. REPOSITORY FACTS (grep over curriculum/, labs/ and docs/ on 2026-10-20, English and Chinese): zero files mention Fourier, eigen, phase portrait, convolution, matrix exponential or impulse response in either language; Laplace appears only in curriculum/taxonomy.json (f.signals summary) and, as the Chinese term, in curriculum/01-foundations/prerequisite-path.zh-CN.md; Euler appears only as the fixed-step semi-implicit Euler integrator of labs/power-electronics/buck_switching.py and in the paragraph of curriculum/power-electronics/dc-dc-conversion/buck-converter-fundamentals.md that describes that scheme; damping ratio appears only in that buck fundamentals lesson (zeta = sqrt(L/C)/(2R) for the start-up transient); phasor appears in taxonomy.json (f.ac summary), in the phasor recap of curriculum/power-systems/ac-power-networks/three-phase-fundamentals.md, as a forward reference in curriculum/foundations/circuits/dc-circuit-fundamentals.md, in labs/power-systems/three_phase.py and, in Chinese, in the zh-CN prerequisite path; transfer functions, Bode plots and LC resonance appear in the draft tutorial curriculum/03-converters/buck-converter.md (duty-to-output transfer function, natural frequency, Q, resonant peak, phase margin, Type III compensation), in the stage outlines curriculum/04-modeling-and-control/README.md and curriculum/03-converters/README.md, in docs/ecosystem-v0.1.md and in taxonomy.json; curriculum/catalogue.json (15 entries) attaches lessons or labs only to f.dc-circuits, pe.buck, ps.three-phase and re.pv, so no lesson or lab exists for f.calculus, f.dynamics, f.ac, f.signals, f.linear-algebra or f.computation. INFERENCES (AIPE Academy judgement): every coverage level and module mapping, including the 'partial' rating of f.calculus and the background entries for pe.inverters and pe.rectifiers; the reading of the Numerical Methods session as introductory relative to the f.computation summary (the session page names Euler's method, its errors and further methods, but note contents were not opened); the lists of concepts missing in AIPE, which combine the taxonomy module summaries, the catalogue and the keyword scan above; and the modern gaps, recommended lesson slugs, recommended simulation scripts and prerequisite relationships, which are proposals in the repository's naming style and are not endorsed by MIT.
