course_facts.scope_summary: 18.06SC is the OCW Scholar self-study version of MIT's undergraduate linear algebra course (Prof. Gilbert Strang, Fall 2011), organised in three units: (I) solving Ax = b, elimination, LU, inverses and the four fundamental subspaces; (II) orthogonality, projections and least squares, determinants, eigenvalues, diagonalization and the matrix exponential exp(At) for systems of differential equations, Markov matrices and Fourier series; (III) symmetric and positive definite matrices, complex matrices and the FFT, similar matrices and Jordan form, SVD, linear transformations, change of basis and pseudoinverses. Each lecture session pairs a lecture video with a lecture-summary PDF, suggested textbook sections and a recitation (problem-solving) video; 31 of the 36 lecture sessions also carry a problem set with solutions (the overview session, the three exam-review sessions and the final review have none); three unit exams and a final exam with solutions are provided. Applications named on the pages read include electrical networks via incidence matrices, least-squares fitting of data, Markov matrices, Fourier series/FFT and image compression; the course does not treat circuits, converters or power systems as subjects.
stated_prerequisites: 18.02 Multivariable Calculus is the formal prerequisite for MIT students taking 18.06, but the syllabus says calculus itself is not needed to follow this course.
Learners need working familiarity with vectors, matrices and 3-D coordinates; the syllabus notes this is taught early in 18.02 and is covered again within this course.
The Instructor Insights page lists the prerequisite as the Mathematics GIR (MIT general institute requirement).

mit_topics: Systems of linear equations, elimination, row reduced form
Matrix multiplication, inverses, transposes, permutations, LU factorization, block matrices
Vector spaces, independence, basis, dimension, the four fundamental subspaces, rank
Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, diagonalization, powers of A, exp(At) for du/dt = Au
Symmetric and positive definite matrices, similar matrices, Jordan form

mapped_modules.rationale: The syllabus course-goal list (18 goals, from systems of linear equations to the singular value decomposition) and all three units are exactly the subject matter of AIPE's 'Linear algebra and state space' module; the exp(At) session supplies the mathematical core of state-space response that the module summary names. This is the course's central content, hence core (inference on coverage; topics are facts from the syllabus and unit pages).

Of the items in the f.signals summary (LTI systems, step and frequency response, Laplace transforms, poles, Bode plots, negative feedback) the course teaches three in matrix form: poles as the eigenvalues of A in the natural response of an autonomous LTI system du/dt = Au (exp(At) session), the discrete-step recursion behind 'Diagonalization and Powers of A', and Fourier series as an orthogonal expansion together with the FFT matrix. Step response, frequency response, Laplace transforms, transfer functions, Bode plots and feedback are absent from all pages read, so the coverage is introductory (inference).

The session page says the session applies linear algebra to electrical networks and the Internet and to results in graph theory; it names no circuit law (fact). The electrical network is an application example for matrices: the course supplies the incidence-matrix view (node-edge matrix A, A^T and A^T C A) that AIPE's DC-circuits module can later use, but teaches none of that module's own content (Ohm's law, KCL, KVL, series/parallel and equivalent circuits), and only one of the 32 lecture sessions touches networks, so background (inference).

du/dt = Au solved through eigenvalue modes generalises the single time constant of the RC and RL responses in AIPE's energy-storage-dynamics module to networks with several storage elements (each mode decays with time constant 1/|eigenvalue|); the course teaches the mathematics only and no capacitor or inductor circuit appears on the pages read, so background (inference).

Elimination and LU are the algorithms behind every numerical linear solver AIPE's computation module uses. The home page names a selection of Java demonstrations and a MATLAB-coded figure, but no demonstration is linked on any page read, and no programming, step-size or numerical-error topic appears on the pages read, so background only (inference).
The exp(At) session extends the scalar exponential solution of dy/dt = ky to systems; the syllabus states that calculus is not needed for the course. Tangential to AIPE's calculus module (inference).

Complex vectors and matrices and the Fourier matrix are the algebra behind phasors and harmonic analysis in AIPE's waveforms/AC module, but the course never treats sinusoidal steady state or impedance; tangential (inference). Evidence note: 'Markov Matrices; Fourier Series' is a Unit II title listed on https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/pages/least-squares-determinants-and-eigenvalues/ and appears on the cited Unit III page only in the course navigation.

State-space averaged converter models are matrix ODEs whose poles are eigenvalues; the course supplies that toolset but never mentions converters, linearisation of switching systems or transfer functions. Assumed mathematics for AIPE's converter-modelling module (inference). Evidence note: the Unit III titles 'Similar Matrices and Jordan Form' and 'Symmetric Matrices and Positive Definiteness' are listed on https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/pages/positive-definite-matrices-and-applications/ and appear on the cited Unit II page only in the course navigation.

mit_topics: Solving Ax = b: Row Reduced Form R
mapped_modules.rationale: Solving Ax = b by elimination/LU and describing a network by its incidence matrix are the linear-algebra prerequisites of the Newton-Raphson power-flow iteration and the Ybus formulation; power flow itself is not on any page read (inference).

Small-signal (modal) stability analysis of grids rests on eigenvalues of a linearised state matrix and on quadratic (energy/Lyapunov-type) forms; the course teaches the mathematics but no power-system application appears on the pages read (inference). Evidence note: the Unit III titles 'Symmetric Matrices and Positive Definiteness' and 'Positive Definite Matrices and Minima' are listed on https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011/pages/positive-definite-matrices-and-applications/ and appear on the cited Unit II page only in the course navigation.

The Fortescue symmetrical-components transform is the 3x3 Fourier (DFT) matrix, and sequence networks arise from a change of basis that diagonalises a balanced impedance matrix; the course teaches complex matrices, the Fourier matrix and change of basis as mathematics and never applies them to three-phase quantities or faults (inference).

The Clarke/Park (dq0) transformations used in grid-converter current control are changes of basis (a rotation matrix applied to three-phase quantities), and stationary-frame complex-vector notation rests on complex matrices; the course teaches change of basis, linear transformations and complex matrices without any three-phase or converter application (inference).

concepts_missing_in_aipe: Vector spaces, subspaces, span, linear independence, basis and dimension (AIPE has the f.linear-algebra module, legacy F09, but no lesson yet; the module summary names only systems of linear equations, matrices and state-space descriptions)
The four fundamental subspaces (column space, nullspace, row space, left nullspace) and rank

Solution methods for Ax = b: Gaussian elimination, pivots, row reduced echelon form, special solutions, solvability conditions and the complete solution (the f.linear-algebra summary names systems of linear equations and the G2 gate asks for solving a small linear system, but no method is named and no lesson exists)
Matrix inverses, transposes, permutation matrices, LU factorization and block matrices
Orthogonal vectors and subspaces, projections and projection matrices, least-squares fitting via A^T A
Orthogonal matrices and Gram-Schmidt orthogonalisation (QR)
Determinants: properties, cofactor formulas, Cramer's rule, volume interpretation
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalization, powers of a matrix, Markov matrices

Matrix exponential exp(At) and the solution of linear systems of differential equations: state-space descriptions are already named in the f.linear-algebra summary; what is missing is their solution, exp(At), eigenvalue modes and the response of du/dt = Au

Fourier series as orthogonal expansions, complex vectors and matrices (Hermitian, unitary) and the FFT matrix: complex numbers appear in the f.ac summary and harmonics in pe.rectifiers and pe.inverters, but none of these linear-algebra formulations is named in any module summary
Symmetric matrices, positive definite matrices, quadratic forms and minima
Similar matrices and Jordan form
Singular value decomposition, pseudoinverse, left and right inverses
Linear transformations, their matrices and change of basis (with image compression as application)

Graphs and node-edge incidence matrices as the matrix description of electrical networks: the f.linear-algebra summary names node equations and f.dc-circuits teaches KCL/KVL, but the incidence-matrix formulation of those node equations (A, A^T, A^T C A) appears in no module summary
modern_gaps_not_covered_by_mit: State-space models with inputs and outputs (A, B, C, D matrices), controllability/observability, and state-space averaging of switching converters

Discretisation of a continuous model (Ad = exp(A Ts)), discrete-time state space with inputs, and the z-transform needed for digital control; the course does treat the autonomous recursion u(k+1) = A u(k) in 'Diagonalization and Powers of A'
Laplace transform, transfer functions, poles/zeros and Bode plots linking matrix eigenvalues to frequency response (taught in MIT 18.03 / 6.003, not 18.06)

Numerical linear algebra in practice: floating-point rounding, conditioning, sparse matrices and sparse LU or iterative solvers for large networks, implemented with NumPy/SciPy (the course pages mention only MATLAB and Java demonstrations)
Nonlinear systems: Jacobians and Newton-Raphson iteration (power flow), nonlinear least squares and parameter identification
Recursive least squares and Kalman-type state estimation (grid state estimation, battery state-of-charge estimation)
Three-phase transformations as change of basis: Clarke/Park (dq0) and symmetrical components (Fortescue); the course's change-of-basis and complex-matrix material is not applied to them
Admittance (Ybus) and impedance matrix formulation of AC networks with complex phasor entries
Modal and participation-factor analysis for small-signal stability of converter-dominated grids

Data-driven uses in power and energy (PCA of measurement data, regression on PV/wind resource data): least squares is taught as fitting curves to data (Unit II description) and change of basis is applied to image compression, but neither is applied to power or energy measurement data

Lyapunov energy functions for stability of dynamic systems and quadratic cost functions in control design; the course covers quadratic forms, positive definiteness and minima as mathematics ('Positive Definite Matrices and Minima') without the stability or control application
recommended_lessons: la-01-node-equations-as-ax-b (f.linear-algebra, f.dc-circuits): write the KCL node equations of a resistive network as Ax = b, solve by elimination and interpret singular cases such as floating nodes

la-02-incidence-matrix-of-a-network (f.linear-algebra, f.dc-circuits): node-edge incidence matrix, KVL as potential differences A v, KCL as A^T y = 0, conductance matrix A^T C A; original counterpart to the MIT 'Graphs, Networks, Incidence Matrices' session that uses AIPE's own network examples, figures and problems and links to the MIT session page without reproducing its examples or problem set
la-03-rank-nullspace-and-solvability (f.linear-algebra): rank and the four subspaces applied to circuit and measurement equations; when a system has none, one or many solutions

la-04-least-squares-fitting-of-measurements (f.linear-algebra, re.pv, f.magnetism): fit resistor V-I or PV I-V data by projection; residuals, orthogonality and model error; tagged re.pv for the PV I-V example and f.magnetism because the lesson treats measurement range and error, which the taxonomy places in that module
la-05-eigenvalues-and-the-natural-response (f.linear-algebra, f.dynamics, f.signals): eigenvalues of an LC/RLC filter state matrix as poles, damping and oscillation frequency
la-06-matrix-exponential-and-state-space-response (f.linear-algebra, f.signals): x(t) = exp(At) x0 for a second-order filter, then discretisation x[k+1] = exp(A Ts) x[k] for digital control
la-07-energy-as-a-quadratic-form (f.linear-algebra): stored energy 1/2 x^T P x, positive definiteness and what it says about stability
la-08-svd-and-pseudoinverse-for-measurement-data (f.linear-algebra, f.computation): SVD of a measurement matrix, rank reduction and least squares via the pseudoinverse
la-09-change-of-basis-for-three-phase-quantities (f.linear-algebra, ps.three-phase, ps.faults, ps.grid-converters): Clarke/Park and symmetrical components as change-of-basis and similarity transforms
num-01-matrix-numerics-with-numpy (f.computation, f.linear-algebra): LU versus numpy.linalg.solve, condition numbers and rounding error on nearly singular nodal matrices
recommended_simulations: Python/NumPy: resistive ladder network - build the incidence matrix A and conductance matrix C, solve (A^T C A) v = f for node voltages, and cross-check against an ngspice .op run of the same netlist
Python/SciPy + ngspice: LC/RLC filter state-space model - eigenvalues of A as R, L, C vary; step response via scipy.linalg.expm overlaid on an ngspice .tran of the same filter
Python/NumPy: least-squares fit (numpy.linalg.lstsq) of synthetic or measured diode/PV I-V data; verify the residual is orthogonal to the column space and compare with the pseudoinverse solution
Python: hand-written Gaussian elimination/LU with partial pivoting versus numpy.linalg.solve; condition-number sweep on a nearly singular nodal matrix and error versus float32/float64

Python + ngspice: eigenvalues of an averaged small-signal buck converter state matrix (pe.modelling) versus load and capacitor ESR; compare the predicted ringing frequency and damping with a switching simulation
Python: discretisation Ad = expm(A Ts) and the discrete state update versus the continuous solution; effect of sample time Ts (links to the f.computation step-size topic)
Python/NumPy: SVD/PCA of a synthetic matrix of bus-voltage snapshots or converter waveforms; fraction of energy captured by the leading singular values
Python/NumPy: Fortescue symmetrical-components transform as the 3x3 DFT matrix - verify it diagonalises a balanced circulant impedance matrix; Clarke/Park rotation of a three-phase set

course_facts.scope_summary: MIT 2.60J Fundamentals of Advanced Energy Conversion (Spring 2020; the OCW pages display only the number 2.60J, while the catalogue's verified OCW metadata lists the cross-listings 2.62J, 10.390J, 10.392J and 22.40J; instructor Prof. Ahmed F. Ghoniem; listed level Undergraduate, with the syllabus adding that a graduate version runs on identical content with a heavier assignment load) uses thermodynamics, chemical and electrochemical thermodynamics and transport to examine how energy is converted and stored, judging each process mainly by its efficiency, its delivered performance and its environmental footprint. The 26-session schedule moves from thermodynamic tools for conversion efficiency, gas mixtures, liquefaction and chemical thermodynamics into electrochemistry (electrochemical thermodynamics, fuel cells, electrolysis, batteries), then surveys conversion technologies (solar photovoltaics, thermo-mechanical conversion, solar thermal, geothermal, gas separation and CO2 capture, energy-system modeling, wind, materials, biomass) and closes with energy storage and term-project presentations; sessions 13 and 14 were cancelled, so 23 lecture-note sessions and one presentation session were held. The term project is a design analysis of a storage technology for a chosen application and scale. It is a thermal/chemical energy-conversion course: no power-electronics, electric-machine or grid topics are named in the lecture titles (lecture 21, Energy System Modeling and Examples, was not opened).
stated_prerequisites: MIT 2.006 Thermal-Fluids Engineering II, or the pair 2.051 Introduction to Heat Transfer plus 2.06 Fluid Dynamics, or the instructor's permission (syllabus page).

No other prerequisite is stated, and the syllabus page lists no textbook or reading list (the syllabus note on undergraduate versus graduate workload is recorded in scope_summary and access_limitations, not as a prerequisite).

mapped_modules.rationale: The course's central subject is the thermodynamic analysis of energy conversion processes and their efficiency limits across fossil, nuclear and renewable resources (course description and objectives on the syllabus page, https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-60j-fundamentals-of-advanced-energy-conversion-spring-2020/pages/syllabus/). This matches AIPE's re.conversion module (energy, power and efficiency across physical conversion processes; resources and limits of renewable energy) and the course goes far deeper than AIPE's module on the thermal and chemical side. Lectures 3, 19 and 20 (gas-mixture thermodynamics and separation, gas separation technologies, CO2 capture and storage) sit under re.conversion only as thermodynamic work-of-separation content, since no other taxonomy module can host them; their technology content is listed in concepts_missing_in_aipe. All titles appear on the lecture-notes page except that the lecture 20 title is recorded in the form rendered on the calendar page (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-60j-fundamentals-of-advanced-energy-conversion-spring-2020/pages/calendar/), because the lecture-notes page shows an unprocessed subscript shortcode.

mit_topics: Storage, Stationary or Mobile, at Different Scales
mapped_modules.rationale: Five of the 23 delivered lecture titles on the lecture-notes page (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-60j-fundamentals-of-advanced-energy-conversion-spring-2020/pages/lecture-notes/) contain the word storage (lectures 4, 10, 11, 20 and 25); four of these concern energy or gas storage, while lecture 20 (CO2 Capture and Storage) uses the word in the geological-sequestration sense and is not counted here. In addition the term project, worth 34% of the grade, is entirely a storage design analysis (thermal, chemical, electrical or mechanical storage for an application at a chosen scale, per the projects page). That weight is why 'partial' rather than 'introductory' is chosen, and 'core' would be arguable; 'partial' is kept because the course's central thread is conversion and because the treatment is thermodynamic/chemical (gas storage, hydrogen, batteries) rather than AIPE's emphasis on energy/power ratings and bidirectional converter interfaces, which the listed titles do not mention.

Lectures 8-11 form an electrochemistry block covering cell thermodynamics and electrochemical converters (fuel cells, electrolysers, batteries), which is the physics underpinning AIPE's re.batteries module (electrochemical cells, chemistries). State of charge, ageing and battery management systems do not appear in any title, so coverage is partial (inference from titles only).

A single lecture (12) on solar photovoltaics within a survey of conversion technologies; depth within the lecture is unknown (PDF not opened). The module's I-V characteristic, maximum power point and irradiance/temperature effects are not evidenced by the title.

A single lecture (22) on wind energy. Given the course's thermodynamic framing, it most plausibly covers the resource and power-in-the-wind side of AIPE's re.wind module; generators and back-to-back converters are not evidenced by the title (inference).

mit_topics: Storage, Stationary or Mobile, at Different Scales
mapped_modules.rationale: The term project asks students to pick a storage technology, match it to an application anywhere from a bicycle or car up to a building, a grid or a whole country, and carry out a design analysis that weighs the intended power level and rival technologies, with economic and policy constraints allowed only as a brief aside; lecture 21 (title on the lecture-notes page, https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-60j-fundamentals-of-advanced-energy-conversion-spring-2020/pages/lecture-notes/) is an energy-system modeling lecture. This is a design-analysis exercise in the spirit of AIPE's re.system-design but without renewable-system sizing or component selection in the electrical sense.

Not taught as a subject (inference from titles and objectives).

recommended_lessons: re.conversion: Energy conversion chains and efficiency: from fuel or resource to electricity, with first-law efficiency of each stage and overall efficiency of the chain
re.conversion: Why heat engines have a ceiling: Carnot and practical limits of thermo-mechanical conversion, and what that means for solar thermal, geothermal and biomass plants
re.conversion: Minimum work to separate a gas mixture, as the physics behind CO2 capture and air separation energy penalties
re.storage: Comparing storage technologies (thermal, chemical, electrochemical, mechanical) by energy density, power density and round-trip efficiency
re.storage: Hydrogen as a storage pathway: electrolysis, compression or liquefaction, and fuel-cell reconversion, with the round-trip efficiency budget
re.storage: Compressed and liquefied gas storage: the work of compression and liquefaction versus stored energy
re.batteries: From electrochemical thermodynamics to cell voltage: open-circuit voltage, reaction energy and theoretical energy density
re.batteries: Electrochemical converters at finite current: polarisation losses in fuel cells, electrolysers and batteries and the resulting efficiency
re.pv: Photovoltaics as an energy-conversion process: spectrum, bandgap and conversion efficiency limits before the circuit view
re.wind: Power in the wind and the Betz limit as the resource-side foundation of re.wind
re.system-design: A term-project style design analysis: choose a storage technology for an application and scale, and justify it with efficiency, power range and competing options
recommended_simulations: re.conversion: Python (NumPy + CoolProp): Carnot, Rankine and Brayton cycle efficiency versus source temperature and pressure ratio, reproducing the 'tools to analyze conversion efficiency' theme with open property data
re.conversion: Python: minimum isothermal work of separation of an ideal-gas mixture versus concentration (Gibbs free energy of mixing), applied to CO2 capture from flue gas and to air separation
re.storage: Python: compression and liquefaction work for hydrogen and methane storage (isothermal versus multi-stage adiabatic compression) and the fraction of stored heating value it consumes
re.storage: Python: hydrogen round-trip efficiency chain calculator (electrolyser efficiency, compression or liquefaction penalty, fuel-cell efficiency) with sensitivity plots

re.batteries: Python: fuel-cell and electrolyser polarisation curve model (Nernst voltage, Butler-Volmer activation loss, ohmic loss, concentration loss) giving power density and efficiency versus current density
re.batteries: Python: battery open-circuit voltage and internal-resistance discharge model giving voltage, delivered energy and round-trip efficiency versus C-rate
re.batteries: ngspice: Thevenin equivalent-circuit battery model (OCV source, series resistance, RC pair) discharge and charge transients, checked against the Python round-trip efficiency
re.pv: Python: single-diode PV cell model with I-V and P-V curves versus irradiance and temperature; ngspice: single-diode PV cell netlist with a DC sweep as a cross-check
re.wind: Python: wind power density, Betz limit and a Weibull wind distribution giving annual energy yield for a turbine power curve
re.storage: Python: Ragone-style comparison chart of storage technologies (specific energy versus specific power, round-trip efficiency) from openly stated parameters
re.system-design: Python: energy-system efficiency chain model for a fuel-to-electricity-to-storage-to-load path, mirroring the storage term project
prerequisite_relationships: re.conversion requires f.quantities and f.calculus (the course assumes thermal-fluids engineering, heat transfer and fluid dynamics as stated prerequisites, and AIPE's thermodynamic lessons should assume unit-level algebra and calculus). Agrees with taxonomy.json, where re.conversion requires exactly f.quantities and f.calculus.

re.storage builds on re.conversion (lecture 4 on liquefaction and gas storage follows the gas-mixture thermodynamics of lecture 3; lectures 10, 11 and 25 follow the full thermodynamics block of lectures 2-7; the storage term project is posted at lecture 4 and selected by lecture 7 per the calendar, with the projects page asking for topic selection by lecture 5). Difference from taxonomy: re.storage currently requires only pe.topologies and re.conversion lists re.storage as related; this course supports adding re.conversion as a thermodynamic prerequisite of re.storage (proposed taxonomy change, not an existing requirement).

re.batteries requires an electrochemical-thermodynamics foundation before finite-current behaviour (lecture 8 precedes lectures 9-11) and in AIPE should follow re.storage, which agrees with taxonomy (re.batteries requires re.storage). f.dc-circuits is not among re.batteries' listed requirements; the finite-current treatment in lectures 9-11 supports naming it as related (proposed, not existing).

re.pv and re.wind are treated as applications after the conversion fundamentals (lectures 12 and 22 come after the thermodynamics block), consistent with taxonomy listing re.conversion as related to re.pv and re.wind; no change proposed.

re.system-design (term project) requires re.conversion and re.storage (midterm project report at lecture 15 after the thermodynamics and storage block; final report at lecture 25). Agrees with taxonomy on re.storage; re.conversion is not among the taxonomy requires (re.pv-systems, re.storage, re.integration) and is proposed here as a justified addition; re.pv-systems and re.integration are not evidenced by this course.

f.computation supports some homework assignments (the Tools page says EES is used for some of them; which ones is not known because the PDFs were not opened), so AIPE's Python property-calculation lesson should come before the thermodynamic efficiency lessons (inference). Taxonomy does not list f.computation among re.conversion requires, and f.computation itself requires f.dynamics (a circuits module), so a module-level requirement would pull circuits content ahead of thermodynamics; recommend adding f.computation as related to re.conversion, or making the Python property-calculation lesson a lesson-level prerequisite of the cycle-efficiency simulations, rather than a module-level requirement.

courses.facts_vs_inferences: FACTS (read directly from MIT OCW HTML pages on 2026-10-20, all HTTP 200, re-fetched during finalisation with the same result): course title, course number 2.60J (the only number shown on the HTML pages), Spring 2020, level Undergraduate, instructor Prof. Ahmed F. Ghoniem, departments (Mechanical Engineering, Chemical Engineering, Nuclear Science and Engineering), topic tags and the four learning resource types (home page); stated prerequisites (2.006, or 2.051 plus 2.06, or instructor permission), the note that undergraduate and graduate versions differ only in workload, four course objectives, grading split (6 assignments 66%, term report 34% = 9% + 20% + 5%) and the COVID-19 schedule note (syllabus); the 26-session outline with titles and key dates, lectures 13-14 cancelled, project posted at session 4, selected at 7, midterm report due at 15, final report due at 25, presentations at 26 (calendar, with titles identical to the lecture-notes page); 23 lecture-note PDFs, with lectures 21 and 23 credited to named contributors and marked used with permission, and five titles containing the word storage (lectures 4, 10, 11, 20, 25) (lecture-notes page); 5 homework PDFs plus 5 solution PDFs, one of six cancelled (assignments page); the term-project topic on storage at different scales, the hydrogen-as-transportation-fuel example theme, the rule that economic and policy aspects may be addressed only briefly, and the lecture-tied milestones (projects page); EES used for some homework assignments with 3 tutorial PDFs credited to a named contributor (tools page). No textbook is listed on the syllabus and no video or readings page exists. The cross-listed numbers 2.62J, 10.390J, 10.392J and 22.40J are taken from the catalogue record references/mit-ocw-catalogue.json (verified.course_numbers, sourced from OCW course metadata via data.json), not from the fetched HTML pages. INFERENCES (my judgement): all coverage levels and module assignments; the depth attributed to single-lecture topics (PV, wind) and to the storage lectures, since only titles were read and no PDF was opened; the assumption that the wind lecture is resource-side rather than generator/converter-side; the reading of lecture 20's 'storage' as geological CO2 storage; the characterisation of lecture 21 as technology-level rather than grid power-flow modeling; the background mappings to f.quantities, f.calculus, f.dc-circuits and f.computation; which homework assignments use EES; the recommended lessons, simulations and prerequisite ordering, which are derived from the lecture sequence and project milestones; the proposed taxonomy differences (re.conversion as a prerequisite of re.storage and of re.system-design, f.computation as related to re.conversion, f.dc-circuits as related to re.batteries); and the list of concepts missing in AIPE, which is drawn from lecture titles and the course description. Two cautions: the course description's 'combined and hybrid power cycles' refers to thermodynamic power cycles and is deliberately not mapped to AIPE's re.hybrid-systems (microgrids); and none of the modern grid or power-electronics topics listed under gaps are attributed to this course, since no page lists them. The catalogue's academic_level 'graduate' versus OCW's 'Undergraduate' is a recorded discrepancy explained by the syllabus note, not resolved here.

course_facts.scope_summary: MIT 2.627 Fundamentals of Photovoltaics (Fall 2013; the OCW data.json also records the companion number 2.626, which no fetched HTML page shows) is an elective in MIT's undergraduate Energy Studies Minor covering the physics of photovoltaic conversion, how cells are made and evaluated, and the market and policy context in which PV technologies compete. The Fall 2013 calendar has 26 sessions in three units: Unit 1 device fundamentals (solar resource, light management, charge excitation, separation, transport and collection, a 1D device model, materials properties), Unit 2 commercial and emerging technologies (wafer silicon, thin films, efficiency limits, emerging concepts, a Fraunhofer CSE field trip), and Unit 3 cross-cutting themes (efficiency-loss troubleshooting; cost and manufacturability with an industry guest lecture on silicon cell manufacturing costs; modules, systems and reliability; price, markets and subsidies; a DOE SunShot guest lecture; PV innovation; PV in developing countries). Lectures 2-12 ran as a flipped classroom using Fall 2011 lecture videos. Hands-on elements are an Arduino-sourcemeter I-V measurement lab, a manufacturing-line simulation assignment using external Virtual MES software, and a team project that weighs technology, economics, policy and social aspects.
stated_prerequisites: The syllabus has no prerequisites section, and the word prerequisite does not occur on the syllabus or the home page. In a student-professor contract note the instructor acknowledges that enrolees differ widely in prior preparation and seniority and undertakes to pitch the course so that newcomers are not left behind and experienced students are not bored.
An ungraded Background Assessment Quiz is assigned at Lecture 1 (Calendar & Readings page; the PDF is listed on the Readings page) to gauge prior knowledge rather than to gate entry.

The syllabus names a free online PV textbook (Honsberg and Bowden, Photovoltaics: Devices, Systems and Applications CD-ROM) as the main text and lists 13 reference books and articles grouped under solar cells, solid-state physics, semiconductor device characterization, review articles and specialty books. AIPE inference, not stated on any page: the assigned pn-junction and device-physics readings presuppose some comfort with basic semiconductor concepts.

mapped_modules.rationale: Unit 1 sessions Lec 3-9 plus Lec 14 (efficiency limits) and Lec 17 (loss troubleshooting) on the 2013 calendar are the device-level content that AIPE's 'Solar PV fundamentals' module summarises: photovoltaic conversion, the I-V characteristic and the material and temperature effects behind it. The syllabus learning objective asks students to describe the governing phenomena phenomenologically, but the session titles, the assigned Green chapters on device physics and the lecture-note items (pn-junction worksheet, ideal diode equation problems, 'Toward a 1D Device Model' videos) take the treatment to semiconductor-device depth that AIPE's module does not attempt, so the course sets the ceiling of depth rather than the floor. The Fall 2011 videos L3-L9 were assigned viewing for these sessions; 2011 L14 'PV Efficiency: Measurement and Theoretical Limits' and L16 'Solar Cell Characterization' are published on the lecture-videos gallery (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-627-fundamentals-of-photovoltaics-fall-2013/video_galleries/lecture-videos-slides/) but were not assigned in the 2013 calendar (only lectures 2-12 were), so they support the mapping as published material rather than as 2013 class content. The Lec 7 lab (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-627-fundamentals-of-photovoltaics-fall-2013/pages/calendar-readings/iv-curve-measurement/) measures a real cell's I-V curve with an Arduino sourcemeter. The course stops at measuring I-V and efficiency: no fetched page names the maximum power point, MPPT, a converter, an inverter or the grid, so it supplies the device-side input to AIPE's re.mppt and re.pv-systems without covering them.

mit_topics: Worksheet on pn-junctions under dark and illuminated conditions
In-class Problems on PN Junction Band Formation and Ideal Diode Equation
mapped_modules.rationale: The lecture-notes listing carries a 'Diodes in the Dark' slide deck, a worksheet on pn-junctions under dark and illuminated conditions, a set of in-class problems on pn-junction band formation and the ideal diode equation, and a 'Lecture 7 - Device Fundamentals' deck. Their resource slugs (mit2_627f13_lec05, lec06_handout, lec07_prob, lec07) place them with 2013 sessions 5-7; this is read from the anchor URLs, not from the visible titles. Together with the 'Tutorial: Doping' video (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-627-fundamentals-of-photovoltaics-fall-2013/video_galleries/tutorial-videos/, assigned at Lec 5 on the calendar) this is the physical basis of the simplified diode model in AIPE's 'Basic electronic devices'. Substantial but not central: the course never treats diodes as switching components, and no listed title mentions MOSFETs, losses or ratings.

Lec 1-2 frame solar energy as a low-carbon resource (the syllabus course objectives motivate the course with the scale of low-carbon generation needed by 2030) and quantify the solar resource, with the PVCDROM appendix 'Standard Solar Spectra' as reading and the NREL PVWatts Calculator as the Session 2 in-class activity; Lec 14 bounds conversion efficiency theoretically. These are the resource-and-limits half of AIPE's 'Energy conversion fundamentals'; the course treats no other conversion process (wind, thermal, storage), so coverage is partial. taxonomy.json lists re.conversion as related to re.pv, not as a prerequisite.

The words inverter and grid appear on none of the eleven fetched pages, so two of the three clauses of AIPE's 'PV systems, inverters and grid interfaces' summary (string and central inverters; grid-connected and off-grid systems) are unserved. One session of 26 plus a tour and a calculator exercise is introductory, not partial, coverage.

mapped_modules.rationale: Unit 3 and the syllabus learning objective of developing a cost model give substantial treatment of PV economics: Lec 18 'Cost and Manufacturability' with an industry guest lecture on silicon cell manufacturing costs and three cost-modelling readings listed on the calendar (a 2012 cost-analysis framework for crystalline silicon, a 2013 IEEE Journal of Photovoltaics paper whose title includes 'Minimum Sustainable Price', and a 2013 paper on regional drivers of PV manufacturing), Lec 20 price, markets and subsidies, the Lec 21 DOE SunShot guest lecture and Lec 22 PV innovation, backed by the 2011 videos L18-L19 'Cost, Price, Markets, & Support Mechanisms' (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-627-fundamentals-of-photovoltaics-fall-2013/video_galleries/lecture-videos-slides/). The team project (30% of the grade on the syllabus, https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-627-fundamentals-of-photovoltaics-fall-2013/pages/syllabus/; described on the assignments page) weighs technology, economics, policy and social aspects. This maps to the economics strand of AIPE's 'Renewable energy system design' only; sizing, component selection and verification of an installed system are not listed, and the module's other taxonomy prerequisites (re.storage, re.integration) have no content here.

mapped_modules.rationale: Only the measurement half of AIPE's 'Magnetism and measurement' applies, and only as an assumed skill: the Fall 2011 quizzes hand students measured data to interpret (EQE data, I-V curves with calculated resistances, Suns-Voc data), and the Lec 7 lab (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-627-fundamentals-of-photovoltaics-fall-2013/pages/calendar-readings/iv-curve-measurement/) measures a cell's I-V curve with a homemade Arduino sourcemeter. The lab page states its purpose in one sentence and otherwise gives driver-installation steps; measurement range, sampling, calibration and error are not discussed on any fetched page, and nothing magnetic appears. The 2011 video L16 'Solar Cell Characterization' (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-627-fundamentals-of-photovoltaics-fall-2013/video_galleries/lecture-videos-slides/) is the closest taught content, but it is device characterization, not measurement technique as AIPE's module frames it.

mit_topics: Dark and Illuminated I-V Measurement Data
Hypothesis Testing of New Wafer Supplies
mapped_modules.rationale: Problem set 3 is built on a measured dark and illuminated I-V data file, and the manufacturing-line challenge is an assignment on hypothesis testing of new wafer supplies run in the external Virtual MES simulator (the page heading is 'Manufacturing Simulation'; the assignment title is listed separately), so students analyse data and run a simulation, which exercises the skills of AIPE's 'Computation and numerics'. None of that module's content (scripts, plots, numerical integration, step size, numerical error) is taught by any listed item, so the module is assumed background, consistent with how this record treats f.dc-circuits and f.electromagnetism. The Session 2 PVWatts Calculator activity (calendar page) and the Suns-Voc quiz data (quizzes page) are further data-driven exercises.

The course assumes I-V curves, resistance, voltage-current-power relations and equivalent-circuit thinking rather than teaching them: Lec 9 charge collection, contacts and metallization is paired with the Schroder review of solar cell contact resistance as the Lec 7 reading, and the Lec 7 lab measures an I-V curve. The Quiz 2.2 data title 'IV curves, calculated resistances data' (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-627-fundamentals-of-photovoltaics-fall-2013/pages/quizzes/) points the same way. AIPE's 'DC circuits' is therefore a background prerequisite that the solar-cell equivalent circuit can later exercise.

Charge, the electric field in a junction, photon energy and light absorption are used from Lec 3-4 onward (the 2011 video 'Light Absorption and Optical Losses' assigned for Lec 3, the Lec 4 session 'Charge Excitation', and the 'Tutorial: Photoconductivity' video assigned at Lec 5), and the syllabus (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-627-fundamentals-of-photovoltaics-fall-2013/pages/syllabus/) points to solid-state physics reference books rather than teaching introductory physics. AIPE's 'Electricity and magnetism' is assumed background; the course's optics and semiconductor content goes beyond what that module covers.

concepts_missing_in_aipe: Semiconductor device physics of solar cells at the depth of a 1D device model: band gap and absorption coefficient, generation and recombination, carrier lifetime and diffusion length, drift and diffusion in the junction (AIPE re.pv and the existing solar-pv-fundamentals lesson stay at the current-source-plus-diode level).
Light management and optical losses: surface texturing, anti-reflection, reflection and absorption losses (course Lec 3, 2011 video L3, Texturing tutorial).

The PV-specific, band-gap-dependent detailed-balance efficiency limit and a systematic loss-mechanism troubleshooting method (course Lec 14 'Theoretical Photoelectric Efficiency Limits', Lec 17 'Troubleshooting Photoelectric Conversion Efficiency Losses'). re.conversion's summary names the generic limits of renewable energy, but no module summary names the PV limit or loss analysis; the detailed-balance naming is AIPE's, the MIT pages say only 'Theoretical Photoelectric Efficiency Limits'.

Solar-cell characterization beyond the I-V curve that re.pv already names: dark-versus-illuminated I-V comparison, external quantum efficiency, Suns-Voc, contact resistance (Schroder review reading) and resistance extraction from measured I-V data (Quiz 2.2 data title 'IV curves, calculated resistances'; no page names shunt resistance) (2011 video L16, Quiz 1 and Quiz 2 data files).
Charge collection, contacts and metallization of cells (course Lec 9, 2011 video L9 'Charge Extraction').

PV technology landscape and manufacturing: wafer-silicon feedstock, crystal growth and wafering, thin-film materials and manufacturing, advanced and emerging concepts, organics and multijunction devices (lecture-note deck 'Organics and Multijunction Devices', 2011 video L15 'Advanced Concepts'), and perovskites as 2013 student project topics.

PV manufacturing cost and manufacturability modelling, minimum sustainable price (Lec 18 reading title), and a manufacturing-line simulation with statistical hypothesis testing (Virtual MES assignment).

Markets, price, subsidies and support mechanisms, R&D investment and innovation dynamics, PV in developing countries, and technology risk and life-cycle analysis (course description and syllabus synopsis).
A hands-on I-V measurement lab built around a low-cost Arduino sourcemeter (course Lec 7 lab page).
modern_gaps_not_covered_by_mit: PV inverters and DC-DC stages: MPPT algorithms, string, central and micro-inverter and power-optimizer architectures (no fetched page names MPP, MPPT, a converter or an inverter).
Grid-connected PV behaviour: anti-islanding, grid codes, reactive-power and ride-through requirements, inverter-based-resource stability (the word grid appears on no fetched page).

Post-2013 cell and module technologies and their commercial status: PERC, TOPCon, silicon heterojunction and bifacial modules, and the commercial maturity of perovskite-silicon tandems. The course covers perovskites only as two 2013 student project topics, and treats organics and multijunction devices (lecture-note deck of that title) and emerging or advanced concepts (Lec 15, 2011 video L15) at 2011-2013 depth.
PV combined with storage, hybrid systems, forecasting and energy management (no storage or forecasting title is listed).

Scriptable open-source PV system modelling: pvlib-style irradiance transposition, module temperature models, performance ratio and degradation analysis from field data, plus post-2013 LCOE and cost data. The course's Session 2 PVWatts Calculator activity is a PV-system yield model, and its cost and market data are 2011-2013 vintage.

System-level safety and reliability practice as it stands today: arc-fault and rapid-shutdown requirements, potential-induced degradation and soiling analytics with modern field data. The course's Lec 19 covers module and system reliability at 2011-2013 level.

prerequisite_relationships: re.pv requires f.electronics (pn-junction diode behaviour, ideal diode equation) and f.dc-circuits (I-V curves, resistance, power), as taxonomy.json already states: the course builds Lec 4-9 charge excitation, separation and collection on diode physics and equivalent-circuit reasoning before any technology lecture.

re.pv benefits from re.conversion (solar resource and spectrum) taught first: the course places 'The Solar Resource' (Lec 2) before light absorption and device physics (Lec 3-9), and the renewable-energy-intro learning path puts the conversion stage before the pv stage. taxonomy.json lists re.conversion only as related to re.pv (re.pv.requires = f.electronics, f.dc-circuits); this record keeps it as recommended-before and does not change the taxonomy. Proposed taxonomy change for maintainers to consider: add re.conversion to re.pv.requires.

re.pv-systems requires re.pv: modules, systems and reliability (Lec 19 / 2011 video L17) come only after the device-fundamentals and technology units. The module's other taxonomy prerequisites (pe.inverters, ps.grid-converters) are not evidenced by this course.

re.system-design (economics strand) requires re.pv and re.pv-systems: cost and manufacturability, price, markets and subsidies (Lec 18, 20-22) form Unit 3 after Units 1-2 and feed the team project. taxonomy re.system-design.requires = [re.pv-systems, re.storage, re.integration]; this course evidences only the re.pv-systems dependency and offers no storage or grid-integration content, so re.storage and re.integration remain taxonomy-level prerequisites not supported by this source.

re.mppt (taxonomy: requires re.pv and pe.buck) is not evidenced by this course, which stops at measuring the I-V curve and efficiency and never names the maximum power point; the existing lesson solar-pv-fundamentals covers re.mppt as an AIPE extension with pe.buck as the tracking converter.

f.magnetism (measurement half) and f.computation are assumed by the course's lab, data-driven problem sets and quizzes (I-V measurement lab at Lec 7, Problem set 3 data file, Quiz 1-2 data files, Virtual MES simulation) and are mapped as background rather than taught.

f.electromagnetism is a background prerequisite: the syllabus has no prerequisites section and an ungraded background quiz is used instead, but charge, fields and light are assumed from general physics.

course_facts.scope_summary: 22.081J Introduction to Sustainable Energy (Fall 2010, undergraduate and graduate, listed under six departments: Nuclear Science and Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, Chemical Engineering, Civil and Environmental Engineering, Urban Studies and Planning, Engineering Systems Division) is a survey course that assesses present and future energy systems from resources through extraction, conversion and end use, judged against engineering, economic, political, social and environmental goals. Part I (sessions 1a-9b) builds a quantitative 'toolbox' (energy units and flows, conversion and efficiency, resource depletion, storage and transmission, systems analysis, electric power sector, electrical system dynamics, economic feasibility, thermodynamics, carbon policy); Part II (10-19b) surveys specific technologies (nuclear, fossil, wind, policy, transport, fusion, carbon management, geothermal, solar PV and thermal, biomass); Part III (20a-25b) covers end use, option assessment and trade-offs (vehicles, biomass LCA, wind system dynamics, electrochemical storage, buildings, probabilistic risk analysis, climate negotiations, hydropower, electricity in Sub-Saharan Africa). Electrical-engineering content is limited to a few sessions on the power grid and system dynamics (7a, 7b, 8a); no session title or listed sub-topic indicates power-electronics or circuit-level content (slides not read, so this is an inference).
stated_prerequisites: The syllabus page lists no formal prerequisite subjects (no prerequisites section appears on the syllabus or home page).

Course description says students learn a quantitative framework for evaluating energy technology proposals; graduate students enrol in the companion 'Sustainable Energy' subject and complete extra assignments and a 20-30 page term paper (paraphrased).

Textbook readings (Tester et al., Sustainable Energy: Choosing Among Options, 2nd ed., MIT Press, 2012) are keyed to individual sessions: chapter or section numbers appear for 22 of the 45 session parts, and a separate 20-item bibliography sits on the Related Resources page (own wording).

The Lectures and Readings page carries a notice that the posted slide decks appear with their authors' permission, and many sessions are guest lectures by external speakers (Harvard Kennedy School, PSEG, Cape Wind, MTechnology), so individual decks may carry third-party restrictions beyond the OCW licence. The course assumes only general undergraduate quantitative skills (units, algebra, basic thermodynamics) rather than circuits or power-electronics modules, so it suits AIPE learners entering the renewable-energy domain before the pe.* modules or the network-analysis track (ps.power-flow, ps.faults, ps.protection). Justified difference: MIT teaches storage technologies and roles (5a, 6b, 21b) and wind fundamentals (5b) with no power-electronics prerequisite, whereas AIPE's re.storage requires pe.topologies and re.wind requires ps.grid-converters (which requires pe.control and ps.three-phase); the survey-level strands of these modules are therefore reachable earlier in MIT's sequence than in AIPE's requires graph. Inference; no requires change proposed, the alternative being to teach those survey strands inside re.conversion.

course_facts.scope_summary: MIT 6.002 (Spring 2007, Prof. Anant Agarwal; the home page states the course materials were created collaboratively with Prof. Jeffrey H. Lang) is MIT's first undergraduate circuits course, built on the lumped circuit abstraction. Over 25 lectures and 26 recitations it moves from resistive network analysis (KVL/KCL, node method, superposition, Thevenin/Norton) through the digital abstraction and MOSFET switch and amplifier models (large- and small-signal), into capacitors, inductors and first- and second-order transients, then sinusoidal steady state, impedance methods and filters, operational-amplifier feedback circuits, and energy and power in digital/CMOS circuits, ending with a lecture on the limits of the lumped abstraction. Five lab assignments (Lab 0 familiarization; Thevenin/Norton equivalents and logic gates; MOSFET amplifiers and first-order circuits; second-order networks; a mixed analog/digital audio playback system), eleven homework sets, two evening quizzes and a final accompany the lectures. The required textbook is Agarwal and Lang's Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits (title recorded only).

MIT 18.03 Differential Equations is listed as a prerequisite on the syllabus page.

Meeting times (2 lectures + 1 recitation per week), 8 course objectives, 16 learning outcomes, 2 stated prerequisites, textbook, homework/lab/quiz/final policies and grading weights (homework 5%, labs 5%, two quizzes 50%, final 40%). prerequisite_relationships: f.dc-circuits and the MIT prerequisites: MIT lists 8.02 (electricity and magnetism) and 18.03 (differential equations) as prerequisites for its circuits course, and L1 derives the lumped abstraction from physics (syllabus, calendar). The AIPE taxonomy deliberately differs: f.dc-circuits requires only f.quantities, f.electromagnetism is 'related' rather than required, and f.calculus is introduced through charging and discharging circuits (the foundations-first-circuits path runs quantities -> dc-circuits -> calculus/dynamics). Recommendation: keep the AIPE order and cite 8.02/18.03 as optional background reading, since AIPE targets learners without university physics.

f.electronics requires f.dc-circuits: the MOS switch (L5) and nonlinear resistors (L6) are introduced only after KVL/KCL, nodal analysis and Thevenin/Norton (L1-L3). Difference from the taxonomy: MIT teaches the MOSFET switch, gate and amplifier models (L5-L12, Lab 1, Lab 2's amplifier part) before any energy-storage element (L13), so the taxonomy requirement f.electronics -> f.dynamics is not supported by MIT's ordering; it is justified only by AIPE's switching-converter aim (switching transients and losses in f.electronics need RC/RL responses). Either keep it with that justification or relax f.electronics.requires to ['f.dc-circuits'].

pe.modelling (linearisation around an operating point) should follow the f.electronics operating-point work: the course introduces nonlinear networks and operating points (L6) before incremental/small-signal analysis (L7, R7), and revisits operating-point and biasing analysis (R8) before the MOSFET amplifier small-signal lectures (L10-L12). This supports placing pe.modelling after the Foundations electronics work and does not contradict the taxonomy's direct requires (pe.topologies, f.signals).

f.dynamics requires f.dc-circuits and f.calculus: first-order circuits (L13) come after all resistive and MOSFET material, second-order systems (L16-L17) after first-order (L13-L14), and course objective 3 presumes students can formulate and solve the differential equations (prerequisite 18.03). Agrees with taxonomy f.dynamics.requires ['f.dc-circuits', 'f.calculus'].

f.ac requires f.dynamics: sinusoidal steady state and impedance (L18-L19) are derived after second-order transients (L16-L17), and R18 previews frequency response. Quiz 2 (Q2) falls between L18, the first sinusoidal-steady-state lecture, and L19 Impedance methods (one day after L18 per the syllabus), so second-order transients and the first SSS lecture are examined together before impedance methods and filters. Agrees with taxonomy f.ac.requires ['f.quantities', 'f.dynamics'].

f.signals requires f.ac: filters, Q and op-amp feedback (L20-L23, R20-R23) build on impedance methods (L19); R22 op-amp filters assume both. Agrees with taxonomy f.signals.requires ['f.dynamics', 'f.ac'].

pe.losses builds on f.dynamics and f.electronics: energy and power in gates and CMOS (L24, R24, R6) use capacitor energy and MOSFET switch models. The taxonomy's direct requires for pe.losses are pe.devices and pe.topologies; f.electronics and f.dynamics are upstream of those, so this relationship is consistent with but weaker than the taxonomy, and L24/R24 map to a precursor of pe.losses rather than to its converter content.

pe.devices requires f.electronics: the switch-resistor model (L5, R5) and the 2N7000 datasheet row in Lab 1 are the course's entry point to a real switch. Agrees with taxonomy pe.devices.requires ['f.electronics'].

Measurement practice (the measurement half of f.magnetism) versus the taxonomy: the taxonomy sequences f.magnetism after f.dynamics and f.electronics, but MIT's lab key dates (Lab 0 out L1, due 1 day before L3; Lab 1 out R4a, due R8; Lab 2 out L11, due R15; Lab 3 out L15, due R20; Lab 4 out L18, due R23) show instrument use and discrepancy analysis starting as soon as the resistive material is done. AIPE should either split measurement practice into early lab exercises attached to f.dc-circuits/f.dynamics or keep f.magnetism's requires and treat Labs 0-1 as f.dc-circuits lab content.

course_facts.scope_summary: MIT 6.003 Signals and Systems (Fall 2011, undergraduate, Prof. Dennis Freeman) is a one-semester course in signal and LTI-system analysis that develops the discrete-time and continuous-time cases side by side. The syllabus groups the material into two strands: ways of representing signals (singularity functions, complex exponentials, the Fourier, Laplace and Z transforms, and sampling) and ways of representing linear time-invariant systems (block diagrams, difference or differential equations, system functions with their poles and zeros, convolution sums and integrals, and the impulse, step and frequency responses). The 25 lecture titles run from DT and CT systems through the Z and Laplace transforms, convolution, frequency response, Bode plots and feedback/control to the four Fourier representations, sampling and quantization, modulation and an Audio CD capstone; MIT names control, communications and signal processing as application areas. Format stated on the syllabus: two one-hour lectures and two one-hour recitations per week, graded from three midterms (10%, 15%, 20%), a final exam (40%) and homework, participation and other factors (15%). No lecture, reading, supplementary-note or exam title on the pages read mentions power circuits or converters; nothing is asserted about lecture content beyond those titles.
stated_prerequisites: The syllabus lists a single prerequisite: MIT subject 6.02 (Introduction to EECS II)

No other prerequisite, corequisite or required mathematics background is listed on the syllabus or the course home page (the textbook, meeting format and grading are recorded under teaching_resources and scope_summary, not as prerequisites)

mapped_modules.rationale: AIPE f.signals is defined as LTI systems, step and frequency response, Laplace transforms, poles, Bode plots and negative feedback. All of these except step response appear as lecture titles in sessions 1-13 (systems: 1, 2, 4; poles: 3; Laplace: 6; frequency response: 9, 11; Bode: 11; feedback: 3, 10, 12, 13); impulse and step responses are named in the official course description on the syllabus rather than in a lecture title. The CT and DT Fourier lectures (sessions 14-20) extend the same module. 6.003 is the canonical full-semester treatment of f.signals and goes well beyond it (DT systems, Z transform, Fourier transforms).

The course introduces the feedback fundamentals that pe.control builds on: the four lecture titles listed (sessions 3, 10, 12 and 13) cover feedback in DT and CT, and supplementary-notes chapters 7 'Control' and 8 'Proportional and derivative control' on the readings page (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-003-signals-and-systems-fall-2011/pages/readings/) add proportional and derivative control by title. No lecture, reading or supplementary-note title names loop design, compensation, phase or gain margins, voltage- or current-mode control or digital implementation, which are the pe.control summary items. The Z transform (session 5) and sampling and quantization (sessions 21-22) lectures supply mathematics behind digital control rather than its implementation and are therefore not listed here. Because the feedback material itself is credited to f.signals (negative feedback), pe.control coverage is introductory.

AIPE f.computation covers scripts, plots and simulation models together with numerical integration, step sizes and numerical error. Only one of 25 lecture titles, session 7 'Discrete Approximation of Continuous-Time Systems', suggests the step-size and discretisation-error strand (an inference from the title; the PDF was not opened), supported by the DT-systems lecture and by supplementary-notes chapter 1 'Difference equations' on the readings page (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-003-signals-and-systems-fall-2011/pages/readings/), which give the discrete-time vocabulary a simulation lesson needs. No software, scripting or plotting workflow is listed on any page, so coverage is introductory.

mapped_modules.rationale: The course assumes complex exponentials and sinusoidal reasoning (its sole stated prerequisite is 6.02) and extends them to frequency response and Fourier series, which is the mathematics behind f.ac's complex numbers, phasors and impedance and behind decomposing periodic converter waveforms into harmonics. None of period, frequency, duty cycle, average, RMS or impedance is a listed topic, and Fourier series exceeds f.ac (it appears under concepts_missing_in_aipe). Supplementary-notes chapter 6 'The perfect (sine) wave' on the readings page (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-003-signals-and-systems-fall-2011/pages/readings/) is the one chapter whose title points to sinusoids. Consistent with prerequisite_relationships (f.signals requires f.ac), f.ac is background for this course rather than taught by it.

Only the measurement half of AIPE f.magnetism (measurement range, sampling, reference points and error) overlaps: sessions 21-22 and the Audio CD capstone treat, by title, sampling and quantization of signals. Nothing on the pages concerns flux, induction, magnetic circuits or saturation.

mapped_modules.rationale: System functions, poles and zeros and Bode plots are the language AIPE pe.modelling applies to averaged converter models, and supplementary-notes chapter 3 'Block diagrams and operators: two new representations' on the readings page (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-003-signals-and-systems-fall-2011/pages/readings/) adds the block-diagram and operator view. No converter, averaging or small-signal linearisation topic is listed; the course is the assumed background (taxonomy: pe.modelling requires f.signals).

CT systems are introduced through differential equations and DT systems through difference equations (the syllabus description lists both; supplementary-notes chapter 1 'Difference equations' is on the readings page, https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-003-signals-and-systems-fall-2011/pages/readings/). The course uses rather than teaches calculus, so f.calculus is assumed background; the only stated prerequisite is 6.02.

Impulse and step responses, poles and fundamental modes generalise the RC/RL time-constant behaviour of AIPE f.dynamics, but the course pages list no circuit-specific content (MIT describes its applications as coming from engineering and physics generally); AIPE's RC/RL lesson is the natural prerequisite and worked example (taxonomy: f.signals requires f.dynamics).

Supplementary-notes chapters 4 'Modes' and 5 'Repeated roots', together with lecture 3 'Feedback, Poles, and Fundamental Modes' on the lecture-notes page (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-003-signals-and-systems-fall-2011/pages/lecture-notes/), are the transfer-function counterpart of eigenvalues in AIPE f.linear-algebra's state-space description, but no matrix or state-space topic is listed, so the link is tangential (taxonomy lists f.linear-algebra as related to, not required by, f.signals).

Replacing a CT system by a DT approximation, which the session-7 title suggests, is what every fixed-step circuit simulator does, so the lecture is background for judging simulation step size and plausibility (inferred from the title); no converter simulation or software tool is listed.

Fourier series, sampling and modulation are the analysis tools for PWM harmonic spectra and output filters in AIPE pe.inverters. The lecture titles say only 'Modulation, Part 1/2'; the course description lists communications among its application areas, and PWM, inverters and output filters are not listed on any page, so this is tangential background only.

Harmonic analysis of line current and the power-factor definitions in AIPE pe.rectifiers rest on Fourier series; the course supplies the mathematics but lists no rectifier, harmonic-distortion or power-factor content.

mit_topics: Continuous-Time (CT) Frequency Response and Bode Plot
mapped_modules.rationale: Second-order frequency response and Bode plots, with damping and Q read from pole locations (inferred from the session 3, 9 and 11 titles), are the vocabulary of resonant-tank gain curves in AIPE pe.resonant; the taxonomy lists f.signals as a pe.resonant requirement. No resonant-converter, LLC or soft-switching content is listed.

Convolution as a system representation and its link between impulse response and transfer function

The s-plane-to-z-plane pole-mapping view of discretisation (forward Euler z = 1 + sT, backward Euler, CT poles mapped to DT poles for a given step size); f.computation names numerical integration, step size and numerical error but not this interpretation (inferred from the session-7 title)

Fourier series and Fourier transform (CT) as formal signal representations, and the DT Fourier series/transform with the relations among all four Fourier representations (DFT/FFT link); harmonics are named in pe.rectifiers and pe.inverters, but no module names Fourier series or Fourier transforms

Python: convolution of a test input with an impulse response compared with direct ODE integration (scipy.integrate.solve_ivp) for the same system
Python: Fourier-series synthesis of square, triangular and PWM waveforms; FFT of a simulated buck inductor-current ripple; verify Parseval's relation between harmonic RMS sum and time-domain RMS
Python: sampling and aliasing of a switching-ripple waveform at a chosen ADC rate, with and without an anti-alias filter; quantise to N bits and compute quantisation-noise RMS versus N

Python: proportional and PD control of a second-order plant; sweep the gain, plot pole trajectories and step responses, then apply the same loop to the averaged buck model used in the existing buck-converter tutorial (catalogue slug buck-converter, covers pe.modelling and pe.control)

prerequisite_relationships: f.signals requires f.dynamics and f.ac (agrees with taxonomy). The course's only stated prerequisite is 6.02; the pages do not say which skills 6.02 supplies, but the syllabus description lists differential equations and complex exponentials among the course's representations and session 4 is titled 'Continuous-Time (CT) Systems', so circuit-level differential equations and complex exponentials are inferred to be assumed rather than taught

f.signals requires f.calculus transitively (taxonomy: f.signals requires f.dynamics, which requires f.calculus); no taxonomy change. Difference and differential equations are the entry representations (sessions 2 and 4, supplementary-notes chapters 1-2)

Sequencing suggestion, not a prerequisite relation: 6.003 teaches DT systems and the Z transform (sessions 2-3, 5) before CT systems and Laplace (sessions 4, 6); AIPE can adopt the same DT-first order so that f.signals leads directly into the digital-implementation part of pe.control

pe.control requires f.signals via pe.modelling (taxonomy: pe.control requires pe.modelling; pe.modelling requires f.signals). Differs from taxonomy: f.magnetism.requires lists f.dynamics and f.electronics only, so a sampling/quantisation lesson for f.magnetism's measurement half cannot assume the Fourier-transform part of f.signals. Session 7 (discrete approximation of CT systems) links f.calculus and f.dynamics to f.computation and pe.simulation (taxonomy: f.computation requires f.dynamics; pe.simulation requires f.computation): numerical step size is a DT-system question (inferred from the title)

pe.modelling requires f.signals (agrees with taxonomy); the course supplies the transfer-function vocabulary (system functions, poles and zeros, Bode plots) that pe.modelling applies to averaged converter models

f.linear-algebra is a useful co-requisite rather than a prerequisite (taxonomy lists it under f.signals.related): fundamental modes and repeated roots (session 3, supplementary-notes chapters 4-5) correspond to eigenvalues in the state-space view, which the course does not list
pe.resonant requires f.signals (agrees with taxonomy): the second-order frequency-response and Bode material (sessions 9, 11) should precede resonant-tank gain curves

course_facts.scope_summary: MIT presents 6.012 Microelectronic Devices and Circuits (Fall 2005, undergraduate, Prof. Jesús del Alamo) as the entry course for its EECS devices/circuits/systems concentration. It starts from semiconductor carrier physics (electron and hole populations, doping with donors and acceptors, drift and diffusion), builds the electrostatics of p-n junctions and MOS structures, derives MOSFET current-voltage characteristics and equivalent-circuit (large-signal and small-signal) models, then applies them to NMOS/CMOS inverter logic (transfer characteristics, delay, scaling, dynamic power). A second device block covers p-n diode I-V, charge storage and diffusion capacitance, and the bipolar junction transistor; the final block treats MOSFET and BJT single-stage and multistage amplifiers, current sources and sinks, and amplifier frequency response (Miller effect, open-circuit time constants). Assessment consists of ten problem sets (the tenth is marked optional on the calendar), two quizzes, a final exam and a SPICE/Cadence circuit design project (an optical receiver). Readings are assigned from the Howe and Sodini textbook for lectures L1-L25.

access_limitations: No lecture videos exist for this course: the learning resource types are Exams, Lecture Notes, Problem Sets and Projects only, so topic evidence comes from the calendar and lecture-notes listing pages, not from recorded lectures. The calendar's R1 Topics cell carries a second line, 'Video: Silicon Run I (The 200 mm Era)', beneath 'Basic MOSFET Description'; this names a film (presumably shown in recitation, an inference) and no video file is provided on OCW.

All lecture notes (26 + 24 annotated), 10 problem sets, 6 exam/solution files, the project brief, 3 OCW-hosted Cadence support files and 8 study-material files are PDFs; per the licensing rules none were opened, so this record holds titles and counts only. Annotated notes are missing for L1 and L24. A fifth Projects-page item (Cadence Waveform Calculator Functions) is an off-site third-party PDF link, not OCW content.
The MIT Microelectronics WebLab (Tools page) requires registration and is described as available to MIT students and collaborating institutions; AIPE learners cannot rely on it.

The design project depends on commercial Cadence EDA software (the Projects page describes Cadence as the commercial circuit CAD tool used for the project); all three OCW-hosted Cadence support files carry Used with permission notices (two courtesy of Kerwin Johnson, one courtesy of Cadence Design Systems, Inc.), and the waveform-calculator manual is hosted on a third-party site (media.advico-microelectronics.com) under its own terms.
Assigned readings are sections of a commercial 1996 textbook (Howe and Sodini, Prentice Hall); no open reading files are provided, and the L26 wrap-up has no assigned reading.

The course edition is Fall 2005 (over 20 years old); device examples and the CMOS scaling discussion reflect that era. The calendar and readings pages use typographic quotes in the L4 title that rendered as encoding artefacts in the text fetch; the straight-quote form is recorded here.

The instructor name contains a non-ASCII character (ú). references/mit-ocw-verification.json and references/mit-ocw-catalogue.json store 'Prof. Jesús del Alamo' as correct UTF-8; a Windows console using a non-UTF-8 code page renders the ú as ?? when these files are printed, which is a display artefact, not a data defect.

mapped_modules.rationale: AIPE's f.electronics is 'simplified models of diodes and MOSFETs, operating points, losses and ratings'. The central subject of 6.012 is the physics-based derivation of diode, MOSFET and BJT models and their use at an operating point (syllabus objectives B-D and the measurable outcomes on large-signal and incremental LEC models). MIT goes far deeper than AIPE needs (full device physics, BJTs, amplifiers), so this course is the authoritative deep reference behind AIPE's simplified-model treatment rather than a one-to-one lesson source.

It is substantial but not central to pe.devices because it treats small-signal integrated devices only: no power MOSFET structures, IGBTs, SiC/GaN, ratings, SOA or datasheet reading, which matches the catalogue's 'Device foundations' / supplementary classification.
