concepts_missing_in_aipe: Semiconductor carrier physics: electrons and holes, donors and acceptors, carrier statistics, drift and diffusion, majority and minority carriers, excess carriers, low-level injection, minority-carrier lifetime, quasi-neutrality and quasi-statics (L2-L4, R3, R5; syllabus outcome on semiconductor concepts)

Electrostatics of the p-n junction and MOS structure: depletion approximation, built-in potential, depletion width and depletion capacitance, threshold voltage, MOS C-V behaviour from accumulation to inversion (L5-L8, R5-R9, problem sets 2-4)

Physics-based derivation of MOSFET I-V in the linear and saturation regions, including back-bias (body) effect, and the physics-based derivation of the resulting large-signal and small-signal equivalent circuits with capacitances (L9-L11); AIPE names the simplified models themselves in f.electronics and pe.modelling but not their derivation
Minority-carrier charge storage and diffusion capacitance of the p-n diode, the physics behind reverse recovery (L16)
Bipolar junction transistor operation (forward active and other regimes) and its equivalent-circuit models; AIPE has no BJT content although the IGBT it teaches is a BJT-MOSFET hybrid (L17-L18)
Digital CMOS logic: inverter transfer characteristics and noise margins, NMOS versus CMOS inverters, propagation delay, dynamic power and CMOS scaling (L12-L14, R13-R15)

Analog amplifier building blocks: common-source and other single-stage MOSFET/BJT amplifiers, multistage and cascode amplifiers, current sources/sinks and mirrors (L19-L22, R19-R21); relevant to op-amp, compensator and current-sense design but absent from AIPE
Amplifier frequency response methods: Miller effect and the open-circuit time-constant technique (L23-L25, R23, R24)

Physics-based SPICE device models and their parameter extraction (a SPICE MOSFET model in R12; Cadence Spectre MOS1 model files on the Projects page; syllabus outcome on determining model parameter values from device structure, dimensions and bias)
Integrated-circuit fabrication and microelectronics industry trends (syllabus measurable outcome on fabrication and industry trends; the film Silicon Run I listed under R1)
Experimental device characterization (diode and MOSFET I-V measurement, as in problem sets 1 and 6 and the WebLab tool)
modern_gaps_not_covered_by_mit: Power semiconductor device structures: vertical (planar, trench, superjunction) power MOSFETs, IGBTs, PiN and Schottky power diodes, voltage/current ratings and safe operating area

Wide-bandgap devices (SiC MOSFETs, GaN HEMTs) and power-device technology after 2005: material properties, gate-drive requirements, reverse conduction without a body diode, fast switching and device-level reliability; the course's only technology-trend content is 2005-era CMOS scaling (L14) and the syllabus outcome on fabrication and industry trends

Hard-switching loss mechanisms at converter level: gate charge and Miller plateau, Coss energy, reverse-recovery loss, dead-time and body-diode conduction loss, and efficiency budgets (the Miller effect itself is taught in L24 in the amplifier context; its gate-charge/Miller-plateau form for power switches is not)
Power-device datasheet interpretation: R_DS(on) versus temperature and gate voltage, thermal resistance and junction temperature, avalanche and SOA curves
Thermal management of power devices (junction-to-case and heatsink thermal networks)
Gate drivers, dead time, bootstrap supplies, isolation and overcurrent/overvoltage protection for power switches
Open-source simulation workflow (ngspice/Python) with behavioural switch models and vendor SPICE models for converters, replacing the course's commercial Cadence flow
Package and layout parasitics (ESL, commutation-loop inductance) and their effect on switching waveforms and EMI

Converter-level small-signal modelling (averaging, state-space averaging, converter transfer functions) and digital control, which build on but go beyond the amplifier small-signal methods taught here
recommended_lessons: f.electronics / pn-diode-from-physics-to-model: how depletion and diffusion capacitance and the exponential I-V law arise, and when the piecewise-linear diode model AIPE uses in converters is valid (academic reference: mit-6-012-2005 L5, L6, L15, L16)

f.electronics / mosfet-operating-regions-for-switching: threshold voltage, linear (ohmic) and saturation regions, body effect, and why a power switch is driven hard into the linear region (reference L9-L11)

f.electromagnetism / charge-field-potential-in-a-junction: integrate a charge distribution to field and potential for a parallel-plate capacitor and then for a depleted p-n junction, as the electrostatics bridge into the pn-diode lesson (reference L4-L8, R5-R9)
pe.devices / mos-capacitance-and-gate-charge: MOS C-V from accumulation to inversion, nonlinear Cgs/Cgd/Cds, the Miller effect and the gate-charge curve read from a datasheet (reference L8, R9, L24)
pe.devices / minority-carrier-storage-and-reverse-recovery: diode charge storage and diffusion capacitance as the physics behind reverse-recovery loss in converters (reference L16)
pe.devices / from-bjt-to-igbt: BJT forward-active and saturation regimes as the bridge to IGBT conduction, saturation voltage and tail current (reference L17-L18)
pe.losses / switching-loss-from-the-cmos-inverter: energy-per-transition and CV^2f dynamic power as the archetype of capacitive switching loss, extended to a half-bridge (reference L14, R15)

pe.modelling / linearisation-around-an-operating-point: large-signal versus incremental models, built first for a transistor stage and then reused for an averaged converter (reference L11, L19, syllabus outcome on LEC models)

pe.simulation / level-1-mosfet-model-in-ngspice: meaning of VTO, KP, LAMBDA, GAMMA and capacitance parameters, and checking an ngspice I-V sweep against a hand square-law model (reference R12; the Cadence Spectre MOS1 model files are the historical pointer, with level-1 correspondence an inference)

f.signals / amplifier-frequency-response-and-miller-effect: poles, open-circuit time constants and bandwidth of a gain stage, as groundwork for compensator and current-sense amplifier design in pe.control (reference L23-L25)
recommended_simulations: Python (numpy/matplotlib): Shockley diode I-V versus temperature and saturation current, with a least-squares fit of ideality factor and series resistance to synthetic measured data, mirroring the course's diode-characterization exercises without using its data

Python: abrupt p-n junction depletion width and depletion capacitance versus reverse bias from the depletion approximation; plot C(V) and compare its shape with a datasheet-style output-capacitance curve

Python: MOS capacitor C-V curve (accumulation, depletion, inversion) in low- and high-frequency limits for a given oxide thickness and doping; show how threshold voltage shifts with doping and body bias

ngspice: level-1 NMOS I-V families (ID-VDS for several VGS, ID-VGS with body-bias sweep); extract threshold voltage, transconductance parameter and linear-region resistance and compare with the Python square-law model

ngspice: MOSFET-as-switch study, sweeping gate voltage and temperature (TEMP/TNOM) to show how linear-region on-resistance changes, as the first loss term to add to labs/buck_open.py, which currently assumes ideal switches and carries no device model

ngspice: CMOS inverter DC transfer characteristic and noise margins, then transient propagation delay versus load capacitance and average supply current versus frequency to verify the CV^2f dynamic-power law
ngspice: p-n diode reverse-recovery transient using a diode model with transit time (TT) and zero-bias junction capacitance (CJO); relate recovered charge to forward current and diffusion capacitance
ngspice: common-source amplifier with Cgd, AC sweep for gain and -3 dB bandwidth; compare with an open-circuit time-constant estimate computed in Python and show the Miller multiplication of Cgd
ngspice: simple current mirror and cascode current source, output resistance versus bias, as an optional analog building-block exercise for learners heading to control-IC design

course_facts.scope_summary: MIT 6.013 (Fall 2005, undergraduate; listed under Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and the Engineering Systems Division; instructors listed as Prof. David Staelin, Prof. Erich Ippen and Markus Zahn) is an applied electromagnetics course that builds Maxwell's equations from the Coulomb-Lorentz force law, through boundary conditions, potentials, media and the electro-/magneto-quasistatic approximations, and then applies them in six units: Maxwell's equations, plane waves, transmission lines and waveguides, fields and forces (field energy, virtual-work forces, rotating and self-excited machines), antennas and radiation, and acoustics. The course page names applications spanning wireless and optical communications, circuits and computer interconnects, microwave links and radar, sensors, MEMS, motors, and power generation and transmission. Delivery was 23 lectures and 25 recitations with 11 problem sets, two quizzes and a final; the treatment is analytical (the only computational reference on the calendar is a radiation-pattern 'computer simulations' demo in R23) and no lecture videos are published.
stated_prerequisites: MIT 18.01 and 18.02, or equivalent (the syllabus lists subject numbers only; their subject names, single- and multivariable calculus, are inferred from the MIT catalog)
MIT 8.01 and 8.02, or equivalent (subject numbers only on the syllabus; inferred from the MIT catalog to be introductory mechanics and electricity and magnetism)
MIT 6.002 and 6.003 (subject numbers only on the syllabus; inferred from the MIT catalog to be circuits and electronics, and signals and systems)

The syllabus glosses these subject numbers as working knowledge of complex arithmetic, vector differential operators and elementary matrix algebra, basic calculus, RLC circuit analysis, Maxwell's equations and Fourier-transform methods.

teaching_resources.summary: Course description, 3 instructors, 2 departments (Electrical Engineering and Computer Science; Engineering Systems Division), level/term, topic tags and the resource-type list (Lecture Notes, Problem Sets, Problem Set Solutions, Exams, Exam Solutions); no lecture videos listed.

Meeting times (2 lectures, 2 recitations and optional tutorials per week), stated prerequisites, 2 texts cited by title (Staelin course notes 'Electromagnetics and Applications'; Haus and Melcher 'Electromagnetic Fields and Energy', described as out of print and linked as OCW supplemental resource RES.6-001, Spring 2008), quiz/final/homework policy and a grade formula.

R2 Superposition and integral forms of Gauss' and Ampere's laws (volume charge and current densities)
L2 Boundary conditions; surface charge and surface current problems
R3 Boundary condition problems (conducting sphere or cylinder around a point or line charge or line current)
L3 Maxwell's equations in differential form; electroquasistatics and magnetoquasistatics
R4 Problem solutions using the differential form of Maxwell's equations
L4 Electric field, electric scalar potential and the gradient; Poisson's and Laplace's equations
L5 Method of images; R6 Method of images problems with planes, cylinders and spheres
L6 Dielectric, conducting and magnetic constitutive laws; charge relaxation
R7 Capacitance, resistance, inductance and charge relaxation from field solutions

mapped_modules.rationale: The course's first unit (7 lectures and 7 recitations) plus the Poynting and field-energy lectures covers the whole of this module's summary (charge, electric field and potential, current, magnetic fields, Faraday's law as part of Maxwell's equations, energy stored in fields) but at a vector-calculus, Maxwell's-equations level. Electromagnetic field theory is the course's central subject, so this is the one module the course covers as core; AIPE should treat it as the advanced reference and the ceiling of the module. The recitations R2, R3, R4 and R6 are confirmed on the calendar page but omitted from the capped topic outline.

mit_topics: L7 Magnetic dipoles and circuits; reluctance
L6 demo: H/M 9.4.1 measurement of B-H characteristic (magnetic hysteresis loop)
R19 Ohm's law for moving media; Faraday's disk (homopolar generator)
mapped_modules.rationale: Flux, induction, magnetic circuits, reluctance and the B-H (hysteresis) characteristic are treated in two lectures and a demonstration, which covers the magnetic-circuit and saturation half of the module substantially. The measurement half of the module (range, sampling, reference points, error) is not listed anywhere in the course.

mit_topics: L16 Principle of virtual work to find electric and magnetic forces
L18 Self-excited electric and magnetic machines
R18 Force problems in capacitive and inductive systems
R19 Faraday's disk (homopolar generator); torque; equivalent circuit
R21 Torque-speed characteristics of rotating machines
mapped_modules.rationale: Unit IV is a field-based treatment of electromechanical energy conversion (forces from stored energy, torque, homopolar generator, synchronous machine, self-excited machines, torque-speed curves) across roughly six sessions, which is the first half of this module. Induction machines and machine models for system studies are not listed, and the course page names motors and power generation only as applications, so coverage is substantial but not central.

mit_topics: L10 Parallel plate transmission lines; wave equation; sinusoidal steady state
L11 Gamma plane; Smith chart; VSWR; quarter-wave transformer
L12 Transient waves on transmission lines
L13 Reflections from ends; driven and initial value problems
R12 Short-line limits as circuit approximations to capacitors and inductors
R14 Impedance and VSWR problems; single-stub tuner
mapped_modules.rationale: The distributed-parameter transmission-line theory (characteristic impedance, standing waves, input impedance, reflections, travelling-wave transients) that underlies the power long-line model and surge/travelling-wave analysis is taught in depth over Unit III, but in an RF and communications framing. Only the distributed-line theory behind the module's 'line models' is taught, in an RF framing (Smith chart, VSWR, stub tuner); lines, cables, buses, loads, transmission and distribution structure and power-frequency line parameters are absent, so with respect to this module the coverage is introductory.

mit_topics: R7 Capacitance, resistance, inductance, and charge relaxation problems
R12 Short-line limits as circuit approximations to capacitors and inductors
mapped_modules.rationale: RLC circuit analysis is a stated prerequisite, so the module's own content (RC/RL responses, time constants) is assumed rather than taught. The course does briefly show where lumped capacitance, resistance and inductance and the charge-relaxation time constant come from in field terms, and when a short line reduces to a lumped C or L, which is a short but useful complement to this module.

mit_topics: L10 Sinusoidal steady state on transmission lines
mapped_modules.rationale: Complex numbers and phasor sinusoidal steady state are stated prerequisites, reviewed in the first recitation and then used throughout rather than taught. The impedance concept is extended to distributed lines (L10-L11, Smith chart), which goes beyond the module's scope.

mit_topics: R1 Review of vector and integral calculus; coordinate systems; gradient, curl, and divergence
mapped_modules.rationale: Calculus (18.01/18.02) is a stated prerequisite; the course only reviews it, and what it reviews (vector and integral calculus, divergence and Stokes' theorems) is beyond the module's first-order differential equations and is recorded as a concept missing from AIPE.

mit_topics: Syllabus prerequisite: 6.003 and Fourier transforms (syllabus page)
L12-L13 transient waves; driven and initial value problems (calendar page: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-013-electromagnetics-and-applications-fall-2005/pages/calendar/)
mapped_modules.rationale: Signals and systems and Fourier transforms are listed as prerequisites (syllabus page) and are leaned on by the transient and sinusoidal-steady-state analyses of L12-L13 (calendar and lecture-notes pages); nothing in this module is taught by the course.

mit_topics: L7 Magnetic dipoles and circuits; reluctance
mapped_modules.rationale: No transformer session is listed (the 'lambda/4 transformer' in L11 is a transmission-line impedance transformer, not a magnetic one). The magnetic-circuit and reluctance sessions supply only the physical basis on which the transformer equivalent circuit is later built, so the relationship is tangential.

mit_topics: L6 demo: B-H characteristic (magnetic hysteresis loop)
R9 effects of ohmic loss; skin-depth
mapped_modules.rationale: Hysteresis, reluctance and skin depth are the physics behind core loss, gapped-inductor design and AC winding loss, but the course lists no inductor or transformer design content, so it serves only as physical background for this module.

mit_topics: R9 Snell's law: Brewster and critical angles; effects of ohmic loss; skin-depth
L6 demo: H/M 9.4.1 measurement of B-H characteristic (magnetic hysteresis loop)
mapped_modules.rationale: Skin depth and the hysteresis loop are the physics behind AC winding loss and core loss, but the course lists no loss budgeting, switching or converter content; the module is mapped so that the skin-depth lesson below attaches to it.

mit_topics: R7 Capacitance, resistance, inductance, and charge relaxation problems (field origin of C, R and L)
R12 Short-line limits as circuit approximations to capacitors and inductors
L6 demo: B-H characteristic (saturation and hysteresis)
mapped_modules.rationale: The course derives C, R and L from field solutions and shows the B-H loop, which is the physical background for capacitors and inductors as real components, but it lists no ESR, ESL, ripple-current rating, tolerance or component-selection content.

mit_topics: L12-L13 transient waves and reflections on transmission lines
L19 Radiation by charges and currents
mapped_modules.rationale: The course description names circuits and computer interconnects among its applications, and line reflections, skin depth and radiation are the physics behind signal integrity and radiated EMI. EMI, EMC, layout or filtering are not listed anywhere, so the course is background only for this module.

concepts_missing_in_aipe: Vector calculus for fields (gradient, divergence, curl; divergence and Stokes' theorems) and Maxwell's equations in integral and differential form; AIPE's f.electromagnetism stops at Faraday's law without the vector-calculus formulation
Electroquasistatic and magnetoquasistatic (EQS/MQS) approximations: the formal criterion for when a lumped circuit model of a physical structure is valid
Boundary conditions at interfaces, Poisson's and Laplace's equations, the method of images and the electric dipole
Constitutive laws of dielectric, conducting and magnetic media; charge relaxation and the conservation-of-charge boundary condition (origin of leakage in capacitors and insulation)
Plane waves, Poynting's theorem as an electromagnetic power-flow statement, reflection and transmission at interfaces, and skin depth (basis of AC resistance of conductors and windings)

Wave equation on a transmission line, standing waves and VSWR, the Smith chart, quarter-wave transformer and single-stub matching. Note: characteristic (surge) impedance and travelling-wave transients and reflections are the basis on which ps.components is mapped above, but that module's summary item 'line models' does not yet make them explicit
Waveguides, cavity resonators, dispersion and group versus phase velocity; dielectric waveguides and fibre optics; lasers and optics

The virtual-work/coenergy method for deriving force and torque from stored field energy, and its homopolar (Faraday disk) and electrostatic (van de Graaff, Kelvin) generator examples, which ps.machines' 'electromechanical energy conversion' and f.electromagnetism's 'energy stored in fields' do not yet name
Antennas and radiation: dipole radiation, radiation resistance, arrays and antenna gain, wireless and optical links
Acoustic waves and acoustic boundary-value problems (outside AIPE Academy's power and energy scope; recorded for completeness, no lesson recommended)
modern_gaps_not_covered_by_mit: Numerical field solving (finite-difference, finite-element or FDTD) with open tools, which AIPE needs for reproducible simulations of inductors, busbars and cables; the course lists no student-facing numerical-methods content, and computer simulations appear only as a radiation-pattern demo in R23
Power-frequency transmission-line parameters (R, L, C per km from conductor geometry, bundling), cable models and the ABCD/long-line and per-unit treatment used in power systems
Power magnetics losses for switching converters: Steinmetz-type core loss, high-frequency winding (skin and proximity) loss, leakage and winding capacitance

Electromagnetic compatibility for power electronics: conducted and radiated emission limits, measurement setups, common-mode noise paths and PCB commutation-loop layout; high dv/dt effects of wide-bandgap devices (none of this is listed in the course)
Electromagnetic transient simulation of power networks (lightning and switching surges, insulation coordination) with EMT-type tools
Wireless power transfer and near-field magnetic coupling design (e.g. for EV charging)

Permanent-magnet machines, finite-element machine design and converter-fed machine models. Induction machines are also absent from this course but are classical rather than modern; the machines baseline for AIPE is MIT 6.685 (catalogue id mit-6-685-2013), not 6.013

The course description names sensors among its applications, but no session on sensing is listed; magnetic and current sensing for engineering measurement (Hall sensors, Rogowski coils, current transformers), which AIPE's f.magnetism module needs, is therefore a gap
High-voltage insulation and dielectric engineering for power equipment (partial discharge, breakdown)
recommended_lessons: f.electromagnetism: From Faraday's law to Maxwell's equations - Gauss's and Ampere's laws applied to a coaxial cable, a busbar and a solenoid, deriving capacitance and inductance per metre
f.electromagnetism: Quasistatics - when is a circuit model valid? Electrical size versus wavelength and switching edge rates
f.electromagnetism: Where does the power flow? Poynting's theorem in a coaxial cable and a transmission line (lesson-level prerequisite: f.ac for the sinusoidal case)
f.dynamics: Charge relaxation - where C, R and L and the RC time constant come from in field quantities (epsilon/sigma)
f.magnetism: Magnetic circuits and reluctance - from field laws to the inductance of a gapped core, with B-H loop and saturation
ps.components: Transmission lines as distributed circuits - characteristic (surge) impedance, reflections and the long-line model (lesson-level prerequisites: f.electromagnetism, f.ac)

ps.components / pe.emi-pcb: Travelling-wave transients - lightning and switching surges, cable reflections and gate-drive ringing (shared lesson; lesson-level prerequisite: the distributed-line lesson above)
pe.magnetics / pe.losses: Skin depth and the AC resistance of conductors and windings
ps.machines: Forces and torque from stored field energy - virtual work, the Faraday disk and the synchronous machine
pe.emi-pcb: Why loops radiate - dipole radiation and the physics behind radiated EMI (optional enrichment; radiation is not yet in any AIPE module)
recommended_simulations: Python (numpy/matplotlib): 2-D finite-difference Laplace solver for a coaxial cable and a parallel-plate capacitor with dielectric; compute capacitance per metre and compare with the analytical formula
Python: method-of-images field plot of a line charge above a ground plane (overhead conductor above earth) and the resulting capacitance per unit length
Python + ngspice: charge-relaxation time epsilon/sigma for several materials compared with the RC decay of an equivalent leaky capacitor simulated in ngspice
Python: reluctance-network model of a gapped magnetic core; inductance versus air gap and versus current with a saturating B-H curve
Python: skin depth versus frequency for copper and aluminium, and the AC/DC resistance ratio of a round conductor from 50 Hz to 1 MHz
ngspice: lossless transmission line (T element) driven by a step into open, short, matched and resistive loads; compare the transient with a hand-drawn bounce diagram
ngspice: lossy line (LTRA) energisation of a long cable showing the surge-impedance step and reflections; Python overlay of the analytical travelling-wave solution
ngspice + Python: sinusoidal steady state on a line - input impedance versus electrical length, quarter-wave matching, and a Python Smith-chart plot of the reflection coefficient
Python: 1-D FDTD plane wave at normal incidence on a dielectric slab and on a conductor, extracting reflection/transmission coefficients and skin-effect decay
Python: virtual-work force of a gapped electromagnet versus gap and current, and torque of an idealised two-pole synchronous machine versus load angle
Python: Poynting vector in a coaxial cable integrated over the cross-section to recover V times I
Python: radiation pattern of a two-element dipole array (array factor) as an intuition demo for radiating loops
prerequisite_relationships: f.electromagnetism requires f.calculus: agrees with taxonomy.json (f.electromagnetism requires f.quantities and f.calculus); the course assumes 18.01/18.02 and opens with the R1 review of vector and integral calculus. Vector calculus itself is beyond f.calculus and is listed under concepts_missing_in_aipe

Difference from taxonomy, not a requirement: f.electromagnetism does not require f.ac. Taxonomy gives f.electromagnetism requires [f.quantities, f.calculus] and places the physics track before circuit models; 6.013's complex-exponential/phasor notation (R1, used from Unit II onward) is needed only for the plane-wave, transmission-line and antenna content, which lies outside the module. f.ac is therefore attached as a lesson-level prerequisite of the proposed Poynting and transmission-line lessons, not of the module

f.magnetism and f.electromagnetism: taxonomy has f.magnetism requires [f.dynamics, f.electronics] with f.electromagnetism only 'related'. 6.013's order (L7 magnetic dipoles, circuits and reluctance after L1-L6 Maxwell's equations and media) supports a recommended-but-not-required sequencing of f.electromagnetism before f.magnetism; recorded as a sequencing suggestion for maintainers, not as an existing requirement

f.dynamics benefits from f.electromagnetism (R7 derives C, R, L and charge relaxation from fields) while the course assumes RLC circuit analysis (6.002) beforehand; taxonomy f.dynamics requires [f.dc-circuits, f.calculus], unchanged

ps.components: f.ac agrees with taxonomy transitively (ps.components requires ps.three-phase, which requires f.ac). f.electromagnetism is not a taxonomy prerequisite of ps.components; it is a lesson-level prerequisite of the proposed distributed-line/surge-impedance lesson only (difference from taxonomy, justified by Unit III building on the wave equation of Units I-II)

ps.machines: f.magnetism agrees with taxonomy (ps.machines requires [ps.transformers, f.magnetism]). f.electromagnetism is a difference: 6.013 reaches machines through field energy (L16) and magnetic circuits (L7) without any transformer session, so the field-based route is a justified alternative for the force/torque lesson, not a replacement of the taxonomy prerequisite ps.transformers

pe.emi-pcb: taxonomy requires [pe.practical] only, unchanged. The shared lesson 'ps.components / pe.emi-pcb: Travelling-wave transients' draws on the transmission-line transients of L12-L13, and the optional radiation lesson draws on Unit V radiation concepts, which are not yet in any AIPE module (see concepts_missing_in_aipe); neither makes a power-electronics module depend on a power-systems module
f.signals is an assumed prerequisite of the course (6.003, Fourier transforms) for the transient and steady-state line analyses; taxonomy f.signals requires [f.dynamics, f.ac], unchanged

course_facts.scope_summary: MIT 6.061 (with a graduate variant 6.690) is an advanced-undergraduate (OCW level: Undergraduate) introduction to electric power systems and electromechanical energy conversion, taught by Prof. James L. Kirtley Jr. in Spring 2011 with two 1.5-hour lectures per week. The 23-lecture calendar starts with a review of network theory, first-order transients (using buck and boost converters as examples) and sinusoidal steady state, then covers transmission lines, polyphase circuits, transformers and per-unit, symmetrical components, faults, protection, phase control and HVDC, and load flow. The second half turns to electromechanics (forces, virtual work) and synchronous, induction, DC and permanent-magnet machines including drive control, and closes with switching power-electronic circuits and inverters. Published materials are a 12-chapter set of course notes labelled '2007 Course Notes' (11 chapter PDFs; chapter 7 not available on OCW), also offered as a single open-textbook PDF, plus 11 problem sets with solutions, one small load-flow program file with problem set 7, and 2 quizzes with solutions; the syllabus names the instructor's Wiley textbook as the text.

prerequisite_relationships: ps.three-phase requires f.ac (taxonomy agrees: requires [f.ac]; f.dynamics is reached transitively through f.ac): the course reviews network theory, first-order transients and sinusoidal steady state (L2-L5) before polyphase systems (L7-L8), and MIT assumes a circuits course (6.002)

ps.components: MIT teaches single-phase transmission-line theory (L6) before polyphase systems (L7), then combines them (L8); the taxonomy dependency ps.components requires ps.three-phase holds for the polyphase-line lectures only; f.calculus (ODE/PDE methods) is an additional prerequisite the taxonomy reaches transitively via f.ac -> f.dynamics -> f.calculus

ps.per-unit and ps.transformers are taught together (L9) and both require ps.three-phase (taxonomy agrees); the taxonomy's f.magnetism requirement for ps.transformers is not reflected in the course order, which places transformers (L9) before the forces and induction lectures (L14-L15) and relies on the 6.013 electromagnetics prerequisite and the Ch6 magnetic-circuit chapter instead

ps.faults: taxonomy has ps.faults requires [ps.power-flow]; MIT teaches symmetrical components and faults (L10-L11, Ch4) before load flow (L13, Ch5), so sequence-network fault analysis needs ps.three-phase, ps.transformers and f.linear-algebra but not power flow; recommend relaxing the taxonomy requires to [ps.per-unit, ps.transformers] or recording the AIPE ordering as a deliberate design choice. ps.protection follows ps.faults (L11, L13), as the taxonomy has it

ps.power-flow requires ps.per-unit and f.computation (taxonomy: [ps.three-phase, ps.per-unit, f.computation]); ps.components is an addition suggested by the course order, since line models (L6-L8) precede load flow (L13, Ch5), which also carries the supporting program file

ps.machines requires ps.transformers and f.magnetism (taxonomy; the course order L9 -> L16 agrees, and the magnetic-circuit chapter Ch6 precedes the machine chapters); f.electromagnetism is an addition justified by the 6.013 prerequisite and the forces, Poynting-flow and virtual-work lectures (L14-L15) that precede the machine lectures (L16-L21)

pe.topologies (buck and boost) is introduced early with only f.dynamics and f.calculus as prerequisites (L3-L4), as an ODE example rather than as converter theory; the taxonomy's requires [pe.devices, f.ac] stands for converter theory proper

ps.dc-grids: taxonomy has ps.dc-grids requires [ps.grid-converters] (VSC view); MIT's line-commutated HVDC (L12) rests on pe.rectifiers (phase control) and ps.components and is taught before switching circuits and inverters (L22-L23)

pe.applications (motor drives, L20) and pe.inverters (L22-L23) are placed after ps.machines in this course; the taxonomy has no such dependency (pe.inverters requires [pe.topologies, f.ac]; pe.applications requires [pe.control, pe.practical]), so MIT's placement is a sequencing choice for a power-systems audience, and AIPE's power-systems path may likewise sequence inverter basics after machines even though the power-electronics track teaches them earlier

course_facts.scope_summary: MIT 6.302 Feedback Systems (Spring 2007, listed by OCW as Graduate; instructors James Roberge, Joel Dawson, Kent Lundberg) is an introductory feedback-control design course that this record characterises as classical and continuous-time (the record's own terms; no OCW page uses either). Judging from the session titles, it moves from the properties of feedback (desensitivity, linearisation), plant modelling and first/second-order dynamics, through stability tools (root locus, Nyquist criterion, Hall/Nichols charts, Bode gain and phase margins) to compensation design (lead/lag series compensation, minor-loop compensation, internal and external op-amp compensation, lightly damped plants) and finally nonlinear topics (describing functions, oscillators, conditional stability). Physical applications run through a servomotor laboratory (Lab 1A-1D) and a design project chosen from three options (Phase Locked Loop, Thermal-Control System, Magnetic Levitator). The course description's topic list closes with the quoted phrase 'modeling and compensation of power converter systems, and phase lock loops' (11 words, quoted from the home and syllabus pages), although no calendar session title mentions converters explicitly.

mapped_modules.rationale: The course's central subject is the analog half of AIPE's 'Feedback and digital control' module: loop gain, stability margins, series and minor-loop compensation. The course description's topic list includes the quoted phrase 'modeling and compensation of power converter systems', but no session title names converters, so the depth of converter-specific treatment is unknown. Reading minor-loop compensation as the classical form of the inner current loop used in current-mode control is this record's inference. The digital-implementation half of pe.control (sampling, z-domain compensators) is not covered by this course; only R23 'Time delays' touches the delay problem. This is the only module for which the course is core coverage.

concepts_missing_in_aipe: Root locus method (Evans' rules) for seeing how closed-loop poles move with gain or compensator parameters (L7, R7-R8); AIPE lists only Bode-margin thinking.
Nyquist stability criterion and its examples, including conditional stability and gain-window stability (L9, L10, L23, R9-R10).
Degree-of-stability measures beyond phase margin: Hall and Nichols charts, closed-loop peaking M-circles, gain setting from the open-loop plot (L11).
Steady-state error analysis and system type / error constants (L5, R6).
Properties of feedback stated quantitatively: desensitivity, linearisation via feedback, Black's formula, return ratio and loop-gain measurement concepts (L2, R17, R22).

The explicit procedure for turning closed-loop regulation, bandwidth and noise specifications into open-loop Bode constraints (L13-L14, R14-R15); AIPE's pe.control summary lists loop design, but no lesson teaches this specification-to-loop-shape step.

Minor-loop (inner-loop) compensation as a general technique and its relation to series compensation (L17-L18, R18-R20); AIPE mentions current-mode control but has no lesson on the minor-loop principle.

Operational amplifier circuits as feedback systems, analog computers, and internal/external op-amp compensation (R5, L16, L18, L19). AIPE has no op-amp circuit lesson: the taxonomy summary of f.electronics names only diodes and MOSFETs, op-amps appear only as a keyword in the README row for legacy module F06, and the buck tutorial (curriculum/03-converters/buck-converter.md) names the error-amplifier and compensation-network blocks without analysing them.

Describing-function analysis of nonlinear loops, limit cycles and intentional oscillators (L21, L22, R24, Describing Functions Demo) - directly relevant to hysteretic/bang-bang converter control and PWM saturation, absent from AIPE.
Nonlinear compensation for conditionally stable loops (L23).
Time delays in feedback loops and their phase cost (R23) - the foundation for digital-control delay budgeting in pe.control.

Compensating lightly damped quadratic (resonant) plants as a general method (L20). AIPE's buck tutorial already quantifies the LC resonant peak (f0 about 1.3 kHz, Q about 3.9, about 39 dB) and prescribes Type III compensation to cross above it, but there is no general lesson on lightly damped plants beyond that single buck example.

The phase-locked loop analysed as a generic feedback system (linearised phase-detector/loop-filter/VCO model, loop-filter design, lock-in and hold range; R11, R12, Lab 2 option 'Phase Locked Loop'). AIPE's ps.grid-converters names synchronisation, but no module treats PLL loop dynamics as such.

Non-converter physical plants as feedback case studies: servomotor position/velocity control (Lab 1), inverted pendulum (L8), thermal-control system and magnetic levitation (Lab 2 options; the levitator is an unstable plant, inference from the physics).

A hands-on feedback laboratory sequence with a motor mechanism, prelabs and a take-home quiz (Lab 1). AIPE currently has only software-only Python labs (labs/buck_open.py ideal CCM calculation, labs/foundations/dc_circuits.py, labs/power-electronics/buck_switching.py time-domain switching simulation, labs/power-systems/three_phase.py, labs/renewable-energy/pv_model.py); none closes a feedback loop and there is no hardware lab (the buck tutorial's bench section describes an intended comparison that no lesson has yet carried out).
modern_gaps_not_covered_by_mit: Digital control of converters: sampling, z-domain compensators, ADC and PWM quantisation, computational and PWM delay, anti-windup and firmware implementation (AIPE pe.control 'digital implementation').

Averaged and small-signal modelling of switching converters (state-space averaging, PWM-switch model), control-to-output and line-to-output transfer functions, output impedance, and the right-half-plane zero of boost/buck-boost stages (AIPE pe.modelling, pe.boost) - only named generically in the course description phrase 'modeling and compensation of power converter systems'; whether the unpublished lectures go further is unknown.

Current-mode control specifics: peak and average current-mode control, slope compensation, sampled-data current-loop effects; Type II/Type III compensator design and realisation in converter controller ICs.

Grid-connected converter control: dq-frame current control, synchronous-reference-frame PLLs for three-phase grids, grid-code requirements, grid-support functions (AIPE ps.grid-converters, re.integration).

Impedance-based stability of interconnected converters (Middlebrook input-filter criterion, source-load impedance ratio), small-signal stability of converter-dominated grids, grid-forming and droop control (AIPE ps.converter-dominated, ps.microgrids).

Python-based control tool chain (scipy.signal / python-control) and SPICE-level loop verification with ngspice. The course uses MATLAB and Octave for problem sets (Octave is itself open-source software, so the gap is the specific Python/ngspice chain, not open-source tooling as such) plus Java applets written for Java Plug-in 1.4, which are unlikely to run in current browsers (inference).

Loop-gain measurement of switching converters by injection (Middlebrook/Tian methods, frequency-response analyser) and hardware-in-the-loop verification. Caveat: the course has four hands-on motor labs (1A-1D) and R22 'Return ratio', whose handouts were not read, so general loop-measurement practice may well be covered; only the converter-specific methods are asserted as absent.

State-space and observer-based design, model predictive control and MPPT-style search controllers used in renewable interfaces (AIPE f.linear-algebra, re.mppt); judging from the titles the course is purely classical transfer-function control.
Wide-bandgap-era bandwidth constraints (high switching frequency, EMI filter interaction with control loops) - not attributable to a 2007 classical control course.

block-diagrams-from-circuits-and-physical-systems (pe.modelling): deriving transfer functions and block diagrams from a converter, a DC motor and a thermal system; linearisation about an operating point
first-and-second-order-systems-and-the-s-plane (f.signals): poles, damping, step and frequency response, pole-zero maps
steady-state-error-and-system-type (pe.control): why an integrator removes output-voltage error, error constants
stability-from-the-loop-gain-nyquist-and-bode-margins (pe.control): Nyquist criterion, gain and phase margin, degree of stability and closed-loop peaking
root-locus-for-converter-loops (pe.control): Evans rules applied to a buck voltage loop with PI and lead compensation
loop-shaping-from-specifications (pe.control): turning regulation, bandwidth and noise specifications into open-loop gain constraints and forbidden regions on the Bode plot
lead-lag-and-pi-compensation-design (pe.control): series compensation on first- and second-order plants
minor-loop-compensation-and-current-mode-control (pe.control): inner loops as compensation, link to peak/average current-mode control

lightly-damped-plants-and-type-iii-compensation (pe.control/pe.modelling): an extension of the compensation section of curriculum/03-converters/buck-converter.md (which already quantifies the LC peak and prescribes Type III) into a general method for resonant plants, including boost stages and input-filter interaction
op-amp-error-amplifiers-and-compensator-realisation (pe.control/f.electronics): op-amp circuits, compensation networks and op-amp internal/external compensation
describing-functions-limit-cycles-and-hysteretic-control (pe.control): predicting limit cycles in relay/hysteretic converter loops, intentional oscillators
conditional-stability-saturation-and-nonlinear-compensation (pe.control): startup, large-signal saturation and conditionally stable loops
time-delay-in-digital-control-loops (pe.control): delay phase cost, Pade approximation, sampling and PWM delay budgets
phase-locked-loops-for-grid-synchronisation (ps.grid-converters): PLL as a feedback loop, loop-filter design, single-phase and SRF-PLL

servomotor-position-control-open-lab (f.signals/pe.control): an original low-cost DC-motor position-loop experiment (encoder, H-bridge, microcontroller) designed around AIPE's own buck-open-lab format, with proportional, lead and tachometer-feedback stages
recommended_simulations: Python (scipy.signal / python-control): Bode, Nyquist and root-locus plots of a buck control-to-output transfer function with PI, lead-lag and Type III compensators; compute gain/phase margins and closed-loop step and load-step responses.

Python: desensitivity demonstration - sweep plant gain by +/-50% with and without feedback and plot the closed-loop gain change versus loop gain (Black's formula), plus disturbance rejection versus frequency.
Python: steady-state error versus system type - step and ramp references for type 0/1/2 loops, linked to output-voltage regulation of a converter.
Python: root-locus animation of a second-order plant as gain and lead-zero location vary; identify when closed-loop poles cross into the right half-plane.
Python: Nyquist plot of a conditionally stable loop showing stability only inside a gain window, then a time-domain simulation of what happens when the loop saturates (gain reduction instability).
Python: Hall/Nichols chart construction and closed-loop peaking (M-circles) for a given open-loop response, compared with the measured step overshoot.

Python: describing-function prediction of a limit cycle in a relay/hysteretic buck controller versus a time-domain switching simulation; build an original interactive describing-function/limit-cycle demo in Python (matplotlib widgets) for a relay-plus-hysteresis buck controller.
Python: time-delay effects - exact exp(-sT) phase versus Pade approximations; phase-margin loss from one-sample plus half-PWM-period delay in a digital voltage loop.
Python: PLL model (phase detector, loop filter, VCO) - linearised loop Bode/root locus versus nonlinear time-domain lock-in; extend to a single-phase grid-voltage PLL with a frequency step.
Python: DC servomotor position loop (motor electrical and mechanical model) with proportional, lead and tachometer minor-loop compensation; compare step responses.
ngspice: op-amp error amplifier with Type II and Type III compensation networks - AC analysis of the compensator transfer function compared with the hand-designed poles and zeros.
ngspice: closed-loop averaged buck model (behavioural sources) with a voltage-mode compensator; measure loop gain by injection (Middlebrook/Tian method) and run a load-step transient.
ngspice: two-pole op-amp macromodel with external (minor-loop) compensation versus series lead compensation; show the effect on loop gain and closed-loop bandwidth.
prerequisite_relationships: pe.control requires pe.modelling (AIPE's existing direct requirement), which in turn requires f.signals and pe.topologies: the course places plant modelling and linearisation (L2-L3, R2-R3) and first/second-order dynamics (L4) before any stability or compensation topic, and officially requires a linear-systems course (6.003 level).

f.signals requires f.dynamics and f.ac (AIPE's existing requirement, confirmed): the course assumes first-order responses and complex variables, giving only a one-recitation review of complex variables and the s-plane (R4) before using frequency response throughout.

pe.control (compensator realisation) requires op-amp circuit skills beyond AIPE's f.electronics: the course assumes a circuits laboratory course (6.002/6.071) and reviews op-amp circuits in R5 before the op-amp compensation lectures L16-L19.

Within pe.control, stability analysis precedes compensation design: root locus (L7, R7-R8), Nyquist (L9-L11, R9-R10) and Bode margins (L12) come before series compensation (L15, R16), minor-loop compensation (L17-L18, R18-R20) and lightly damped plants (L20).
Within pe.control, linear compensation precedes nonlinear topics: describing functions, oscillators and conditional stability (L21-L23, R24) are the last block, after all linear tools.

ps.grid-converters (PLL synchronisation) requires pe.control's linear loop analysis (consistent with AIPE's existing requirement ps.grid-converters -> pe.control): the PLL recitations R11-R12 and the PLL design option are scheduled after the Nyquist sessions (R9-R10) and alongside the Bode-margin lectures.
pe.control digital implementation requires an understanding of time delay in loops: R23 'Time delays' is treated as an advanced topic after compensation design.

f.computation is a tool prerequisite for loop-design exercises: the syllabus states MATLAB/Octave are needed for some problem sets, which AIPE should satisfy with Python before learners reach pe.control problem work.

ps.stability (small-signal stability methods) builds on pe.control's Nyquist and describing-function tools, consistent with AIPE's existing requirement that ps.stability needs pe.modelling (confirmed in the taxonomy).

course_facts.scope_summary: MIT 6.334 Power Electronics (Spring 2007, graduate, Prof. David Perreault) is a one-semester graduate course on using electronic circuits for energy conversion and control, worth 6 engineering design points. Its 37 calendar lectures run from analysis methods and rectifier basics (AC-side reactance, power factor and distortion) through DC-DC converters, magnetics, isolated DC/DC converters, DC-AC inverters and PWM, EMI filtering, loss computation and snubbers, soft switching, thermal design and resonant/RF converters, to averaged modelling and control, three-phase (multi-pulse) rectifier systems, practical layout and gate-drive issues, switched-mode rectifiers and a closing design example. Assessment is weekly problem sets (40%), two evening quizzes (50%, no final exam) and a design project (10%); the required text is Kassakian, Schlecht and Verghese, Principles of Power Electronics, and the OCW site publishes lecture notes and problem sets but no videos.
stated_prerequisites: The syllabus states a single prerequisite, given by number only: 6.012. Its title, Microelectronic Devices and Circuits, is taken from the AIPE catalogue record mit-6-012-2005 (Fall 2005, undergraduate), not from any 6.334 page.

teaching_resources.summary: Course description, instructor (Prof. David Perreault), level (Graduate), term (Spring 2007), 2 MIT topic tags (Electric Power, Electronics), 2 learning-resource types (Lecture Notes, Problem Sets); no video resource type listed. The course image shows, per its caption, an automotive bidirectional DC/DC converter (an illustration, not a lecture topic).

Meeting times (3 one-hour lectures per week), 1 stated prerequisite (6.012, by number only), homework policy, 2 evening closed-book quizzes timed just after Lec 19 and Lec 34 (2 and 1 days later respectively) and no final, 3-component grading scheme (homework 40%, two quizzes 50%, design project 10%), 1 required textbook title (1991), 4 additional reference-book titles (1998, 1995, 1997 and 2006 editions), 1 industry field-trip note (Synqor, a DC/DC converter maker for telecommunications, Boxborough MA).

37 numbered lecture entries with topic titles (unit titles as headings with sub-topic lines), plus key dates for 11 homework sets (0-10), 2 quizzes with review sessions, practice exams (out at Lec 33), the design project (out at Lec 21, due at Lec 37) and a SynQor field trip entry in the Lec 34 cell.

access_limitations: No lecture videos: the course lists only Lecture Notes and Problem Sets as learning-resource types, so there is no video gallery to cite.

The lecture-notes page lists 16 chapter PDFs that do not map one-to-one onto the 37 calendar lectures (chapter numbering differs from lecture numbering). Only 8 chapter titles are included in topic_outline because of the 45-item cap; the other 8 closely parallel calendar lecture titles and are: ch. 1 Introduction and analysis methods, ch. 3 Power factor and measures of distortion, ch. 5 Introduction to DC/DC converters, ch. 6 Introduction to magnetics, ch. 7 Isolated DC/DC converters, ch. 9 Inverters (DC/AC converters), ch. 12 Soft-switching techniques, ch. 15 Three-phase systems (all read on the lecture-notes page). mapped_modules.mit_topics may cite these chapters although they fall outside topic_outline; each such item carries the [lecture-notes] page tag.
No quiz, practice-exam or exam-solutions page is published, although the syllabus and calendar mention two quizzes, quiz review sessions and practice exams.

No design-project page or project description is published; the project is known only from the syllabus grading table (10%, issued early April, due Lec 37) and the calendar key dates (project out at Lec 21, due at Lec 37).
Lecture 27 is listed only as 'Guest lecture' with no topic title.

Lecture-note PDFs, the 11 problem-set PDFs, the .LIB/.SLB/.CIR example files and the whole-course download were not opened, in line with the metadata-only rule; coverage judgements rest on page-level titles only.

The related-resources page names proprietary or external tools (PSpice/OrCAD, PSIM demo, LTspice/SwitcherCAD III, a Microsim DesignLab Release 8 evaluation download) and an external SMPS design database; only OrCAD, Powersim and a university SPICE tutorial are hyperlinked, LTspice, the DesignLab download and the database are text mentions, and none of the external sites or files were fetched or checked for current availability.

The course dates from 2007; four of its five listed books are 1990s editions (1991-1998) and the SPICE reference is a 2006 edition. The AIPE catalogue ranks the course 'historical' behind MIT 6.622 (Spring 2023), so it should not be used as evidence for post-2007 practice.

Title conventions in topic_outline and mit_topics: where the calendar shows a unit heading plus a sub-topic line, the record joins them with a colon after the unit number; OCW's parenthetical expansions of abbreviations (LC, CSI, VSI, PWM, EMI, RF, LLC) are dropped from every title for consistency and the 12-word cap, while the parenthetical in Notes ch. 9 'Inverters (DC/AC converters)' is kept because it is part of the chapter title; Lec 17 joins two separate heading blocks on the page (DC-AC Converters 3 and EMI Filters 1). Lec 36 is shortened from the page's 14-word title to 12 words: the page reads 'New topologies and methods' where the record has 'New topologies'. All other titles are otherwise as listed.

The only stated prerequisite is 6.012, which the AIPE catalogue record mit-6-012-2005 identifies as MIT's Microelectronic Devices and Circuits subject; in AIPE terms this is the f.electronics layer (diode and MOSFET models, operating points).

concepts_missing_in_aipe: Linear versus switching regulation as the motivating comparison for power conversion (Lec 1); no AIPE module summary names linear regulators.

General periodic-steady-state analysis methods for switching circuits beyond volt-second and charge balance (Lec 2 'Introduction to analysis methods', Notes ch. 1; which methods, e.g. assumed-states or piecewise-linear analysis, is not stated in the titles). The pe.topologies summary names only the two balance conditions.

Rectifiers with AC-side (commutating) reactance: commutation overlap and its load-regulation effect (Lec 3; the related-resources page lists example rectifier circuit files with commutating inductance).

Decomposition of power factor into distortion factor and displacement factor, and THD as a defined metric (Lec 4, Notes ch. 3); pe.rectifiers and ps.three-phase name harmonics and power factor but not these metrics.

Thyristors (SCRs) as power devices and phase-control operation (Notes ch. 4): pe.devices lists diodes, MOSFETs, IGBTs, SiC and GaN but no thyristor, and pe.rectifiers names 'controlled rectifiers' without a lesson for them (see recommended_lessons).
Multi-pulse three-phase rectifiers: six-pulse and twelve-pulse schemes with phase-shifting transformer connections and interphase transformers (Lec 32-33).
Multiple-output isolated converters and the effect of leakage inductance on their regulation (Lec 14).
Multi-winding transformer modelling and high-frequency winding effects in magnetics (Lec 11-12; skin and proximity effects are inferred from the title 'Losses and high-frequency effects', not named).

Current-source versus voltage-source inverters, selective harmonic elimination, harmonic cancellation and multilevel waveform synthesis (Lec 15-16); AIPE's pe.inverters summary stops at bridges, PWM and filters.
EMI filter damping and the interaction of an input filter with converter control (Lec 18 'Damping; Control impact').
Snubber design and diode reverse-recovery effects (Lec 20-21, Notes ch. 11); AIPE's pe.losses summary does not mention snubbers.
Matching networks and RF power circuits as an extension of resonant conversion (Lec 26, Notes ch. 16).

Fourier-series decomposition of switching waveforms as an explicit analysis tool (Lec 15 'Fourier'); pe.rectifiers and pe.inverters name 'harmonics' but no AIPE foundation module summary names Fourier series.

Structural gap rather than a missing concept: no design-project brief or worked end-to-end design example exists as a lesson (Lec 37 'Advanced design example', syllabus design project). The power-electronics-core G3 gate already demands a design with specification, device constraints and a verification record, so the concept exists but is unlessoned.
modern_gaps_not_covered_by_mit: Wide-bandgap devices (SiC MOSFETs, GaN HEMTs), their figures of merit, fast-edge gate-drive and dv/dt considerations (pe.devices, pe.gate-driving).
Digital control implementation: sampling, discretisation, PWM resolution, microcontroller/DSP compensators (pe.control).

Bidirectional and dual-active-bridge isolated converters as a taught topology (pe.isolated): no lecture or chapter title names a bidirectional or dual-active-bridge converter; Lec 36 'New topologies' is unspecified, and the home-page image caption mentions a bidirectional automotive DC/DC converter only as an illustration.
Grid-connected converter control: synchronisation/PLL, current control in rotating frames, grid codes, anti-islanding (ps.grid-converters).
Grid-forming converters, inverter-dominated grids and converter-interaction stability (ps.converter-dominated) - not listed on any 6.334 page and must not be attributed to this course.
Open-source simulation workflow (Python, ngspice) replacing the PSpice/PSIM-era tooling on the related-resources page (pe.simulation).
Renewable-energy and storage interfaces: PV maximum power point tracking converters, battery charging and bidirectional storage converters (re.mppt, re.storage, re.pv-systems).
Modern bridgeless/totem-pole power-factor-correction stages with wide-bandgap devices (pe.rectifiers); only 'Switched mode rectifiers' / 'Switching-mode rectifiers' is listed.

EMC standards and pre-compliance measurement practice (CISPR/IEC limits) alongside filter design (pe.emi-pcb): no title names EMC standards or limits; Lec 17 'Intro to EMI' is unspecified and may touch conducted-EMI limits.
Datasheet-driven loss measurement methods such as double-pulse testing and calorimetric efficiency measurement (pe.losses).
Reliability, lifetime and thermal-cycling considerations in converter design (pe.thermal, pe.practical).
Wireless power transfer and modern resonant/high-frequency applications beyond RF amplifiers (pe.resonant, pe.applications).

prerequisite_relationships: pe.devices requires f.electronics, and pe.topologies requires f.electronics through pe.devices (taxonomy pe.topologies.requires = [pe.devices, f.ac]): the syllabus states MIT 6.012, a devices-and-circuits subject, as the sole prerequisite. By extension through the taxonomy's own chains this presupposes f.dc-circuits and f.dynamics; f.dynamics is mapped as background, f.dc-circuits (two levels below the course) is left unmapped.

pe.topologies requires f.ac directly (taxonomy) and f.dynamics indirectly (f.ac requires f.dynamics): the course front-loads 'analysis methods' (Lec 2) for periodic steady state before any converter is studied.

pe.rectifiers requires f.ac (harmonics, RMS, phasors): rectifier and power-factor lectures (Lec 3-4) are taught immediately after the analysis-methods lecture and before DC-DC converters. Differs from taxonomy.json, where pe.rectifiers requires pe.topologies: 6.334 teaches diode rectifiers, AC-side reactance and power factor (Lec 3-4, Notes ch. 2-4) before any DC-DC converter (Lec 5-8). The diode-rectifier/power-factor part of pe.rectifiers needs only f.ac; only switched-mode rectifiers/PFC (Lec 35, Notes ch. 10) need pe.topologies and pe.control. Recommend relaxing pe.rectifiers.requires to [f.ac] with pe.topologies required by the PFC lessons, or recording the current order as a deliberate AIPE sequencing choice.
pe.isolated requires pe.magnetics: the four magnetics lectures (Lec 9-12) directly precede the isolated DC/DC lectures (Lec 13-14), matching the taxonomy's existing requirement.
pe.magnetics requires f.magnetism (taxonomy): Lec 9 is an explicit review of inductance and reluctance before transformer modelling and inductor design.

pe.inverters requires f.ac (taxonomy): Lec 15 opens the DC-AC unit with Fourier analysis, a tool that no AIPE foundation summary names (see concepts_missing_in_aipe); f.signals is the nearest home for it.

pe.emi-pcb follows the converter units and benefits from pe.modelling: EMI filters (Lec 17-19) come directly after the inverter unit and Lec 18 covers filter damping and its control impact. Differs from taxonomy.json, where pe.emi-pcb.requires is [pe.practical] only (pe.topologies is reached through pe.practical); the MIT order places EMI filters before the practical-issues lecture (Lec 34). Recommend adding pe.modelling as related to pe.emi-pcb for the filter/control interaction content.
pe.thermal requires pe.losses (taxonomy): loss computation, snubbers and soft switching (Lec 20-22) precede thermal design (Lec 23).

pe.resonant requires pe.isolated (taxonomy; confirmed by the MIT order, isolated DC/DC Lec 13-14 precede soft switching and resonant converters Lec 21-26) and f.signals (taxonomy; Lec 24 is a resonant-circuits review). Proposed addition to the taxonomy: promote pe.losses from related to requires for pe.resonant, because loss computation and reverse recovery (Lec 20-21) directly precede soft switching.

pe.modelling requires pe.topologies and f.signals (taxonomy), and pe.control requires pe.modelling (taxonomy): the control unit (Lec 28-31) comes after all topology units and moves from averaging to a control example and current-mode control. Proposed addition: f.linear-algebra is not in taxonomy pe.modelling.requires ([pe.topologies, f.signals]); it is proposed here as an addition justified by state-space averaging (Lec 29) and is already a G2 gate module.

Multi-pulse rectifier content requires ps.three-phase and ps.transformers (connection groups): three-phase systems are introduced (Lec 32) immediately before six- and twelve-pulse rectifiers (Lec 33). In the taxonomy ps.three-phase is only related to pe.rectifiers; the dependency applies to the multi-pulse lessons, not to the whole module.

Switched-mode rectifiers (PFC) require pe.rectifiers and pe.control: Lec 35 is placed after the control unit. This is a lesson-level dependency within pe.rectifiers, not a module-level requirement in the taxonomy.

pe.practical requires pe.devices and pe.topologies (taxonomy): practical issues (Lec 34), the design example (Lec 37) and the design project close the course after all technical units. Differs from the draft reading: taxonomy pe.practical.requires is [pe.devices, pe.topologies]; pe.magnetics is only related and pe.control is absent (it is required by pe.applications). The MIT order (Lec 34 and Lec 37 after the magnetics and control units) supports promoting pe.magnetics to requires; the pe.control dependency attaches to the design example/design project, i.e. pe.applications, not pe.practical.

course_facts.scope_summary: MIT 6.622 Power Electronics, Spring 2023, is a graduate subject taught by Prof. David Perreault on the modelling, analysis, design and control of switching circuits that convert electrical energy. Its 38 numbered lectures open with rectifiers, load regulation and power factor, continue with a four-lecture DC/DC block (inferred to be the non-isolated converter family, since isolated converters follow the magnetics block), four magnetics lectures, two lectures on isolated DC/DC converters, switching losses and snubbers, and thermal modelling and heat sinking; the second half covers a three-lecture inverter block, switched-mode rectifiers, three-phase systems and three-phase inverters, converter control including current-mode control, EMI filters (including common-mode and differential-mode noise), switched-capacitor converters, soft switching, resonant power conversion with matching networks, and finally gate drive, level shift and layout. Assessment is by 12 problem sets (Problem Set 0 to 11; homework weighted 40%), 10 short assessments issued roughly weekly in place of exams (50%) and a buck-converter design project (10%) whose deliverables are the power stage, input and output filters, device and heatsink selection, passive components and a closed-loop controller. The textbook is Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese and Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics (Cambridge University Press, 2023), used as a preprint of the second edition and referred to as KPVS.

mapped_modules.rationale: A four-lecture DC/DC block plus the analysis-methods lecture form the backbone of the course's first third; steady-state switching-converter analysis (conversion ratios, ripple, conduction modes) is exactly this module's subject. Inference: the specific topologies within 'DC/DC Parts 1-4' are not named in the titles.

Project item: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-622-power-electronics-spring-2023/pages/design-project/. The design project asks students to design a buck converter and to specify its power stage, input and output filters, power devices and heatsinks, passive components and a feedback controller that stays stable across line and load variation; this makes the buck the course's worked reference converter and is the factual anchor of this mapping. Inference: L5-L6 are assumed to introduce the buck converter; their titles say only 'Intro to DC/DC, Part 1' and 'DC/DC, Part 2'.

Inference: four graduate lectures on DC/DC conversion and a later switched-mode rectifier lecture presuppose step-up and indirect (buck-boost type) converters; the titles themselves only say 'DC/DC, Part N', so the boost/buck-boost attribution, and therefore this core label, is inferred from the block length and the standard scope of the KPVS textbook.

Three opening lectures treat rectifiers, their load regulation and power factor, and a later lecture covers switched-mode rectifiers (inference: these are power-factor-correcting rectifiers; the title does not say so). Together they match this module's diode rectifiers, harmonics, power factor and power factor correction; controlled (thyristor) rectifiers are not named in any title.

A three-lecture inverter block plus a dedicated three-phase inverter lecture. AIPE's module names half- and full-bridge inverters, PWM, harmonics and output filters, so the three-phase lecture extends beyond the module's current summary. Inference: Inverters Parts 1-3 are taken to be single-phase because a separate three-phase lecture follows.

prerequisite_relationships: All pe.* modules in this baseline assume f.electronics, f.dc-circuits, f.dynamics and f.ac: the syllabus names a single prerequisite (6.2500 Nanoelectronics and Computing Systems) and the course starts directly with rectifier analysis (L2)

pe.rectifiers: taxonomy requires [pe.topologies, f.ac], but MIT teaches rectifiers (L2-L4) before switching converters (L5-L8). Justified difference: diode-rectifier, load-regulation and power-factor lessons need only f.ac and f.electronics; the switched-mode rectifier lesson (L20, taught after the DC/DC block) needs pe.topologies and pe.boost. Proposal: either split the requirement at lesson level or change pe.rectifiers.requires to [f.ac, f.electronics] and make pe.boost a lesson-level prerequisite of the switched-mode/PFC lesson

pe.topologies and pe.buck precede pe.boost and pe.isolated: the DC/DC block (L5-L8) comes before magnetics and isolated converters, consistent with the taxonomy (pe.boost requires pe.buck; pe.isolated requires pe.topologies)
pe.isolated requires pe.magnetics: the four magnetics lectures (L9-L12) immediately precede the isolated-converter lectures (L13-L14), consistent with the taxonomy
pe.thermal requires pe.losses: switching losses (L15) are taught immediately before thermal modelling and heat sinking (L16), consistent with the taxonomy

A three-phase inverter lesson in pe.inverters requires ps.three-phase (lesson-level addition; the taxonomy lists ps.three-phase only as related to pe.rectifiers): L21-L22 (Three-Phase Systems) precede L23 (Three-Phase Inverters)

pe.control requires pe.modelling and f.signals: the control block (L24-L26) follows all topology blocks and precedes current-mode control (L27), so current-mode control should follow voltage-mode loop design; consistent with the taxonomy (pe.control requires pe.modelling, which requires f.signals)

pe.emi-pcb: taxonomy requires [pe.practical] only; pe.modelling is a proposed additional requirement for an input-filter/control-loop interaction lesson (inference from the EMI-filter lectures L28-L30 following the control block L24-L27)

pe.resonant: taxonomy requires [pe.isolated, f.signals], consistent with the MIT order (L13-L14 before L35-L37); pe.losses is only 'related' in the taxonomy, but soft switching (L33-L34) is motivated by switching loss (L15), so pe.losses is proposed as an additional requirement

The L38 gate-drive and level-shift content (pe.gate-driving) requires pe.devices and pe.losses, consistent with taxonomy pe.gate-driving.requires = [pe.devices]; the L38 layout content belongs to pe.emi-pcb itself and follows the EMI block L28-L30

The capstone buck design project requires pe.buck, pe.passives, pe.magnetics, pe.losses, pe.thermal, pe.control and pe.emi-pcb together (the project page lists power stage, input and output filters, devices and heatsinks, passive components and a controller)

courses.facts_vs_inferences: FACTS (read on 2026-10-20 from the MIT OCW HTML pages listed in evidence_urls, all HTTP 200, re-fetched after review): course title Power Electronics, number 6.622 (no other current number appears on any fetched page), Spring 2023, graduate level, instructor Prof. David Perreault; 3 one-hour lectures per week; the single stated prerequisite 6.2500 Nanoelectronics and Computing Systems; the textbook citation (Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese, Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics, Cambridge University Press 2023, used as a second-edition preprint denoted KPVS and supplemented by notes and handouts); grading weights homework 40%, assessments 50%, design project 10%; the 38 lecture titles and their order (identical on the handwritten list, the typed list and the video gallery except that the Lecture 1 video is titled 'Introduction to Power Electronics'); 38 handwritten and 38 typed note PDFs and 38 videos; 12 problem sets (0-11) with 11 solution sets (none for Problem Set 11); 10 assessments with 9 solution sets (none for Assessment 9), stated to replace exams and to be issued approximately weekly; the design project's subject (a buck converter) and deliverable categories (power stage, input and output filters, power devices and heatsinks, passive components, a feedback controller stable across line and load variation, with simulations accepted as supporting evidence); its 1 OCW project-description link plus 25 third-party links (24 URLs naming PDF files and 1 archive.org catalogue-viewer page); the six capacitor datasheet labels (conductive polymer, multilayer ceramic, CS Capstick series, U767D large tubulars, aluminum electrolytic HD series, LXG snap mount); the former course number 6.334; the absence of a calendar page (HTTP 301 redirect loop returning an empty body). INFERENCES (AIPE judgement): every coverage level and module assignment; what the 'Part N' lectures contain (that DC/DC Parts 1-4 are non-isolated and include boost/buck-boost, that Inverters Parts 1-3 are single-phase, that Control Parts 1-3 begin with averaged/small-signal models, that Magnetics Part 1 revisits magnetic circuits and Parts 3-4 treat core and copper loss); that Switched-Mode Rectifiers (L20) are power-factor-correcting rectifiers; the interpretation of 'Load Regulation' (L3) as a rectifier topic; that 6.2500 is a devices-and-circuits subject; that the Paktron Capstick capacitors are film capacitors (an inference dropped from the record because the page does not say so); that devices are treated via datasheets rather than device physics; the prerequisite relationships beyond the one stated on the syllabus; the lists of missing concepts and modern gaps, which rest on what the titles do and do not name (no PDF, video or assignment content was read). The core labels for pe.boost and pe.modelling depend on inferred 'Part N' content and are flagged in their rationales. No lecture numbers, instructors or resources were invented; titles were recorded as listed, shortened only by dropping the 'Lecture N:' prefix and the '(Handwritten Notes)' suffix; the project outline title combines the page heading 'Design Project' with the task subject stated in the page's first sentence.

course_facts.scope_summary: A graduate course on electromechanics that uses electric machinery as its running example. It starts from field- and energy-based force calculation and magnetic circuits, then covers windings and air-gap fields and the major machine classes: round-rotor and two-reaction (Park transform) synchronous machines with their dynamics and simulation, induction machines (transformer model, squirrel-cage, drives and control, doubly-fed, single-phase, linear), DC commutator machines, variable-reluctance machines and permanent-magnet brushless DC motors, plus transformers, per-unit normalisation, machine sizing and power density, and design evaluation. The stated approach is deliberately classical and analytical, using numerical methods only when necessary; students are expected to be able to design the main classes of rotating and linear machines and to estimate their dynamic parameters. Research-motivated examples named on the syllabus are doubly-fed induction machines (wind turbines, microgrids, ship propulsion) and induction motors for traction drives.
stated_prerequisites: MIT's introductory electric power systems subject (6.061/6.690), or the instructor's consent; both the syllabus and the instructor-insights page give this as the only formal prerequisite.

The instructor-insights page describes the typical student background as some electromechanics (6.061) and circuits (6.002 Circuits and Electronics and 6.003 Signals and Systems, which the page groups together under circuits).

course_facts.license_notes: MIT OpenCourseWare materials are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (non-commercial, share-alike), which is incompatible with AIPE Academy's CC BY 4.0, so this record holds metadata only: page URLs, short lecture and chapter titles as listed, resource counts and prerequisites paraphrased in our own words; no lecture-note, problem-set, solution or quiz text is reproduced and no PDF or zip was downloaded (the resources and download listings were read as HTML only). The lamination-steel data excerpt attached to problem set 3 is explicitly marked as third-party copyrighted (2007, Electric Motor Education and Research Foundation, used with permission) and cannot be reused under any CC terms. The three reference books named on the syllabus (Fitzgerald/Kingsley/Umans 'Electric Machinery'; Kirtley 'Electric Power Principles'; Beaty and Kirtley 'Electric Motor Handbook') are commercial publications cited by title only.

recommended_lessons: NOTE: the items below are AIPE lesson proposals derived from the lecture order; their explanations, derivations, figures, exercises and code are to be written independently of the MIT notes, and MIT lecture titles are not to be turned into lesson files mechanically (task section 4.2).
Forces from energy and coenergy: solenoid plunger and reluctance actuator (f.electromagnetism -> ps.machines)
Magnetic circuits for machines: air gaps, saturation and lamination steel (f.magnetism)
From windings to rotating fields: MMF, winding factors and the air-gap field (ps.machines)
Round-rotor synchronous machine: phasor model, V-curves, sizing and rating (ps.machines)
Park's transformation: dq0 models of synchronous machines (ps.machines)
Synchronous machine dynamics: swing equation and transient reactances in per-unit (ps.stability, ps.per-unit)

Extension of the existing lesson three-phase-fundamentals (ps.three-phase, covers ps.per-unit): per-unit normalisation of machine parameters and base changes for simulation, rather than a new standalone per-unit lesson (ps.per-unit)
Induction machine as a transformer: equivalent circuit and torque-speed curve, with the single-phase motor as a special case (ps.machines, ps.transformers)
Variable-frequency induction motor drives: V/f and field-oriented control (ps.machines -> pe.applications)
Doubly-fed induction generator for wind turbines: sub- and super-synchronous operation (re.wind)
DC commutator machines and permanent-magnet brushless DC motors (ps.machines)
Variable-reluctance (switched reluctance) machines: principles and electronically commutated operation (ps.machines)
Eddy currents and loss mechanisms in machine iron (f.magnetism, pe.magnetics)
Machine sizing: shear stress, power density and ratings (ps.machines)
recommended_simulations: Python: coenergy-based force on a plunger or reluctance actuator from W'(i, x) by numerical differentiation; force versus position and current (f.electromagnetism, ps.machines)
Python: nonlinear magnetic-circuit solver with a synthetic B-H curve (fixed-point or Newton iteration), showing air-gap dominance and saturation (f.magnetism)
Python: MMF harmonic spectrum and rotating-field animation of a three-phase distributed winding; winding-factor calculator (ps.machines)
Python: round-rotor synchronous machine phasor model producing power-angle curves, V-curves and a capability chart (ps.machines)

Python: abc-to-dq0 Park transform demo on balanced and unbalanced currents, then a dq synchronous-machine model integrated with scipy solve_ivp for a three-phase short circuit (ps.machines, ps.stability)
Python: single-machine infinite-bus swing-equation simulation with equal-area criterion plot (ps.stability)

Python: extend labs/power-systems/three_phase.py per_unit() with machine-parameter base conversion (reactances in pu on machine and system bases, base change across a transformer) instead of a new standalone script (ps.per-unit)
Python: induction-machine equivalent circuit sweeping slip to give torque-speed curves versus rotor resistance and V/f ratio; dq-model direct-on-line start transient (ps.machines)
Python: DFIG steady-state stator and rotor power versus slip in sub- and super-synchronous operation (re.wind)
ngspice: transformer equivalent circuit with coupled inductors (K statement), magnetising and leakage inductance, open- and short-circuit tests to extract referred impedances (ps.transformers)
ngspice: Cauer ladder network representing a laminated-iron eddy-current path, AC sweep showing frequency-dependent surface impedance (f.magnetism, pe.magnetics)
ngspice: DC machine model with armature RL, back-EMF behavioural source and an electrical analogue of the mechanical load; start-up transient (ps.machines)
ngspice: six-step commutated brushless DC motor with trapezoidal back-EMF behavioural sources, showing phase currents and torque ripple (ps.machines)
Python: machine sizing calculator from shear stress and rotor volume, plotting power density versus speed and pole count (ps.machines)
