course_facts.scope_summary: MIT 6.691 (Spring 2006, graduate, Prof. James L. Kirtley Jr.) is a seminar on how bulk electric power systems are planned and operated, taught mainly from an engineering viewpoint with some attention to the economics of a restructured industry. Its self-described 'straw man' calendar runs from a review of complex power and polyphase systems through transmission-line two-port models and sending/receiving-end circle diagrams, transformers, Newton-Raphson and decoupled load flow, synchronous-machine modelling and per-unit models, electromechanical dynamics, voltage regulators and power system stabilizers, small-signal behaviour, generation costs and economic/optimal dispatch, symmetrical components, fault modelling and relaying. The home-page course description (the only fetched page that carries the 'core topics' list) additionally names, as core themes, system protection, multimachine dynamics and control, stability in both its steady-state and transient senses, isolated and mobile power systems, and computation together with simulation; the syllabus page has its own, shorter description, which says the 2006 offering expected to look at DC distribution systems and perhaps renewable sources. Assessment: seven published problem sets with solutions (many problems drawn from the Bergen & Vittal text), two quizzes planned in the straw-man calendar (Q1, Q2; the syllabus says 'perhaps two quizzes' and no quiz materials are published), no final exam, and a term project written at the scale of a conference paper and presented in class. Two sample project reports and two MATLAB simulation scripts are published; there are no lecture videos.
stated_prerequisites: Prior exposure to power systems at the level of MIT 6.061, or alternatively strong network-theory preparation plus some controls and electromagnetics. The syllabus and Lecture Notes pages show only the anchor text '6.061'; its link target is the OCW offering 6.061 Introduction to Electric Power Systems, Spring 2011 (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-061-introduction-to-electric-power-systems-spring-2011/), so the course title comes from the link target, not from visible text.
Economics background is called helpful because part of the seminar examines why the electricity industry was deregulated and restructured.
Rather than providing per-lecture notes, the Lecture Notes page refers readers to the 6.061 notes (same link target) for power-systems background.

Reference text named on the syllabus and assignments pages (bibliographic data only): Bergen and Vittal, Power Systems Analysis, 2nd ed., Prentice Hall, 1999; it supplies background reading and the source of many problem-set problems.

teaching_resources.summary: Course description, level (Graduate), term (Spring 2006), one instructor, MIT topic tags (Energy > Electricity; Engineering > Electrical Engineering > Electric Power), and four learning-resource types: Lecture Notes, Problem Sets, Problem Set Solutions, Projects with Examples. No lecture videos are listed. Carries the only copy of the 'Core topics include' course description, whose listed themes are (in our grouping): component representation (lines, transformers, plants, loads) and an overview of how the system is structured and run; power flow analysis; multimachine dynamics and control with steady-state and transient stability; protection; economic dispatch; isolated and mobile systems; and computation plus simulation. The syllabus page has a different, shorter description paragraph. The page image (a small power system from the lecture notes) is credited to the instructor.

Meeting times (2 sessions/week, 1.5 h), the syllabus's own short description with expected background, textbook (bibliographic data only), assessment outline (several problem sets, 'perhaps two quizzes', no final exam, final project), and a straw-man calendar of 20 lecture sessions (L1-L20), 2 planned quizzes (Q1, Q2) and project sessions (P1 ideas, P2-P4 presentations).
1 PDF ('Plans and Directions'); the page points readers to the notes of 6.061 for background. There are no per-lecture note files.
7 problem sets, each with a solutions PDF (14 PDFs in total); the page states that many problems come from the Bergen & Vittal text. Titles are generic (Problem Set 1-7).

Project brief (individual or 2-3 person teams; conference-paper-scale report plus class presentation; topics agreed with the instructor) and 2 sample student project reports (PDF), each credited to named students and marked as used with permission.

2 MATLAB .m files: a derivative function (it returns the state-variable derivatives that ode23 integrates) and a main script that runs the simulation. The page does not state which physical system is simulated.
Bergen & Vittal, Power Systems Analysis, 2nd ed. (Prentice Hall, 1999), named on the syllabus and assignments pages as the source of background material and many problems.
Linked as 'Download Course' from every course page and listed in the verification subpages; not fetched, format not verified.

course_facts.license_notes: Every fetched page links to the MIT OCW licence, Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/). The two sample project reports are credited to named students and marked as used with permission, so they are third-party works with their own permission status; the home-page image is credited to the instructor; the Tools page marks MATLAB as a registered trademark. For AIPE Academy (CC BY 4.0) this record keeps metadata only: page URLs, short listed titles (at most 12 words, one visibly truncated), resource counts, bibliographic data and prerequisites paraphrased in our own words. No lecture notes, problem text, solutions, project reports, scripts or the download archive were downloaded or copied, and any AIPE lesson or simulation on these topics must be written independently from standard engineering knowledge, not adapted from the OCW materials, because NC-SA terms cannot be relicensed under CC BY.

concepts_missing_in_aipe: [taxonomy gap] Sending- and receiving-end power circle diagrams for transmission lines (L3-L4): no AIPE module or lesson treats power-circle loci.

[taxonomy gap] Two-port network parameters (Z, Y, H and, by extension, ABCD) as a line-modelling tool (L4): ps.components names line models, but no module or foundations lesson names two-port networks.

[lesson gap in ps.power-flow] Load-flow solution algorithms: Newton-Raphson Jacobian formulation and fast-decoupled load flow (L7). The module names the power-flow problem; no lesson exists and the algorithms are named nowhere in AIPE.

[lesson gap in ps.machines] Per-unit synchronous-machine parameters (transient and subtransient reactances and time constants) and the operational-impedance / frequency-response view of the machine (L9-L10). ps.machines already names machine models for system studies; no lesson exists yet.

[taxonomy gap] Excitation control: automatic voltage regulator and power system stabilizer design and their effect on small-signal damping (L12). ps.grid-control names voltage control generically and ps.stability names rotor-angle stability, but no module or lesson names excitation control, AVR or PSS.

[lesson gap in ps.stability] Eigenvalue / modal analysis method for electromechanical modes of multimachine systems (L13). ps.stability names rotor-angle stability, which includes small-signal rotor-angle stability, but no module names the eigenanalysis method and no lesson exists.

[lesson gap in ps.grid-control] Generation cost curves, incremental cost and lambda iteration, loss penalty factors and the optimal-dispatch / optimal power flow formulation (L14-L16). ps.grid-control names dispatch only as a word; no economics or optimisation content exists in AIPE.
[taxonomy gap] Economics of electricity industry deregulation and restructuring (syllabus description): no AIPE module covers electricity markets or regulation.

[taxonomy gap] Power system planning and reliability, including cascading-failure and blackout post-event analysis (home-page description: planning and operation; one sample student project on the August 2003 blackout): no AIPE module covers planning, reliability or post-event analysis.
[taxonomy gap] Mobile, shipboard and isolated power systems as a class (home-page core topic; ship-to-shore student project): AIPE has microgrids but no module for mobile or shipboard power systems.

[lesson gap in ps.stability / f.computation] Time-domain simulation of power-system dynamics (home-page core topic 'computation and simulation'; the Tools page distributes an ode23-based simulation whose modelled system is not stated). f.computation covers numerical integration generically and pe.simulation covers converters; the gap is a power-system dynamic simulation lesson, not the concept of numerical integration.
modern_gaps_not_covered_by_mit: Grid-connected converter modelling and control: synchronisation (PLL), current control and grid-support functions (ps.grid-converters).
Inverter-dominated and low-inertia grids, grid-forming converters and converter-interaction stability (ps.converter-dominated); the course's stability content is purely synchronous-machine based.
Fault behaviour and protection of converter-fed networks, including limited fault current and inverter-based-resource ride-through (the converter part of ps.protection).

Grid integration of variable renewable generation: variability, grid codes, hosting capacity (re.integration); the syllabus only says renewable sources might perhaps be discussed and no session is listed.
Energy storage in system operation and frequency support (re.storage, re.batteries).
Microgrid droop control, power sharing and energy management, and DC distribution beyond the syllabus's one-sentence mention (ps.microgrids, ps.dc-grids).
HVDC and solid-state transformer interfaces between AC and DC networks (ps.dc-grids, ps.sst).

Dispatch and unit scheduling with variable renewables and storage, and stochastic, forecast-driven scheduling (re.energy-management, ps.grid-control). Security-constrained economic dispatch and locational pricing are not listed as gaps: they may have been touched in L16 'Optimal Dispatch' and the deregulation discussion, and lecture content was not read.

recommended_lessons: Existing coverage first: three-phase-fundamentals (status available; module ps.three-phase; covers ps.per-unit; lab labs/power-systems/three_phase.py) already teaches complex power for balanced wye and delta loads and per-unit conversion, so no new lesson is proposed for L2 or for the per-unit item of L10. It is the only lesson attached to any module mapped here; the learning path power-systems-intro lists no lessons for ps.transformers, ps.components, ps.power-flow, ps.machines, ps.faults, ps.protection, ps.stability or ps.grid-control.

Priority 1 - transmission-line-and-transformer-models (ps.components, ps.transformers): pi and ABCD two-port line models with sending/receiving-end circle diagrams as a worked result, three-phase transformer connections and phase shift, and per-unit base change across transformers and machine ratings as an extension of three-phase-fundamentals rather than a repeat of it (coverage evidence L3-L5).

Priority 1 - power-flow-analysis (ps.power-flow): Ybus construction, bus types and mismatch equations, the Newton-Raphson Jacobian and iteration, convergence checks and the fast-decoupled approximation in one lesson (L5-L7).

Priority 2 - synchronous-machines-and-electromechanical-dynamics (ps.machines, ps.stability): steady-state and transient synchronous-machine models in per unit, the swing equation, equal-area criterion and transient stability (L8-L11); electromechanical energy conversion and induction machines are left to the 6.685 mapping.
Priority 2 - fault-analysis-with-symmetrical-components (ps.faults): sequence networks and balanced/unbalanced fault calculations (L17-L18).

Priority 2 - protection-and-relaying-principles (ps.protection): overcurrent, distance and differential relaying and coordination (L19), plus a converter-fed-fault section written from independent modern sources to close the AIPE-specific gap.

Priority 3 - excitation-control-and-small-signal-stability (ps.stability, ps.grid-control): AVR and PSS, the linearised single- and multi-machine model, eigenvalues and electromechanical modes (L12-L13).

Priority 3 - economic-dispatch-and-grid-operation (ps.grid-control): cost curves, equal incremental cost, limits and losses, an outline of optimal dispatch (L14-L16), together with frequency control, reserves and AGC, which the course does not list and which must come from other references.

Priority 4, optional case study - grid-reliability-case-study-2003-blackout (ps.grid-control, ps.stability): written independently from public post-event reports; prompted by a student project title, not by taught content.

Priority 4, optional bridge - isolated-and-shipboard-power-systems (ps.microgrids): islanded, shipboard and relief power supply as the introduction to microgrids; justified by the home-page core topic 'mobile and isolated power systems' and written independently.
recommended_simulations: python (standard library): hand-coded Newton-Raphson load flow on a 3-5 bus network - build Ybus with cmath, form the Jacobian explicitly, solve each step with a small Gaussian-elimination routine and log the mismatch per iteration; optional extensions: a fast-decoupled variant, numpy or pandapower cross-check (ps.power-flow, f.computation)

python (standard library, cmath): ABCD two-port model of a medium/long transmission line; sweep receiving-end power and print the sending- and receiving-end P-Q loci as JSON; optional matplotlib plot of the circle diagrams versus line length and voltage (ps.components)

ngspice (optional extension): three-phase source feeding a pi-model line and load; measure sending- and receiving-end P and Q and check one point of the circle diagram against the Python model (ps.components, ps.three-phase)

ngspice (optional extension): Y-Delta transformer bank showing the 30-degree phase shift; export the measured ohmic results and compute per-unit values referred across the bank in Python, reusing the per-unit routine of the three-phase-fundamentals lab (ps.transformers, ps.per-unit)

python (standard library): fixed-step RK4 integration of the single-machine infinite-bus swing equation with a fault and clearing; equal-area check, critical clearing time sweep and a step-size study (halve h, estimate error); optional scipy.integrate.solve_ivp cross-check (ps.stability, f.computation)

python (standard library): classical SMIB small-signal model - 2x2 linearisation with analytic eigenvalues giving the frequency and damping of the electromechanical mode versus operating point and damping coefficient; optional numpy extension adds exciter/AVR and PSS states to show eigenvalue loci versus AVR and PSS gains (ps.stability)

python (standard library): economic dispatch of 3-5 units with quadratic costs and limits by lambda iteration, then with B-coefficient losses and penalty factors; optional scipy.optimize cross-check (ps.grid-control)
python (standard library, cmath): symmetrical-component transformation and sequence-network calculation of SLG, LL and DLG faults on a small system; verify against the three-phase fault (ps.faults)

ngspice (optional extension): transient of a single-line-to-ground fault on an RL feeder showing DC offset and asymmetrical fault current; compare the peak with a closed-form Python estimate (ps.faults)

python (standard library): inverse-time overcurrent relay curves (standard IEC/IEEE equations) and coordination of two radial feeder relays using the fault currents from the sequence-network lab; optional matplotlib plot (ps.protection)
python (pandapower or PyPSA, optional): repeat the load-flow and dispatch exercises on an open test network to check the hand-written solvers (ps.power-flow, ps.grid-control)

ps.power-flow: the taxonomy requires only ps.three-phase, ps.per-unit and f.computation; the course order (L5 transformers, L6 network matrices, L7 Newton-Raphson) suggests adding ps.components and ps.transformers to requires and f.linear-algebra to related. The course does not require pe.modelling, which the taxonomy lists, because converters are absent.

ps.dc-grids and ps.microgrids are only tangential here; a learner following this course order would reach them after ps.power-flow and ps.stability, and the taxonomy additionally requires ps.grid-converters for both, which the course does not teach.

course_facts.scope_summary: MIT 8.02 (Spring 2007) is MIT's first-year electricity-and-magnetism course, the second half of the introductory physics sequence. It is run in the TEAL studio format: short lecture segments alternate with tabletop experiments, electronically polled concept questions and small-group problem work, and one one-hour session a week is given over to problem solving. Its 36 sessions (26 marked Class and 10 marked Problem solving in the Class Topics table) run from electrostatics (charge, field, potential, Gauss's law, conductors and capacitors) through current and DC circuits, magnetostatics (Biot-Savart, Ampere's law, forces and torques on charges, dipoles and current loops), Faraday's law, inductance and transformers, RC/RL/RLC transients and driven AC resonance, to Maxwell's equations, electromagnetic radiation and a closing session on interference. The OCW site offers lecture notes (14 course-note chapters, 36 session summaries, 25 slide decks, 23 concept-question sets), 28 ungraded in-class group problems, 11 Friday problem-solving sets (6% of the grade) and 9 experiment write-ups; there are no lecture videos, and the graded written homework is not published.

mapped_modules.rationale: Series RLC resonance (natural frequency, damping, Q, bandwidth and phase) is the tank of every resonant converter; the course gives the physics but nothing on LLC stages, soft switching or zero-voltage/zero-current switching. Added for consistency with the f.signals and pe.emi-pcb background entries, which map the same kind of physics-only content.

mit_topics: Maxwell's equations, EM radiation and energy flow (Ses 30-31)
mapped_modules.rationale: Displacement current, radiation from time-varying currents and energy flow are the physics underlying EMI and commutation-loop radiation, but the course does not treat EMC, layout, parasitics or filtering; tangential background only.

concepts_missing_in_aipe: Vector-calculus tools for fields: coordinate systems, gradients, line and surface integrals (Ses 3); AIPE's mathematics track (f.quantities, f.calculus, f.linear-algebra) stops at first-order ODEs and linear algebra.
Gauss's law and flux reasoning for symmetric charge distributions (Ses 7-8; charge-slab and spherical-shell group problems).
Electric dipoles and fields of continuous charge distributions (Ses 2, 6; line-of-charge and charged-disk group problems).
Conductors in electrostatic equilibrium and charge measurement with a Faraday ice pail (Ses 9, Exp 2).

Dielectrics inside capacitors: the 'Partially filled capacitor' group problem (Ses 10) is presumably a dielectric-filled capacitor, but the listed title does not say and the word dielectric appears on no cited page.
Biot-Savart law and Ampere's law as field-computation methods (Ses 14-16); AIPE names 'magnetic fields' but no module or lesson lists these laws.

Magnetic forces and torques on moving charges and dipoles and magnetic levitation (Ses 17-19, Exp 4); eddy currents and Lenz's-law repulsion are named only in the home-page image caption (a magnet levitating above a superconducting ring), not in any session or experiment title.
Magnetic field mapping of a bar magnet and a Helmholtz coil (Exp 3).

Second-order LC and undriven RLC transients: natural frequency and damping (Ses 27). AIPE's f.dynamics is first-order only and no module summary names RLC transients; f.signals (step response, poles) and pe.resonant (resonant tanks) are the natural homes, so the gap is a missing lesson or outline item, not a missing module.
Maxwell's equations as a complete set, displacement current, EM wave propagation, energy flow (Poynting) and generation of EM radiation (Ses 30-33).
Interference and diffraction (Ses 35, Exp 9): optics, outside AIPE's scope, noted for completeness.
modern_gaps_not_covered_by_mit: Magnetic materials for power engineering: B-H curves, hysteresis, saturation, core loss in ferrite, powder and electrical-steel cores, and permanent-magnet materials (remanence, coercivity, demagnetisation curves, ferrite versus NdFeB grades); the course only maps a bar magnet's field (Exp 3) and treats magnets as dipoles (Ses 17-18).
Magnetic circuit analysis (MMF, reluctance, air gaps) and the real transformer equivalent circuit (leakage and magnetising inductance, winding resistance).

Eddy-current, skin and proximity effects in conductors and windings at switching frequencies (eddy currents appear in the course as a demonstration phenomenon, the levitating magnet of Ses 18 and the home-page image caption, not as a winding-loss mechanism).
Non-ideal passive components: ESR/ESL, parasitic winding capacitance, ripple-current ratings, dielectric breakdown and insulation.
Waveform analysis for switched circuits: average and RMS of non-sinusoidal waveforms, duty cycle, harmonics and a Fourier view.

Three-phase systems and complex (real/reactive/apparent) power as used in power-system analysis (ps.three-phase). Single-phase average power and power factor of the driven RLC circuit are probably treated in the AC-circuits course notes (Chapter 12, slug cha12ac_circuits, cited for Ses 26-27) but appear in no listed title, so they are not claimed as a gap.
Circuit and field computation with open tools: ngspice transient/AC analysis and Python numerical field solvers; the course relies on pre-made visualisations.
Engineering EMC practice: near-field coupling, commutation loops, shielding and filtering, as opposed to radiation physics.
Current and magnetic-field sensing in practice (shunts, Hall-effect sensors, current transformers, Rogowski coils) and measurement error.
The energy-storage view used in converters: volt-second and charge balance as applied field-energy storage in L and C.
Electromechanical energy-conversion models for synchronous, induction and permanent-magnet machines beyond torque on a current loop.
recommended_lessons: f.electromagnetism: From Coulomb's law to the capacitor: electric field, potential and energy stored in a capacitor
f.electromagnetism: Gauss's law as a flux-counting tool, with the fields around cables and bus bars as examples
f.dc-circuits: Current, resistance and Ohm's law from the microscopic picture to a circuit model
f.electromagnetism: Biot-Savart and Ampere's law: field of a straight wire, a loop, a solenoid and a toroid
f.electromagnetism -> ps.machines: Force and torque on a current loop: the principle behind every motor
f.magnetism: Faraday's law and Lenz's law: induced EMF, eddy currents and the generator principle
f.magnetism -> ps.transformers: Self and mutual inductance: solenoid, coaxial cable and the ideal transformer
f.electromagnetism -> pe.topologies: Energy stored in electric and magnetic fields, and why converters move energy through L and C
f.dynamics: RC and RL step responses: time constants from field physics to circuit practice
f.ac -> pe.resonant: LC and RLC circuits: natural oscillation, damping and driven resonance with phasors
f.electromagnetism -> pe.emi-pcb: Maxwell's equations and displacement current on one page: what a power engineer needs
recommended_simulations: Python (numpy/matplotlib): electric field and equipotential map of point charges and a dipole by superposition, with E = -grad V checked numerically (same physical system as Exp 1 Equipotential Lines and Electric Fields, written independently).
Python: numerical Gauss's-law check, computing the flux through a closed surface around a charge distribution by numerical surface integration (Ses 7-8).
Python: Biot-Savart numerical integration for a circular loop and a Helmholtz coil pair, comparing the on-axis field with the analytic formula (same physical system as Exp 3, written independently).
Python: field and inductance of a finite solenoid and of a coaxial cable, compared with the ideal formulas (same geometries as the Solenoid and Coaxial cable group problems, written independently).

Python: Faraday's law, EMF induced in a loop by a moving dipole-field magnet and by a rotating loop (generator), including the Lenz's-law sign (Ses 20-21; same physical system as the Generator group problem, written independently).
ngspice: RC and RL step responses with time-constant extraction and comparison to the analytic exponentials (same circuits as Exp 6, written independently).
ngspice: undriven RLC in under-, critically and over-damped cases, then an AC sweep of the driven RLC for resonance, bandwidth, Q and phase (same circuits as Exp 7-8, written independently).

ngspice: coupled inductors (K statement) with k = 1 and large L to approximate the ideal transformer, then finite L to show the magnetising current and k < 1 to show leakage, as a bridge to real transformer models (Ses 22).
Python: energy balance during RC charging (source energy = stored + dissipated) and energy stored in an inductor during RL turn-on (Ses 23, 25).
Python: torque on a current loop versus angle in a uniform field and a minimal commutated DC-motor model (Ses 19).
Python (optional): 1D FDTD solution of Maxwell's equations for a plane wave with Poynting-vector energy flow (Ses 30-33).
prerequisite_relationships: f.electromagnetism requires f.quantities and f.calculus (taxonomy): consistent with the course, which reviews coordinate systems, gradients, line and surface integrals (Ses 3) before computing fields. That the course assumes calculus is an inference from the Ses 3 title; the syllabus names only 8.01 mechanics.

Course order versus AIPE order for DC circuits: MIT places electrostatics and capacitors (Ses 1-11) before Current, Resistance, and DC circuits (Ses 12). AIPE differs: taxonomy f.dc-circuits requires only f.quantities and lists f.electromagnetism as related, and the foundations-first-circuits path goes f.quantities -> f.dc-circuits with no physics module. The physics-first order is the course's, not a proposed new requires edge.

f.dynamics requires f.dc-circuits and f.calculus (taxonomy); the course order Ses 12 -> Ses 23, 25-26 agrees. The course additionally derives capacitance and inductance from field physics (Ses 9-11, 22-23); AIPE treats that as f.electromagnetism background (related to f.dc-circuits), not as a prerequisite.
f.ac requires f.quantities and f.dynamics (taxonomy): driven LRC circuits (Ses 28-29) follow RC/RL (Ses 25-26) and undriven LC/LRC (Ses 27), in agreement.

f.magnetism requires f.dynamics and f.electronics and lists f.electromagnetism only as related (taxonomy). The course's order, Biot-Savart and Ampere's law (Ses 14-16) before Faraday's law and inductance (Ses 20-23), suggests a stronger dependency on magnetostatics than AIPE declares; recorded as a difference, not as agreement. f.electromagnetism is absent from all four learning paths, consistent with AIPE's circuits-first design.

ps.transformers requires ps.three-phase and f.magnetism (taxonomy): the ideal transformer appears as an application of mutual inductance and Faraday's law (Ses 22), which supports the f.magnetism edge; the course has no counterpart to the ps.three-phase requirement.

ps.machines requires ps.transformers and f.magnetism (taxonomy). The force-and-torque-on-a-current-loop physics (Ses 19, Exp 4) and the generator problem (Ses 20) live in f.electromagnetism, which the taxonomy reaches only indirectly (related to f.magnetism); an indirect dependency, not a requires edge.

pe.passives requires f.dynamics and f.ac; pe.magnetics requires f.magnetism and f.ac (taxonomy); both reach f.electromagnetism only indirectly. Evidence for the field-physics background: the readings page cites Chapter 5 for Ses 11 (Capacitors cont.) and also for Ses 7-8 (Gauss's law), Chapter 10 for Ses 20-22, Chapter 11 Section 11.1 for Ses 21, Sections 11.1-11.4 for Ses 24 and Sections 11.5-11.6 for Ses 25 (RC and RL circuits); Ses 23 has no reading. Chapter titles are not displayed, so identifying Chapters 5 and 11 as the capacitance and inductance chapters is an inference, supported only by the resource-link slugs chap5capacitance and chap11inductance.

f.signals (requires f.dynamics and f.ac), pe.modelling (requires f.signals) and pe.resonant (requires f.signals) can use f.ac resonance (driven RLC, Ses 28-29) as the intuitive entry to second-order frequency response.

course_facts.scope_summary: MIT 8.21 The Physics of Energy (Physics Department, Fall 2009, undergraduate; instructors listed as Prof. Robert Jaffe and Prof. Washington Taylor) is a quantitative physics course on energy for students who already have introductory physics, calculus and chemistry: it asks where energy comes from, how it is extracted, moved, stored, lost and finally used, and which physical laws limit each step. Part I (Energy and its Uses) covers energy units and scales, mechanical, thermal and electromagnetic energy, an introduction to quantum energy levels, chemical energy and CO2 flows, entropy and temperature, heat engines, phase-change conversion with refrigeration and heat pumps, internal combustion engines, and steam and gas power cycles. Part II (Sources of Energy) covers fundamental forces, quantum mechanics for nuclear physics, nuclear forces and binding energy, fusion, fission and fission-reactor physics, design and safety, the flow of energy in the universe, solar radiation, solar-thermal and photovoltaic conversion, biological and fossil fuels, wind resource and turbine physics, geothermal and ocean-thermal energy, and tidal, wave and hydro power. Part III (Systems and Synthesis) covers nuclear radiation, fuel cycles, waste and proliferation, climate change (three sessions), energy storage and energy conservation. The syllabus presents it as a quantitative course rather than a survey; political, economic, social and ethical issues are not discussed directly (the syllabus says the course supplies the scientific foundation for evaluating them).
stated_prerequisites: Introductory physics: MIT 8.01 (classical mechanics) and 8.02 (electricity and magnetism)
Mathematics: MIT 18.01 single-variable calculus and 18.02 multivariable calculus
Chemistry: Principles of Chemical Science (listed as 5.111 and 5.112) or Introduction to Solid State Chemistry (3.091)
The syllabus states that students need not have taken advanced subjects in thermodynamics, quantum mechanics or nuclear physics beforehand
Target audience stated as MIT sophomores, juniors and seniors from any major; the course is not aimed specifically at physics majors

mapped_modules.rationale: The course's central subject is the physics of energy conversion: Part I builds energy, power, entropy and efficiency across mechanical, thermal, electromagnetic and chemical forms (including the CO2 flow from combustion, session 7, on which the proposed 'Energy and CO2' lesson rests) and heat-engine and power-plant cycles, and Part II applies the same tools to the resources and physical limits of solar-thermal, biological and fossil, geothermal, ocean-thermal, tidal, wave and hydro power. This matches the module summary (energy, power and efficiency across physical conversion processes; the resources and limits of renewable energy) and the energy-conversion track summary (physical and thermodynamic foundations of renewable energy conversion) more closely than any other MIT course in the AIPE catalogue.

mit_topics: Quantum mechanics I: Intro to the quantum, energy quantization
mapped_modules.rationale: Three of 38 sessions (21, 24, 25) treat solar radiation and photovoltaic conversion from the physics side, session 6 supplies the energy-quantization idea behind the band gap, and the course description poses how a photovoltaic works as one of its headline questions. The I-V characteristic, maximum power point and irradiance/temperature effects named in the module summary are not named on the MIT pages, so the course is a substantial but not central physics reference for this module.

mit_topics: Wind I: Fluid dynamics and power in the wind, available resources
Wind II: More about fluids, viscosity, types of fluid flow, lift
Wind III: Wind turbine dynamics and design, wind farms
mapped_modules.rationale: Three dedicated sessions (27-29) cover the resource and aerodynamics half of the module (power in the wind, available resources, fluid flow and lift, turbine dynamics and design, wind farms). Generators and back-to-back converters, the electrical half of the module summary, are not named on any page.

mit_topics: Electromagnetic energy: Storage, conversion, transmission and radiation
mapped_modules.rationale: One dedicated session (36) plus storage named in the electromagnetic-energy session title (5); storage is also one of the processes the course description says the course covers. Phase-change thermal storage may be touched in session 10 (Conversion I), but that title names conversion, refrigeration and heat pumps rather than storage, so this is an inference and the session is not listed as evidence. Energy and power ratings, round-trip efficiency and bidirectional converter interfaces from the module summary are not named, so treatment is judged brief.

mit_topics: Units and scales of energy use
mapped_modules.rationale: One early session (2) is devoted to energy units and the scales of energy use, the syllabus stresses quantitative analysis and practical calculations throughout, and the Related Resources page links the NIST Guide to SI Units. A brief treatment, but the best academic exemplar in the catalogue for an AIPE lesson on energy units and order-of-magnitude estimation beyond the joule, watt-hour and watt basics already taught by dc-circuit-fundamentals and first-circuit-zh.

mit_topics: Electromagnetic energy: Storage, conversion, transmission and radiation

prerequisite_relationships: Framing: the items below are AIPE proposals read off the MIT course ordering and prerequisite list. Where they differ from the current curriculum/taxonomy.json requires (re.conversion: f.quantities, f.calculus; re.pv: f.electronics, f.dc-circuits; re.wind: f.magnetism, ps.grid-converters; re.storage: pe.topologies; re.batteries: re.storage) the difference is stated explicitly; this record changes no taxonomy entry.
re.conversion requires f.quantities and f.calculus: agrees with taxonomy (the course opens with units and scales of energy and lists 18.01 and 18.02 as prerequisites).

re.conversion and f.electromagnetism: MIT lists 8.02 as a prerequisite but only session 5 applies it, so AIPE should keep f.electromagnetism as related/recommended for re.conversion rather than required (taxonomy requires = [f.quantities, f.calculus]), preserving the renewable-energy-intro path that starts at re.conversion.

re.pv and re.conversion: taxonomy re.pv.requires = [f.electronics, f.dc-circuits] and lists re.conversion as related; the MIT ordering (Solar I-V after Part I) supports re.conversion as a soft prerequisite and no change to requires is proposed. f.electromagnetism is not required by taxonomy, and AIPE's single-diode treatment in solar-pv-fundamentals builds on f.electronics instead.

re.wind and re.conversion: taxonomy re.wind.requires = [f.magnetism, ps.grid-converters] and re.conversion lists re.wind as related; the MIT Wind I-III sequence supports re.conversion as a soft prerequisite for the resource/aerodynamics half only (fluid dynamics is introduced inside the course rather than assumed); proposed as related, not as a new requires.

re.storage and re.conversion: taxonomy re.storage.requires = [pe.topologies] (converter-interface view); MIT's physics view places session 36 after Parts I-II, so re.conversion is a justified soft prerequisite for a storage-physics lesson only, and f.electromagnetism should be related, not required.

re.batteries: taxonomy requires = [re.storage]; MIT additionally assumes introductory chemistry (5.111 and 5.112, or 3.091), which has no AIPE taxonomy node, so it is recorded under concepts_missing_in_aipe as an external prerequisite rather than as a requires relationship.

Ordering: the course structure (Part I uses and conversion, then Part II sources, then Part III synthesis including storage and conservation) supports re.conversion -> re.pv / re.wind / re.storage and agrees with the taxonomy's renewable-energy-intro learning path (energy conversion -> solar PV fundamentals -> MPPT -> storage -> wind -> grid integration and system design). MIT's Part III (nuclear waste, climate change, storage, conservation) contains nothing on grid integration or system design, so the path's final step rests on AIPE's taxonomy alone, not on this course.

course_facts.scope_summary: EC.S07 (Edgerton Center, Fall 2004, undergraduate, Prof. Louis Bucciarelli) is a one-session-per-week, two-hour class (the syllabus labels the meetings 'Lectures') on the behaviour and first-order conceptual design of photovoltaic systems, with the emphasis on stand-alone (off-grid) PV-plus-battery systems for any location in the US. The 14-session calendar moves from the solar resource (sun geometry, clearness index, US insolation databases and TMY data) through module I-V behaviour and array networking to stand-alone system elements, three sessions of stand-alone sizing (first-order estimation of average daily performance, then loss-of-load probability with a Markov process model and the effect of day-to-day correlation), evaluation of PV station data, two sessions on grid-connected systems (power conditioning, utility constraints, architectural/structural considerations) and cost/benefit analysis with net present value and government incentives. Assessment is a semester-long project built from five exercises and a final report; no final exam is given. Hardware is treated only at an introductory level, as the course description states.

mapped_modules.rationale: Full-sun-hours ratings, daily energy estimates and present-value arithmetic rely on unit conversion, ratios and simple algebra (inference); the course assumes rather than teaches them.

concepts_missing_in_aipe: Solar resource assessment: sun geometry and direct-beam flux on a tilted surface, extraterrestrial irradiance, clearness index Kt, monthly average daily insolation, TMY data and site databases (calendar S2-S3, lecture note LN1); AIPE has no solar-resource lesson, only the general phrase 'resources and limits' in re.conversion.
Array orientation and tracking: annual output as a function of tilt/azimuth and of tracking (S5.2); not named in re.pv-systems.

'Full sun hours' (peak-sun-hours) module rating and first-order daily energy-balance sizing of array and battery (S4.2, S7.1): re.system-design names sizing generically, but no module or lesson names the peak-sun-hours module rating or the first-order daily energy-balance sizing method.

Probabilistic stand-alone sizing: loss-of-load probability with a Markov process model and the effect of day-to-day correlation of insolation (S8-S9); AIPE has no probability/stochastic-sizing content and no probability-and-statistics foundation module.

Engineering economics for energy projects: present worth of future benefits, net present value, annual savings, government subsidies and incentives (S13, LN2, LN3); re.system-design lists 'economics' in one word with no lesson.
PV technology history, current status, policy and markets (S1.2-S1.3); no AIPE module covers policy/market context.
Architectural/structural considerations of grid-connected (building-mounted) PV (S12.1).

Evaluation of PV station monitoring data, including least-squares fitting of output versus irradiance and temperature (S10, LN4): f.magnetism covers measurement range, sampling, reference points and error in general, but no module names performance monitoring of a PV station or least-squares fitting of output against irradiance and temperature.
modern_gaps_not_covered_by_mit: MPPT algorithms (perturb-and-observe, incremental conductance) and the DC/DC stage between PV and battery or DC link; module-level power electronics (optimisers, microinverters) - only 'Max. Power Tracking' is named on the page. Gap relative to MIT only: AIPE already covers re.mppt with perturb-and-observe in the catalogue lesson solar-pv-fundamentals and labs/renewable-energy/pv_model.py; the DC/DC stage and module-level electronics remain open in AIPE.

Modern grid-tied inverter behaviour and grid codes: anti-islanding, voltage/frequency ride-through, volt-var and frequency-watt functions, grid-support and grid-forming operation (IEEE 1547-2018 era requirements).

Lithium-ion storage, battery management systems, state-of-charge/health estimation and degradation models; hybrid PV-storage inverters - the page lists only 'Battery Characteristics' and 'Charge Control'.
Current PV cell/module technologies and models: single-diode model parameter extraction, PERC/TOPCon/heterojunction/bifacial modules, degradation rates and warranties.
Open data and open tools for resource and yield modelling (NSRDB, PVGIS, satellite irradiance, pvlib-python, SAM) replacing 2004 site data files and a Java applet.

Updated economics: LCOE, net metering and feed-in tariffs, time-of-use pricing, power purchase agreements and the post-2004 tax-credit landscape; the course's S13.2 'Government Subsidies and Incentives' reflects 2004 programmes.
Hybrid systems and microgrids: PV with battery and generator, DC microgrids, EV-charging integration (not listed on the page).
Distribution-level integration: hosting capacity, voltage rise on feeders, curtailment and PV output forecasting.
Electrical safety and installation codes for PV (rapid shutdown, arc-fault protection, grounding, string fusing) - the page lists only architectural/structural considerations.
Reproducible, open-source simulation workflows (Python/ngspice) as the learning backbone, with verification against hand analysis.
recommended_lessons: re.conversion / solar resource: 'Where the energy comes from - sun geometry, tilt, clearness index and TMY data' (grounded in calendar S2-S3 and LN1; use open NSRDB/PVGIS data instead of the 2004 PDFs).

re.pv: extend the existing catalogue lesson solar-pv-fundamentals (which already teaches the single-diode model and irradiance and temperature effects) with module efficiency, module rating and the 'full sun hours' output method, and the step from one module to an array (S4.2, S5); do not re-teach the single-diode model.
re.pv: 'Modules in series and parallel - mismatch, bypass and blocking diodes, partial shading' (S5.1; genuinely new, since pv_model.py explicitly excludes partial shading and bypass diodes).
re.pv-systems: 'Array orientation and tracking - annual energy versus tilt and azimuth' (S5.2).
re.pv-systems + re.storage + re.batteries: 'Anatomy of a stand-alone PV system - battery, charge controller, loads and load management' (S6).
re.system-design: 'First-order stand-alone sizing - daily energy balance with the peak-sun-hours method' (S7).
re.system-design: 'How reliable is my system? Loss-of-load probability, Markov models and day-to-day correlation' (S8-S9); add a short probability primer as a foundations bridge.
re.pv / re.system-design: 'Reading PV station data - least-squares fits of output versus irradiance and temperature' (S10, LN4).

re.pv-systems + re.integration: 'Grid-connected PV - power conditioning, interconnection constraints, mounting and structure, plus modern grid-code functions' (S11-S12, extended with the modern gaps).
re.system-design: 'Does it pay? Present worth, NPV, LCOE and incentives for a PV project' (S13, LN2-LN3).

re.mppt: follow-on to solar-pv-fundamentals (which already explains why a converter is needed and demonstrates perturb-and-observe): the DC/DC stage between module and battery or DC link, incremental conductance, MPPT under partial shading and the tracking-speed versus oscillation trade-off with converter dynamics, bridging to pe.buck/pe.boost (modern gap; the existing lesson's own further-learning section names this continuation).
recommended_simulations: Python: sun-position and clear-sky irradiance on a tilted surface for any latitude and day of year; plot daily and annual irradiation versus tilt and azimuth (an open re-implementation of what the course's Java applet is described as demonstrating on the tools page: how various factors change solar energy collection through the year); cross-check against pvlib-python.

Python: extend labs/renewable-energy/pv_model.py (already: single-diode model, I-V/P-V curves, Voc, Isc, MPP, fill factor, irradiance and temperature sweeps, perturb-and-observe) with a module efficiency/rating report and a 'full sun hours' rating check: integrate the modelled output over an hourly daily irradiance profile and compare it with rated power times peak-sun-hours.

ngspice: PV module as current source + diode + Rs + Rsh; series strings with bypass diodes and parallel strings with blocking diodes under partial shading; sweep load to show multiple local maxima in the P-V curve.

Python: Markov-chain / Monte Carlo synthesis of daily clearness-index sequences with adjustable day-to-day autocorrelation; simulate a PV-battery-load energy balance and compute loss-of-load probability as a function of array size and battery capacity; plot sizing (iso-reliability) curves and show how correlation changes them.
Python: hourly stand-alone system simulation on open TMY-like data (NSRDB or PVGIS) with a charge-controller state-of-charge model; report LOLP, battery cycling and unmet load for a chosen location.
Python: least-squares regression of measured or synthetic PV station output against irradiance and module temperature; estimate the temperature coefficient and compare with the datasheet value.
Python: project economics - present worth of annual savings with discount rate, degradation, price escalation and incentive scenarios; NPV, payback and LCOE with sensitivity plots.

ngspice + Python (modern gap): add the converter dynamics that the steady-state perturb-and-observe in pv_model.py omits: a boost stage between the pv_model.py module and a battery, perturb-and-observe step size and perturbation period, and harvested energy with and without MPPT under a changing irradiance profile.
prerequisite_relationships: re.pv-systems and re.system-design require re.pv: the course moves module (S4) -> array (S5) -> system elements (S6) -> sizing (S7-S9), so module behaviour precedes system and sizing work.

re.system-design (stand-alone sizing) requires solar-resource assessment (S2-S3 come first) and re.storage (battery characteristics in S6 precede sizing); AIPE should place a solar-resource lesson (under re.conversion or a new re.pv sub-lesson) before sizing.

re.pv requires f.electronics and f.dc-circuits: I-V characteristics, series/parallel networking and diode placement assume diode behaviour and series/parallel circuit reasoning (consistent with the taxonomy's requires list for re.pv).

Probabilistic sizing (S8-S9: Markov process model, day-to-day correlation) requires introductory probability and statistics, which no AIPE foundation module currently provides; f.computation and f.linear-algebra cover only part of this.
PV economics (S13, LN2-LN3) requires only f.quantities-level algebra (discounting, compound growth) but AIPE has no engineering-economics lesson to host it.

Grid-connected sessions (S11-S12) follow the stand-alone sizing block and treat power conditioning as a black box, and the stand-alone sizing and cost/benefit sessions (S7-S9, S13) use no converter or grid-stability theory. This suggests AIPE can offer a systems-first entry to re.pv-systems that soft-requires pe.inverters and ps.grid-converters, to re.system-design that soft-requires re.integration (and through it ps.grid-converters and ps.stability), and to re.storage that soft-requires pe.topologies, rather than hard-requiring them as the taxonomy currently does.

The syllabus and home page are silent on prerequisites and the course is an undergraduate class, so the course's own content is reachable from f.quantities, f.dc-circuits and f.electronics (inference from course level and topic list). The taxonomy's hard requires are deeper: re.system-design -> re.integration -> ps.grid-converters and ps.stability; re.storage -> pe.topologies; re.mppt -> pe.buck; and the catalogue lesson solar-pv-fundamentals requires buck-converter-fundamentals. Either a systems-first path that soft-requires those modules should be added, or the requires kept and this course flagged as a reference that is reachable earlier than the modules it supports.
